issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
## Description
Remove sleep-based timing assumptions and clarify real-service integration boundaries in tests.

Primary examples: tests/rl/test_replay_buffer.py, tests/rl/test_rollout_storage.py, tests/rl/integration/test_weight_sync.py, tests/rl/integration/test_rollout_worker.py, tests/integration/iris/test_iris_integration.py, tests/vllm/test_llm_inference.py, and tests/rl/test_checkpoint_transfer.py.

### Definition of Done
- Unit-shaped tests use fake clocks, events, or poll-with-deadline helpers instead of time.sleep.
- Tests that require GCS, TPU, vLLM, or live services are marked and isolated as integration tests.
- Path reconstruction and storage behavior use temp fsspec filesystems or fakes where possible.

Parent audit: #6424

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Analysis — not opening a PR (multi-module, >100 LOC, touches production ordering). Proposing an approach for review first.**

# Research

Five `time.sleep`s and two real-service test files, all confirmed by parent audit #6424 (findings #6 and #9). Two are trivially removable, one masks a latent production ordering weakness, two are in CI-skipped integration tests, and two files need integration isolation / fsspec-fake conversion.

**Relevant code**
- [`replay_buffer.py#L358-L373`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/replay_buffer.py#L358-L373) — `get_rollouts(timeout=)` already polls with a deadline.
- [`rollout_storage.py#L184-L195`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/rollout_storage.py#L184-L195) — file order sorts on **timestamp only**, ignoring the `counter` field; same-microsecond writes tie.
- [`rollout_storage.py#L296-L299`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/rollout_storage.py#L296-L299) — filename is `{ts}_{host}_{counter}.pkl`; counter exists but is unused for ordering.
- [`test_checkpoint_transfer.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/tests/rl/test_checkpoint_transfer.py) — 10 tests drive `_find_latest_checkpoint` through `Mock(fs)` + `patch(fsspec.core.url_to_fs)`; asserts on a private method.
- [`test_llm_inference.py#L33-L42`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/tests/vllm/test_llm_inference.py#L33) — `tpu_ci` + hard-coded `gs://` model path, no behavioral assertion.

# Proposed approach

Per file:

- **test_replay_buffer.py#L140** — drop `time.sleep(0.2)`; `get_rollouts(timeout=...)` already blocks on a deadline, so the sleep is dead. Just call it (raise timeout to ~5s). One-line change, no helper needed.
- **test_rollout_storage.py#L130** — the `sleep(0.01)` exists because ordering ties on timestamp. Fix the root cause: parse `counter` (`parts[2]`) in `_get_available_files` and sort by `(timestamp, counter)`. Then the test writes 3 batches with no delay and asserts `worker_i` order. This is a small **production** change that makes ordering deterministic regardless of fsspec backend — the reason this is not a pure test PR.
- **test_iris_integration.py#L129** — already a `while time.monotonic() < deadline` poll; the `sleep(0.5)` is the poll interval. Convert to `ExponentialBackoff` (already imported and used at L219 in the same file) for consistency with the rest of the suite.
- **test_rollout_worker.py#L61** and **test_weight_sync.py#L64** — CI-skipped `@slow` integration tests. The sleeps cover "let the background worker/queue settle." Replace with a poll-with-deadline on the observable (`read_all_available()` non-empty / `wait_for_result`), or, if a brief startup sleep is unavoidable, keep one short sleep with a comment naming the race (allowed by `TESTING.md` §Timing). Prefer the poll.
- **test_checkpoint_transfer.py** — replace `Mock(fs)` + `patch(url_to_fs)` with a real `fsspec` memory/local filesystem: create `memory://.../step_N/` dirs and drive the public discovery path instead of asserting on `_find_latest_checkpoint` with stubbed `ls`. This is the largest piece (~280 LOC of mock-based tests).
- **test_llm_inference.py** — already `tpu_ci`-marked and skips without vLLM; add an `integration` marker for consistency and a minimal behavioral assertion (generated text non-empty) so it is more than a pulse check. Keep the GCS path behind the TPU marker.

Open questions for a human before implementing:
1. The rollout_storage ordering change is in production code — acceptable here, or should the test instead inject explicit timestamps and leave the sorter alone?
2. For checkpoint_transfer, is testing through a real `memory://` fs preferred over keeping the path-reconstruction logic as a small pure-function unit test (no fs at all)?
3. Is there an existing `integration` marker convention for `tests/vllm`, or should the file stay `tpu_ci`-only?

Suggested split into reviewable PRs: (a) the two unit-test sleep removals + the rollout_storage ordering fix; (b) checkpoint_transfer fsspec-fake rewrite; (c) integration-test poll/marker cleanups.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 # Research

No overlapping open PR exists for #6429. The sleeps in `test_replay_buffer.py`, `test_rollout_storage.py`, and the RL integration tests wait for observable state that can be polled directly; file rollout ordering also has a production tie bug because filenames include a counter that the reader ignores. `test_checkpoint_transfer.py` is skipped in CI and mocks `fsspec`, which hides that real `fs.ls()` returns detail dicts unless `detail=False` is requested.

**Relevant code**
- [`replay_buffer.py#L358-L373`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/replay_buffer.py#L358-L373) - loader deadline poll
- [`rollout_storage.py#L184-L201`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/rollout_storage.py#L184-L201) - timestamp-only sort
- [`rollout_storage.py#L296-L299`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/rollout_storage.py#L296-L299) - counter in filename
- [`checkpoint.py#L158-L186`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/rl/weight_transfer/checkpoint.py#L158-L186) - checkpoint discovery
- [`test_llm_inference.py#L33-L42`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/tests/vllm/test_llm_inference.py#L33-L42) - TPU/GCS integration test

# Proposed Fix

Remove test sleeps by polling `get_rollouts()`, queue reads, worker completion, and Iris logs with deadlines/backoff. Sort rollout files by `(timestamp, counter)` and request `fs.ls(..., detail=False)` for checkpoint discovery so tests can use real local/memory fsspec filesystems instead of mocked `url_to_fs`. Mark the vLLM test as `integration` and assert generated output is non-empty.

issues.author: WhenWen
issues.body:
## Experiment: MuonH magnitude-direction decoupling (per-row / per-column learnable gains)

**User prompt that initiated this experiment:**

> Now I want you to go back to MuonH and test the following ideas, for each weight matrix, implement column and row weight gain and test if you can get the speedup in https://haeggee.github.io/posts/magnitude-direction-decoupling
>
> Magnitude-Direction Decoupling: factorize each weight into a direction Ŵ with a fixed norm (so it lies on a fixed hypersphere) and learnable magnitude gains: W = diag(γ_row)·Ŵ·diag(γ_col), Ŵ on the sphere, with γ_row ∈ R^{d_out} and γ_col ∈ R^{d_in} learnable gains. The two are learned at separately controlled rates. Update the direction with a normalized matrix optimizer (Muon) and project back onto the sphere; update the gains with Adam at their own LR through a softplus reparam (γ = softplus(γ̂), init γ=1). Fused weights: the model holds W, the optimizer recovers Ŵ = W/γ, splits the gradient (G_Ŵ = γ⊙G; g_γ = reduce(Ŵ⊙G)), steps each, projects Ŵ back to the sphere, and reassembles W = γ⊙Ŵ. Claims: ~2× less compute on MoE, LR transfer in width, no warmup, no weight decay needed.

### Implementation
- `optimizer.py`: `scale_with_grug_muonh_decoupled` + `decouple_gains` / `gain_lr` / `gain_mode` flags on `GrugMoeMuonHConfig`. The muonh group's matrices are factorized `W = diag(γ_row)·Ŵ·diag(γ_col)`; `Ŵ` is stepped by the existing MuonH Newton-Schulz + Frobenius-hyperball step (which preserves `‖Ŵ‖` → stays on the sphere), gains `γ = softplus(γ̂)` are stepped by Adam at LR `1e-3`.
- Launcher: `muonh_decouple_sweep.py`. Everything except the decoupling is held at the May-Recipe MuonH anchor (apples-to-apples).

### Plan
- **Gate 1**: run the variant at d512 (3.82e17) and d768 (2.81e18); effective speedup vs baseline (d512 3.5438 @ 530,704 tok/s; d768 3.2330 @ 357,696 tok/s, v4-32). Pass if speedup > 1 at both.
- Gate 2 if gate 1 passes.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 **Gate-1 launched** (v4-32 us-central2, same hardware as the baseline table → comparable tok/s)

Decoupled MuonH (both row+col gains, gain_lr=1e-3, softplus reparam, γ init=1; everything else at the May-Recipe MuonH anchor):

| run | dim | LR×anchor | job |
|---|---|---|---|
| `muonh_d512_decouple-d512-lr0p7` | 512 | 0.7 | 164934 |
| `muonh_d512_decouple-d512-lr1p0` | 512 | 1.0 | 164952 |

d512 gets a small LR bracket (the gains may shift the optimal matrix LR); d768 runs at the recipe LR. Gate-1 targets: d512 paloma **3.5438** @ 530,704 tok/s; d768 **3.2330** @ 357,696 tok/s. comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 **Gate-1 results (first pass)** — decoupling improves loss at both scales; effective speedup currently just under 1.

All runs on v4-32 us-central2 (same hardware as the baseline table), preemptible w/ 3-min checkpointing. Baselines: d512 **3.5438** @ 530,704 tok/s; d768 **3.2330** @ 357,696 tok/s.

### d512 matrix-LR sweep (gain_lr = 1e-3, blog default)
| LR×anchor | paloma | Δbase | tok/s | eff. speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.7 | 3.5444 | +0.0006 | 498,599 | 0.936 |
| 1.0 | 3.5411 | −0.0027 | 496,829 | 0.950 |
| 1.5 | 3.5511 | +0.0073 | 501,935 | 0.909 |

### d512 gain-LR sweep (matrix LR ×1.0) — the key lever
| gain_lr | paloma | Δbase | tok/s | eff. speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1e-3 (default) | 3.5411 | −0.0027 | 496,829 | 0.950 |
| **2.26e-3 (= adam-group LR)** | **3.5329** | **−0.0109** | 496,305 | **0.993** |
| 5e-3 | 3.5369 | −0.0069 | 491,714 | 0.962 |
| 1e-2 (≈ adamh LR) | 3.5351 | −0.0087 | 490,722 | 0.970 |

**Finding:** raising the gain LR to the **adam-group LR** (not the blog's 1e-3) is best — gives +0.008 loss over the default. Working hypothesis: **the gain Adam LR should equal the other Adam-group LR at each scale.**

### d768 (gain_lr = 1e-3)
| paloma | Δbase | tok/s | eff. speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.2313 | −0.0017 | 342,568 | 0.968 |

### Status
- **Loss: decoupling beats MuonH at both scales.** Best d512 = 3.5329 (−0.0109).
- **Effective speedup: ~0.99 best, all < 1 → gate-1 not yet passed.** The ~6.5% throughput overhead (496k vs 530k) nearly cancels the loss gain at the flat scaling exponent (α=0.094). The throughput gap is puzzling (only elementwise recover/split/reassemble + a 1-D gain Adam) — tabled for now.

### In flight / next
- **d768 with gain_lr = its adam_lr (1.932e-3)** running now — testing the gain-LR=adam-LR rule at d768 (d768 was only run at 1e-3 so far).
- TODO: matched MuonH baseline tok/s on this exact v4-32 setup (the 530k is the README number; true same-hardware overhead may be smaller and could flip speedup > 1).

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 **Update: gain-LR rule confirmed at d768 + MFU-sink hypothesis confirmed**

### Loss (decoupling beats MuonH at both scales)
| run | paloma | Δ vs baseline |
|---|---|---|
| d512 gain_lr=adam_lr (2.26e-3, v4-32) | **3.5329** | −0.0109 (base 3.5438) |
| d768 gain_lr=adam_lr (1.932e-3, v5p-8) | **3.2307** | −0.0023 (base 3.2330) |

d768 confirms the rule: base 3.2330 → 3.2313 (gain_lr 1e-3) → **3.2307 (gain_lr = adam-group LR)**. So **the gain Adam LR should equal the other Adam-group LR at each scale** — it's the best setting at both d512 and d768.

### MFU "sink" was a checkpoint artifact, not the gain vectors
The apparent ~6.5% throughput drop (mean 496k vs baseline 530k at d512) was dominated by **checkpoint/eval/data-loader pauses**, not the decoupled optimizer step:
- At **3-min** checkpoints (used for preemptible robustness): **6.1%** of steps were pauses → mean 496k while median was 517k.
- At **10-min** checkpoints: pause fraction dropped to **~1%** (d512 1.1%, d768 0.7%) → mean ≈ clean throughput.
- True decoupling overhead (recover/split/reassemble + 1-D gain Adam) is only **~2.6%**, consistent with the blog's "Fused Weights" design (the model holds the fused W; the optimizer does the split — already implemented).

Made the checkpoint interval env-configurable (`GRUG_CKPT_MIN`, default 10; preemptible runs set 3).

### Gate-1 effective speedup
- **d512: passes** — using the clean (pause-excluded) v4 throughput (517k), eff_speedup = **1.032** (vs 0.994 on the pause-dragged mean).
- **d768: throughput verdict pending a clean v4 run** — the v5p-8 numbers above are loss-valid but not tok/s-comparable to the v4-32 baseline (357,696); v4-32 central2 has been contended (`ready=0`). Will rerun a clean d768 on v4 when capacity frees to lock the d768 speedup.

**Bottom line:** loss win at both scales is solid; the throughput cost is ~2.6% (the gain vectors don't sink MFU); gate-1 passes at d512 on clean throughput, with d768's clean-throughput confirmation outstanding.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
🤖 **Final gate-1 summary — lm_head gains are layer/scale-dependent**

Added decoupled-AdamH (lm_head/output_proj keep the **Adam direction** + get per-row/col gains; not Muon). Results:

| scale | config | paloma | Δ baseline | est. eff_speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| d512 | matrices-only (gain_lr=adam_lr) | **3.5329** | −0.0109 | **1.034 ✓** |
| d512 | + lm_head gains | 3.5408 | −0.0030 | <1 (hurts) |
| d768 | matrices-only | 3.2307 | −0.0023 | 0.989 |
| d768 | + lm_head gains | **3.2286** | −0.0044 | ~1.00 (break-even) |

**Findings:**
1. **Matrices-only decoupling + gain_lr = adam-group-LR passes gate-1 at d512** (1.034 on clean throughput).
2. **lm_head gains are opposite-signed by scale** — hurt at d512 (3.5381→3.5408), help at d768 (3.2307→3.2286, ~doubling the margin). So no single config cleanly passes *both* scales.
3. **d768 is the bottleneck**: even with lm_head gains its loss margin (−0.0044) only buys ~3% baseline compute at the flat α=0.094 + large budget, so it sits at break-even against the ~2.6% throughput cost.
4. **MFU "sink" was a checkpoint-pause artifact**, not the gain vectors (6.1% pause steps at 3-min ckpt → ~1% at 10-min; true overhead ~2.6%). `GRUG_CKPT_MIN` env added.

**Net:** decoupling + gain_lr=adam_lr is a real loss win and passes gate-1 at d512, but the d768 margin is too thin for a clean two-scale speedup; output-head gains help only at the larger scale. Throughput estimates pending a clean v4-32 confirmation when that pool frees (currently `ready=0`).

issues.author: ravwojdyla-agent
issues.body:
## Problem

The Iris dashboard can't be served behind a prefix-stripping reverse proxy (e.g. code-server's `/proxy/<port>/`, `jupyter-server-proxy`, or any similar path-based proxy commonly used in remote dev environments). The page loads, but every JS chunk fails with:

```
Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<' (at lib-vue.57cf2ad8.js:1:1)
Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<' (at lib-router.86f6f5da.js:1:1)
Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<' (at 310.7554ea96.js:1:1)
Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<' (at controller.00517ea2.js:1:1)
```

## Root cause

`lib/iris/dashboard/rsbuild.config.ts` sets:

```ts
output: {
  assetPrefix: '/',
  ...
}
```

so the built HTML references assets root-absolutely (`<script defer src="/static/js/lib-vue.<hash>.js">`). When the dashboard is served under a path prefix (`https://host/some/prefix/`), the browser resolves those URLs against the proxy's origin root (`https://host/static/js/...`), which typically returns the outer server's HTML (404 page / SPA index). The browser then parses HTML as JavaScript — hence `Unexpected token '<'`.

The issue isn't limited to assets: the dashboard's API endpoints are also called root-absolutely (`/api`, `/iris.cluster.ControllerService`, `/finelog.logging.LogService`, `/proxy`, `/bundles`, `/blobs`, `/health`, `/auth`), so even with relative assets, every fetch would escape the prefix the same way.

## Repro

1. Build the dashboard and start the controller as usual (dashboard on `:10000`).
2. Put any prefix-stripping proxy in front of it, e.g. open it through code-server's built-in port proxy: `https://<code-server-host>/proxy/10000/`.
3. Blank page + the syntax errors above; the HTML document itself loads fine.

## Suggested fix

- `output.assetPrefix: 'auto'` (Rspack's `publicPath: 'auto'`) so assets resolve relative to the URL the page was actually loaded from.
- Derive the API/router base from `document.baseURI` / `window.location` (or make the paths relative) instead of hardcoding root-absolute paths.

That would make the dashboard work unmodified under any prefix — dev-environment proxies, IAP-style proxies, etc.

comments.author: ravwojdyla-agent
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

Confirmed. Two layers of root-absolute URLs: the build config (`assetPrefix: '/'`) bakes absolute script/CSS refs into the HTML, and every frontend fetch hardcodes a root-absolute path. The router already uses `createWebHashHistory`, so SPA routing itself is prefix-safe. One complication: the controller/worker also serve the HTML shell at path-based deep links (`/job/{id}`, `/worker/{id}`, `/task/{id}`, `/status`), so purely relative URLs would break those pages without a per-request `<base href>`.

**Relevant code**
- [`rsbuild.config.ts#L16`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/dashboard/rsbuild.config.ts#L16) - `assetPrefix: '/'`
- [`useRpc.ts#L40`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/dashboard/src/composables/useRpc.ts#L40) - root-absolute RPC fetches (×4 in file)
- [`dashboard.py#L495-L496`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/dashboard.py#L495-L496) - shell served at deep paths
- [`dashboard_common.py#L166`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/dashboard_common.py#L166) - `html_shell`, injection point
- [`speedscope.ts#L22`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/dashboard/src/utils/speedscope.ts#L22) - plus `App.vue`, `LoginPage.vue`, `AccountTab.vue`, `ProfileLink.vue` absolute fetches

# Proposed Fix

1. `output.assetPrefix: 'auto'` — HTML asset refs become relative; async chunks resolve via `document.currentScript`.
2. `html_shell(dashboard_type, request_path)` injects `<base href>` pointing at the dashboard root relative to the request path the server saw (`/` → `./`, `/job/a/b` → `../../`). Relative URLs then resolve correctly at any depth and behind any prefix — the server never needs to know the prefix.
3. Frontend: drop the leading `/` from all fetch/asset URLs (`useRpc.ts`, auth calls, speedscope, worker `href="/"` → `href="./"`); they resolve against the base.
4. `_session_bootstrap` redirect `/` → `../` (relative `Location` survives the proxy).

Test: `html_shell` base injection against a tmp dist dir (the `<base href>` is the browser-consumed contract).

issues.body:
<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This experiment tests whether a small transformer trained only on tokenized continuous-time 2D Ising trajectories can learn useful near-critical dynamics without being given the Hamiltonian, flip rates, or critical temperature. The current `v5p-8` runs show clean teacher-forced learning (`validation loss 4.9071 -> 2.1578`, critical probe loss `2.1767`) and rollout samples that do not collapse at `Tc=2.269`. The main unresolved failure is rollout physics: mean wait times and boundary-flip fractions are plausible, but final `|m|` is too low, especially below `Tc`, so sampled trajectories over-disorder the lattice. The recommended next work is to replicate rollout metrics across seeds, add time-series diagnostics around `Tc`, and debug the sampler entropy/top-k behavior before scaling the model or data.

### Helpful links
- Research logbook: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/ising-tokenizer/.agents/logbooks/ising-tokenizer.md
- Strong teacher-forced run: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/tokexplore/runs/i23pldvi
- Rollout-enabled run: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/tokexplore/runs/p6ciu4qo
- Sampler and rollout review: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4104#issuecomment-4122100756
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

🤖 This issue tracks the Ising tokenizer side project as a proper research thread.

## Description

This project asks whether a small tokenized transformer trained on continuous-time 2D Ising trajectories can recover meaningful near-critical dynamics without being given the Hamiltonian, acceptance rules, or the critical temperature. The trajectory language is rejection-free BKL-style event data: an initial spin field encoded as `[pos][spin]...`, followed by flip events encoded as `[pos][dt]...`.

The goal is not engineering scale. The goal is a clean existence proof for the TATT-style claim that useful physics is latent in the trajectory statistics and can be discovered by a token sequence model.

## Hypothesis or Goal

A transformer trained only on off-critical temperatures should:

- learn teacher-forced next-token prediction cleanly on held-out off-critical temperatures,
- assign reasonable probability mass to unseen trajectories near `Tc`,
- and begin to reproduce rollout-level observables near `Tc` without collapsing.

Near-term success metrics:

- held-out validation loss improves substantially from initialization,
- critical probe loss is not catastrophically worse than held-out validation,
- rollout observables at held-out and critical temperatures are in the right ballpark:
  - mean wait time,
  - boundary-flip fraction,
  - final absolute magnetization.

Current confidence level: `exploratory`.

### Links

* Research Logbook: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/ising-tokenizer/.agents/logbooks/ising-tokenizer.md
* Research Branch: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/research/ising-tokenizer
* WandB Project: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/tokexplore
* Latest strong teacher-forced run: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/tokexplore/runs/i23pldvi
* Latest rollout-enabled run: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/tokexplore/runs/p6ciu4qo

## Results

Current state:

- Scaffold, synthetic BKL data generation, tokenization, and TPU path are working.
- A `v5p-8` run at `8192` examples / `4096` steps trains cleanly:
  - train loss `4.9105 -> 2.1618`
  - validation loss `4.9071 -> 2.1578`
  - critical probe loss `2.1767`
- The rollout-enabled run does not collapse at `Tc`.
- Rollout observables are encouraging but incomplete:
  - `T=1.6` wait-time ratio `0.994`
  - `T=2.9` wait-time ratio `0.899`
  - `T=Tc=2.269` wait-time ratio `0.617`
  - boundary-flip fraction is within about `0.03` to `0.06` absolute error across the probed temperatures
  - final `|m|` is too low across all temperatures, especially below `Tc`, so the model still over-disorders its sampled rollouts

Interpretation:

- The model is clearly learning something real about the dynamics.
- Near-critical rollouts are not catastrophically bad.
- The main failure mode at the moment is ordered-phase persistence, not total rollout breakdown.

Immediate next steps:

1. Replicate rollout metrics across additional seeds.
2. Add simple trajectory-level time-series diagnostics near `Tc`.
3. Decide whether to scale data/model modestly or improve the rollout sampler / conditioning before making stronger claims.

comments.body:
🤖 **Code review and feedback on next steps**

Reviewed the full `research/ising-tokenizer` branch: `data.py`, `model.py`, `train.py`, `launch.py`, tests, and logbook.

**On the |m| under-magnetization failure mode**

The rollout sampler (`_sample_rollout_tokens`) uses unconstrained categorical sampling from masked logits — position tokens get a flat mask over all `num_sites` positions, dt tokens get a flat mask over all 64 bins. There is no temperature parameter on the softmax itself (i.e. no sampling temperature distinct from the physics temperature conditioning). At low T where the true flip-rate landscape is very peaked (most sites have near-zero rate, only domain-wall sites flip), the model's position distribution likely has too much entropy, producing spurious bulk flips that disorder the lattice. Two concrete things to try before scaling:

1. **Top-k or nucleus sampling on position tokens only.** The dt distribution is already broad, but position selection at low T should be sharp. Restricting to top-k=16 (or nucleus p=0.9) for position tokens would test whether the model has learned the right ranking but over-smooths the tail.

2. **Log the per-token entropy of the position and dt distributions during rollout.** This is cheap (just `jax.scipy.special.entr` on the softmax of the masked logits) and would immediately show whether the model's position entropy at T=1.6 is much higher than at T=2.9, which it should be if it has learned the rate structure.

**On the three proposed next steps**

- *Replicate rollout metrics across seeds*: agree this is the right first move — the current 16 examples/temperature is noisy. Consider bumping to 64 and running 3 seeds.
- *Trajectory-level time-series diagnostics near Tc*: the current `_rollout_observables` only measures terminal quantities. A cumulative magnetization curve `|m(t)|` vs event index (cheap to add in `_rollout_observables`) would directly show whether the model's rollouts drift monotonically toward disorder or fluctuate as they should near Tc.
- *Scale data/model vs. improve sampler*: the |m| failure is more likely a sampling/decoding problem than a capacity problem, given that teacher-forced loss is already strong. I'd prioritize the sampler diagnostics above before scaling.

**Relevant code**
- [`train.py#L219-L266`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/ising-tokenizer/experiments/ising_tokenizer/base/train.py#L219-L266) — `_sample_rollout_tokens`, no sampling temperature or truncation
- [`train.py#L187-L212`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/ising-tokenizer/experiments/ising_tokenizer/base/train.py#L187-L212) — `_rollout_observables`, terminal-only metrics
- [`data.py#L143-L155`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/research/ising-tokenizer/experiments/ising_tokenizer/base/data.py#L143-L155) — `_glauber_flip_rates`, the peaked rate landscape at low T

<!-- experiment-tldr:start -->
## Summary

This issue compares completed `1e20 d1536` MoE runs in `dial_moe`, with the main result that the GatedNorm + AdamH run is the strongest current point on the listed quality metrics. Even though it stopped earlier than most baselines (`18.69B` tokens versus roughly `19.9B`), it improves `eval/paloma/c4_en/bpb` over the original v2 baseline, dial_moe v2 bs128, dial_moe v3, and the `e128` run. The remaining caveat is that a token-matched comparison would be cleaner, but the current evidence favors the GatedNorm + AdamH recipe.

### Helpful links
- GatedNorm + AdamH run: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/isoflop-moe-adamh-gatednorm-v5p64-r2-1e20-d1536-retry25
- Original v2 baseline: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/isoflop-moe-v2-1e%2B20-d1536-v4-128
- `e128` comparison run: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/moe-e128-d1536-1e20
<!-- experiment-tldr:end -->

## Description

We now have several completed `1e20 d1536` runs in `marin-community/dial_moe`. This issue records the current comparison set, centered on the completed GatedNorm + AdamH run, and keeps the older v2/v3 runs in the same place.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Check where the completed GatedNorm + AdamH `1e20 d1536` run lands relative to the other finished `1e20 d1536` runs, and separate real quality differences from token-count or setup mismatches.

### Links

* WandB Report: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/isoflop-moe-adamh-gatednorm-v5p64-r2-1e20-d1536-retry25
* Original v2 baseline: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/isoflop-moe-v2-1e%2B20-d1536-v4-128
* dial_moe v2 bs128: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/isoflop-moe-v2-1e%2B20-d1536-bs128
* dial_moe v3: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/isoflop-moe-v3-1e%2B20-d1536
* `e128` run: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/dial_moe/runs/moe-e128-d1536-1e20

## Results

Finished runs at `1e20 d1536`:
- GatedNorm + AdamH: `eval/paloma/c4_en/bpb = 0.87868`, `eval/loss = 2.67004`, `paloma macro = 2.88913`, `uncheatable macro = 2.46996`, `18.69B` tokens
- Original v2 baseline (`marin` project): `0.89727`, `2.69720`, `2.95470`, `2.54613`, `19.96B` tokens
- dial_moe v2 bs128: `0.90192`, `2.71354`, `2.96897`, `2.56660`, `19.96B` tokens
- dial_moe v3: `0.89274`, `2.67939`, `2.93814`, `2.52674`, `19.96B` tokens
- `moe-e128-d1536-1e20`: `0.88188`, `2.64626`, `2.90598`, `2.48573`, `19.92B` tokens

On `eval/paloma/c4_en/bpb`, the completed GatedNorm run is:
- `-0.01859` better than the original v2 baseline
- `-0.02324` better than `dial_moe` v2 bs128
- `-0.01406` better than `dial_moe` v3
- `-0.00320` better than `moe-e128-d1536-1e20`

The main remaining caveat is token mismatch: the GatedNorm run stopped at `18.69B` tokens, while most comparison runs are near `19.9B` tokens. The ranking looks favorable even with that handicap, but a fully token-matched comparison is still cleaner.

issues.author: atqamar
issues.body:
## TL;DR

Continue the async non-agentic RL work from #8936 as a structured research program: one
evaluation/task system with a frozen answer contract, a Qwen3-0.6B screening ladder, a MoE rung
(Qwen3-30B-A3B) used only where a dense model cannot answer, and Snowball confirmation with a
pre-registered non-inferiority margin. Weight-sync cost, the largest measured lever at Snowball
scale, is treated as engineering with bit-identical proofs, not as a research question.

## Description

The first epic (#8936) built the async trainer path, the telemetry, and the Grafana dashboard,
and produced controlled 25- and 100-update comparisons on Qwen3-0.6B and Snowball. It also found
that raw GSM8K reward hides nontermination (Snowball scored 120/128 raw with 64 completed
answers), that the cadence lever changes staleness and cost together, and that the drift
metric conflates engine mismatch with staleness. This epic starts from that evidence with a
narrative structure: goal → sub-goals → hypotheses → experiments, each experiment with a fixed
design bucket, a done-when, and a kill criterion.

Scope: non-agentic math; Megatron trainer; vLLM inference with existing flags only; H100.
Out of scope: agentic tasks, vLLM implementation work, GB200.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Snowball RL can run faster in wall-clock and GPU-hours at non-inferior held-out quality by
decoupling the trainer from rollout workers, and there is a measurable safe range of off-policy
age. A speedup is a hypothesis to test; the completion criterion is evidence with confidence
intervals and an operating recommendation.

Sub-goals: trustworthy measurement · a cost model of where training time goes · cheap weight
sync · off-policy tolerance · system balance (cadence, GPU split, admission) ·
learning-quality validity · trainer memory and speed · a scale ladder from Qwen3-0.6B to Snowball.

## How to read this thread

One comment per milestone or per experiment. Each comment has four parts: what we did and why,
results (with numbers and intervals), what this means, and what comes next. Provenance (commits,
receipts, W&B links, audit gates) is in a collapsed block at the end of each comment.

## Status

(one line per milestone, newest first)

- Milestone 1 — prior runs closed out: the isolated-TIS analysis and the canonical results table
  are posted; no configuration graduates on a single seed.
- Milestone 0 — program started: execution branches `atqamar/async-non-agentic-rl-v2` created
  from MarinSkyRL `fa6aae36` / Marin `eb85a25675`; preflight passed; answer contract frozen.

## Milestones

0 program started · 1 prior runs closed out · 2 evaluation and task system in place · 3
telemetry and pause fix landed · 4 answer contract and tasks fixed · 5 weight sync under 1.5 s
with bit-identical proof · 6 correction chosen and safe-bound rule · 7 learner-size decision · 8
system balance measured · 9 MoE-rung verdict · 10 final tradeoff statement with confidence intervals.

## Glossary

- **Cadence C** — sync weights to the rollout workers every C optimizer updates.
- **Age A** — the maximum number of updates a rollout group may lag the trainer and still be used.
- **P/I** — learner GPUs / inference GPUs.
- **Objectives** — behaviour-clip (BC), plain PPO (REG), PPO with truncated importance sampling
  (REG+TIS), and the masked/second-moment corrections to be added.
- **Three cost axes** — optimizer updates, consumed tokens, and GPU-hours plus core seconds.
- **Three quality scores** — the verifier's raw reward; the completed score (correct *and* the
  response ended on its own, not at the token cap), which is the ranking metric; and a semantic
  score (final answer checked after the thinking boundary).
- **Staleness** — policy-version lag in optimizer updates unless stated otherwise.

## Links

- Prior epic: #8936 (results that carry over are in the milestone-1 comments).
- Reference log this format follows: #8765.

## Decision Log

- 2026-09-08 — Eval battery replaces the locked 1,191-row GSM8K window with GSM8K-Platinum + MATH
  items (window at ceiling, some mislabeled items, informative signal collapses after 60
  updates); the old window stays as the legacy battery for closing the prior confirmation.
- 2026-09-08 — Weight-sync design: shard-to-shard NCCL send/recv (expert weights are already in
  vLLM's layout on the trainer under TP1/EP8); delta weight sync gated on density and on
  sync still mattering afterwards.
- 2026-09-08 — Non-inferiority margin: 2 pp on the completed score (default, revisable before the
  Snowball quality stage); seed count derived from the measured Snowball seed spread before
  confirmation launches.

comments.author: atqamar
comments.body:
🤖 Milestone 0: program started, execution branches created, preflight passed

**What we did and why.** This program continues #8936 under a fixed answer contract and a
pre-registered quality margin, so that every later speed claim is measured against usable
answers rather than raw reward. Before any GPU work we created the execution branches, checked
that the devbox can reach the job scheduler, and started freezing the answer contract and prompt
templates. The three work lanes (evaluation system, research, weight-sync engineering) each got
their own worktrees so they can proceed in parallel without touching each other's files.

**Results.** Shared branch `atqamar/async-non-agentic-rl-v2` is pushed in both repositories.
The egress router and a live scheduler listing passed preflight. The ranking metric for every
quality comparison is the completed score (correct and ended on its own), with a 2 pp
non-inferiority margin. No experimental result is claimed at this milestone.

**What this means.** The bookkeeping that the first epic lacked (one contract, one metric, one
margin, separate lanes) is in place before the first run.

**Next.** Close out the prior epic's unanalysed runs (milestone 1), then bring the evaluation and
task system to its gate (milestone 2).

<details><summary>Provenance</summary>

MarinSkyRL `fa6aae365f70e50bca5218ed2f3d49067e6dcc26` / Marin `eb85a256757f55b9ec34f8e4f7ab7f622e42110f`.

comments.author: atqamar
comments.body:
🤖 Answer contract and prompt templates frozen for Qwen3-0.6B and Snowball

**What we did and why.** Every score in this program depends on the exact prompt template and
the rule the verifier applies to an answer. The first epic changed both mid-stream, which is
why its raw rewards were not comparable across runs. We recorded one template per model and
one contract per environment, hashed them, and added a test that fails if either changes.

**Results.** The template hashes for both models are frozen and independently checked:
`8 passed in 3.40s`. As a mutation check, disabling the hash guard produced `1 failed in 18.88s`
with valid syntax, so the test bites.

**What this means.** From here on, any run whose prompt or contract differs from the frozen one
fails at test time rather than silently producing incomparable numbers.

**Next.** Build the enriched task pool and the dual scorer on top of the frozen contract
(milestone 2).

<details><summary>Provenance</summary>

Eval-system step 0 (KE0). SHA pair: MarinSkyRL `fa6aae365f70e50bca5218ed2f3d49067e6dcc26` /
Marin `88f89be1671556f5e3a970e9f22be8865107ac13`.
</details>

comments.author: atqamar
comments.body:
🤖 Without a correction, cadence-1 training completes 2 of 128 answers; TIS or behavior clipping restores 98 or 90, and the effect vanishes at cadence 4

**What we did and why.** The first epic ran a six-arm Qwen3-0.6B screen (two sync
cadences × three objectives) but never analysed it. The question it can answer is whether the
truncated-importance-sampling correction (TIS) helps quality when rollouts are up to three
updates stale, which matters because letting rollouts go stale is how async training gets its
speed. We audited all six runs and compared the arms in pairs on the completed score (correct

1. At cadence 4 (the configuration that saves time), the TIS correction is worth +7.8 pp on
   completed answers with an interval that includes zero, and behaviour-clip is worth +6.3 pp,

**Next.** Measure how much evaluation is needed to separate arms (the power calibration), then

🤖 Task pool built: nine parquet views with train/dev/held-out locks, verified by readback

**What we did and why.** Every experiment in this program samples its prompts from one
versioned pool rather than from whatever rows a recipe happened to slice, so that arms and
seeds compare on identical questions and held-out sets stay held out. This step built that pool:
each prompt carries a content hash, an answer type, the contract it is scored under, a licence
field, its split, and its token count under both models' templates, and the held-out rows are
locked in a manifest the sampler cannot cross.

**Results.** The pool artifact was written and read back: `KE1_ARTIFACT_READBACK_PASS`, all nine
parquet views and the split locks verified against the candidate manifest
`d39aa170289c9637427bb2f6a829b49321875aa1ebc054fbcda7150bd2482cc1`. Independent pool and sampler
tests: `21 passed in 20.19s`.

**What this means.** Prompt identity is now a hash, not a row index, so pairing across arms and
seeds is exact and reordering a file cannot silently break a comparison.

**Next.** The final evaluation battery and the remaining eval-system gates (scorer, harness,
difficulty ratings), towards milestone 2, "evaluation and task system in place".

<details><summary>Provenance</summary>

Eval-system step 1 (KE1). Shared pair MarinSkyRL `fa6aae365f70e50bca5218ed2f3d49067e6dcc26` /
Marin `50bf442de856c870e9ee608dacafcb374db89e2d`.

comments.author: atqamar
comments.body:
🤖 Seeded sampler admits only audited prompts; removing that check fails three tests

**What we did and why.** Experiments request prompts through one function, `sample(pool, bins,
n, seed, model, split)`, which must be deterministic and must refuse two things: crossing a
split boundary, and returning a prompt whose statement or gold answer has not passed the pool
audit. Without the second refusal, a mislabeled question could enter a training or evaluation
set and quietly bias a comparison.

**Results.** `KE3_ACCEPT_ONLY_MUTATION_PASS`: with the audit-eligibility check removed, three
tests fail; with it restored the suite passes 21 tests, and an independent replay also passes 21.
Sampling now requires an accepted audit status bound to the immutable manifest and the verifier;
prompts whose audit entry is missing, pending, flagged, rejected, or belongs to another manifest
cannot enter a sample.

**What this means.** The sampler is proven to bite: the test that guards audit eligibility was
shown to fail when the guard is removed, which is the standard this program holds every gate to.

**Next.** The scorer and harness gates, then the difficulty-rating pass for both models, towards
milestone 2.

Eval-system step 3 (KE3). Shared pair MarinSkyRL `fa6aae365f70e50bca5218ed2f3d49067e6dcc26` /
Marin `50bf442de856c870e9ee608dacafcb374db89e2d`.

comments.body:
🤖 Syncing every 4 updates reduces Snowball core time by 29.3%, but three seeds do not establish equal answer quality

**What we did and why.** We completed the missing run in the legacy Snowball comparison and audited all three seed pairs. The question is whether syncing weights less often makes training faster while preserving completed answers, a prerequisite for recommending an asynchronous operating range. Both configurations trained for 100 updates with behaviour clipping: sync every 2 updates with maximum age 1, versus every 4 updates with maximum age 3. Evaluation used the same locked 1,191 GSM8K questions at the start and finish.

**Results.**

Completed score means the legacy binary verifier marked the answer correct and its stop label was accepted. Truncation means the generation hit its length cap. Semantic scoring is unavailable for these historical dumps.

| cadence and seed | updates | consumed tokens | core s | task H100h | completed score | semantic | trunc % | group age mean/p95 | min ESS fraction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|---:|---|---:|
| 2, seed 17 | 100 | 14,081,797 | 3759.33 | 59.3357 | 200/1191 | NA | 82.70 | 0.50/1 | 0.98897 |
| 2, seed 29 | 100 | 12,293,213 | 3594.76 | 57.6094 | 374/1191 | NA | 67.93 | 0.50/1 | 0.96900 |
| 2, seed 43 | 100 | 14,120,429 | 3768.46 | 58.5634 | 1024/1191 | NA | 7.89 | 0.50/1 | 0.48478 |
| 4, seed 17 | 100 | 18,793,379 | 2874.52 | 49.3480 | 510/1191 | NA | 56.00 | 1.50/3 | 0.98516 |
| 4, seed 29 | 100 | 15,837,574 | 2663.95 | 47.2133 | 6/1191 | NA | 99.41 | 1.50/3 | 0.94917 |
| 4, seed 43 | 100 | 12,043,386 | 2323.28 | 42.4302 | 1056/1191 | NA | 6.88 | 1.50/3 | 0.97464 |

The completed-score differences for cadence 4 minus cadence 2 are **+26.03, −30.90, and +2.69 percentage points**, averaging **−0.73 pp**.

| uncertainty calculation | 95% interval for the mean completed-score difference |
|---|---|
| Paired questions, conditional on these three fixed training seeds | [−2.27, +0.81] pp |
| Paired training-seed effects, fixed question battery, Student-t with 2 degrees of freedom | [−71.82, +70.36] pp |

The question interval uses 10,000 paired bootstrap draws and does not measure uncertainty over new training seeds. The seed interval assumes approximately normal seed effects, which cannot be checked with three seeds; its width exposes how little these runs establish about reproducibility. Both lower bounds fall below the approved −2 pp non-inferiority margin.

Across the three seeds, cadence 4 uses **7,861.75 versus 11,122.55 core seconds** (29.3% less), **138.99 versus 175.51 task H100-hours** (20.8% less), and **46.67 versus 40.50 million consumed response tokens** (15.3% more). These are fixed-update comparisons, not equal-token speedups. The six-run cost is **314.50 H100-hours**, of which **42.43** is the newly executed candidate; the other five runs are inherited.

[Quality versus updates, consumed tokens and core time; audited summary and source](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/artifacts/analysis/async-rl-v2-e02-audited-results/v0).

**What this means.** The slower weight-sync schedule saves measured training time, but answer completion changes direction across seeds, so equal quality is **undecided** and no configuration graduates. Raw verifier reward hides the failure: the cadence-4 seed-29 run has 1,080 raw-correct answers but only 6 completed-correct answers, with 1,184 responses truncated. Sync cadence and permitted age changed together, actual consumed training order was not verified, and these historical runs cannot identify a causal age threshold.

**Next.** Finish the evaluation and task system, calibrate its power, and address nontermination before ranking new schedules. The next milestone is **evaluation and task system in place**; subsequent confirmation will use a frozen protocol and enough training seeds to support the quality decision.

🤖 Weight sync takes a median 20.226 seconds; receiver GPU telemetry is incomplete

**What we did and why.** We measured where Snowball spends time syncing updated weights to its rollout workers, to guide faster training at the same answer quality (E3.0). The run kept the existing five-second pause grace and tensor-by-tensor transfer behavior, using 32 learner and eight inference H100s for five updates. A 128-row training slice with zero data-loader workers exercised an epoch reset, while greedy evaluation ran on the same 128 development rows before training and after update five.

**Results.** [Audited JSON, three vector plots, and reproducible inputs](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/artifacts/analysis/async-rl-v2-weight-sync-baseline/v0) accompany the tables below.

All five updates, both evaluation dumps, and all five GPU tasks completed successfully. The run consumed 698,807 response tokens in 281.748 core seconds and cost 9.522493333 task H100-hours, including startup and evaluation.

| Whole-operation wall time | Median seconds | p95 seconds |
|---|---:|---:|
| Pause generation | 5.151 | 5.502 |
| Weight broadcast | 14.955 | 15.176 |
| Complete weight sync | 20.226 | 20.513 |
| Derived trainer stall | 20.154 | 20.434 |

Each row contains the five post-update syncs; startup is retained in the audit but excluded from these summaries. The stall proxy is the existing whole-sync wall time minus the host-side NCCL-send span; it is not GPU idle time. These are descriptive within-run quantiles, without a paired effect estimate or a confidence interval for a speedup.

| Stage | Wall median / p95, seconds | CUDA-event median / p95, milliseconds | Observation grouping |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Export | 5.569 / 6.937 | 5,738.414 / 7,067.907 | Maximum across 32 learner ranks per sync |
| NCCL send | 0.074 / 0.081 | 2,838.650 / 2,841.202 | Learner rank zero per sync |
| RPC wait | 5.367 / 5.458 | 2,612.828 / 2,688.714 | Learner rank zero per sync |
| Barrier | 6.187 / 6.454 | 6,045.054 / 6,324.449 | Maximum across 32 learner ranks per sync |
| Learner reload finalization | 0.00647 / 0.00686 | 6.493 / 6.890 | Learner rank zero per sync |
| Receive | 0.0602 / 0.0618 | Missing | Maximum receiver wall time per sync |
| Load | 4.544 / 4.630 | Missing | Maximum receiver wall time per sync |
| Receiver finalization | 0.00473 / 0.00490 | Missing | Maximum receiver wall time per sync |

All stage summaries contain five syncs. Export and barrier each have 160 underlying learner-rank observations; the other learner stages each have five. Including startup, 402 native learner stage events were retained. All 25 post-update learner wall maxima match the corresponding W&B driver metrics. Receiver wall maxima are retained in W&B, but individual receiver receipts and their CUDA times were not durably exported. The worker process returns those values over RPC without initializing a telemetry exporter.

Stage spans overlap. CUDA events can include stream waiting, while a host NCCL call can return before transfer completion; neither rank maxima nor stage medians may be summed into critical-path latency or GPU utilization.

The one-second inference polling configuration produced 2,648 cumulative token observations across eight engines. Actual sampling intervals reached 3.521 seconds. Counter differences aligned to each sync are retained with 60-second windows on either side; adjacent windows overlap other syncs and evaluation, so they do not establish a causal throughput effect. The final after-window has only 66.585% coverage and has no reported rate.

| Development evaluation | Contract score, 95% interval | Completed contract score, 95% interval | Length-stop fraction, 95% interval |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Before training | 75.00% [66.84, 81.70] | 73.44% [65.18, 80.32] | 11.72% [7.23, 18.44] |
| After five updates | 92.19% [86.22, 95.70] | 89.06% [82.48, 93.37] | 9.38% [5.44, 15.67] |

Intervals are Wilson intervals over 128 audited rows, not seed uncertainty or a paired treatment comparison. These are the retained legacy verifier and completed-stop scores; independent semantic scoring was not part of this timing gate. All 160 consumed groups have native policy-version age observations: 92 at age zero and 68 at age one. Pooled group-weighted mean age is 0.425 updates and nearest-rank p95 is one update; coverage is 32 groups per update. Behavior-ratio token-weight ESS fraction ranged from 0.991226 to 0.992424.

The separate data-loader gate failed its strict maximum-lag requirement: 373 samples included three values above two seconds, with a maximum of 2.527699 seconds. The three violations overlap weight sync; overlap does not establish their cause. The epoch reset was observed at update five, and evaluation at both required steps was verified. No lag sample reached ten seconds, but that does not satisfy the two-second criterion.

The preliminary Qwen two-GPU tests passed stage readback and the native pause precursor. Across 64 actual in-flight requests, the precursor accounted for 64 aborts and eventual completions, with zero lost requests and native first-token timestamps on every abort response. Those two tests cost 0.278617778 task H100-hours combined. They are engineering checks, not a Snowball speedup or the full repeated-sync pause gate.

**What this means.** The fixed pause and coordination spans are material optimization targets, and the whole-sync wall baseline is usable. The complete GPU-stage observability requirement remains unmet because receiver CUDA receipts were not retained. The loader change remains ungated; this five-update timing run establishes neither a quality improvement nor a recommended off-policy age range.

**Next.** Preserve receiver timing origin while exporting the native RPC receipts through the trainer, then validate the repair before a bounded Snowball rerun. Independently complete the pause-handshake checks with a matched stale-token comparison, and investigate the three lag spikes without excluding them or relaxing the threshold. These steps lead toward the telemetry and pause-fix milestone.

4,096 are identical to the failed trace. Eval runs at 0/5 and the fifth update crosses an epoch.

preemptions. Native terminal/runtime/request/attempt and all 256 eval rows were audited.

🤖 Qwen rates 1,024 questions, then the larger run exposes a renderer mismatch

**What we did and why.**

We tested inference-only difficulty ratings to choose tasks for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. A 16-question functional check preceded a 1,024-question pilot sampled proportionally across eight accepted training bins, with eight responses per question. Independent CPU audits checked original engine tokens, native rewards and completed correctness; the serving path also required exact agreement between API text and token decoding. We then attempted the 13,407-question remainder and a bounded 512-question diagnostic after the remainder failed that check.

**Results.**

| Attempt | Planned questions×responses | Audited rating rows | Audited response tokens | Native task seconds | H100-hours | Outcome |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Functional check | 16×8 | 128 | 36,033 | 158.510 | 0.044031 | Token/reward/completion parity passed |
| Representative pilot | 1,024×8 | 8,192 | 2,068,195 | 242.926 | 0.067479 | Token/reward/completion parity passed |
| Remainder | 13,407×8 | — | — | 234.651 | 0.065181 | Renderer mismatch; no rating dump |

All four attempts used one east H100, with no automatic retries. Total measured cost is 0.220201389 H100-hours. These were inference-only jobs: training updates, off-policy age and ESS do not apply; no training-core speedup is claimed. The pilot's generation plus native scoring took 129.002900501s within its 242.926s task allocation; the functional check predates that timing instrumentation.

Pilot completed correctness was 1,909/8,192=23.30%, with a 95% question-bootstrap interval [22.19%,24.48%]. The functional prerequisite checked 256 original token hashes; the pilot checked 16,384. The functional panel was deliberately small and balanced across bins, so its answer scores are not pooled with the representative pilot.

Completed correctness is full native credit multiplied by an accepted stop. Each question contributes the mean of its eight binary outcomes. Intervals resample questions with all eight responses kept together, 10,000 draws, bootstrap seed 17; the pooled interval preserves the pilot's bin quotas. They are descriptive, pointwise intervals conditional on one engine seed, with no simultaneous-coverage, independent-seed or treatment-comparison claim. The eight-sample per-question ratings remain coarse empirical measurements, not known latent probabilities.

The pilot had 8,175 accepted stops and 17 length stops (0.2075%); all length-stopped responses had completed correctness 0. All 8,192 thinking-boundary fields were populated. Its signed/fractional raw reward mean was −0.086208839; raw values were preserved separately from binary correctness. The diagnostic preserved a 67,207-byte response artifact. Replaying the exact pinned engine's incremental decoder matched the original API text for all eight responses, including the failing one; the other seven also matched whole-sequence decoding. The failed check remained strict, and neither failed attempt produced an accepted rating dump.

**What this means.**

The pilot is retained as an audited functional, cost and difficulty measurement. The full rating stage is held: a real rendering edge escaped the smaller probes, and the captured response now supplies a regression case. The correction must reproduce the engine's incremental decoding while preserving original tokens, forensic text and semantic scoring; it has not yet passed its repair gate. **Next.**

Qualify the incremental renderer against the captured failure, EOS/stop and Unicode controls, and all 8,192 original pilot responses. 🤖 3 seeded controls time out before their first recorded evaluation

**What we did and why.**

We ran a seeded control to test whether synchronous training and asynchronous training with no admitted staleness consume comparable work. This matters for attributing faster Snowball training at the same answer quality to scheduling. An earlier comparison consumed matching question sets but exceeded its prescribed reward-noise band, so the planned follow-up assigned each trajectory a seed derived from its question, sample and installed weight version and enabled the pinned engine's batch-invariance mode. The three arms were synchronous seed 17, asynchronous seed 17 and an asynchronous seed-29 noise reference, each planned for eight updates.

**Results.**

| Arm | Planned updates | Recorded training/evaluation result | Native terminal state | Task H100-hours |
|---|---:|---|---|---|
| Synchronous, seed 17 | 8 | No usable result | Both tasks timed out | Unavailable |
| Asynchronous, seed 17 | 8 | No usable result | Both tasks timed out | Unavailable |
| Asynchronous noise reference, seed 29 | 8 | No usable result | Both tasks timed out | Unavailable |

All six GPU tasks failed on their first attempt, with no preemption or automatic retry. Each arm requested 16 east H100s with a 1,125-second execution timeout. The controller reports execution timeout for every task, but their attempt-finish timestamps are missing. The 15-H100-hour reservation therefore remains held; it is not reported as measured cost, and the job-terminal timestamps are not substituted for allocation ends.

All three W&B runs are marked crashed with zero history rows. Independent regional storage reads found no evaluation exports, successful training receipts or terminal manifests at the exact frozen output paths. Native telemetry contains no recorded optimizer updates, training metrics or completed-work events for these runs. Consumed tokens, training-core time, completed correctness, semantic correctness, truncation, age, ESS and confidence intervals are consequently unavailable.

The runs reached receiver setup and then stopped making visible progress before initial evaluation. Source inspection shows that batch-invariance initialization changes NCCL settings in the rollout workers while the trainer retains its previous settings. That is a transport hypothesis, not a demonstrated cause: the captured stacks cover the waiting launcher, and targeted computational stacks could not be recovered before teardown. The earlier two-request determinism probe passed, but it did not exercise trainer-to-worker weight sync.

**What this means.**

This attempt does not establish synchronous/asynchronous equivalence or non-equivalence. It is a failed startup qualification with no quality comparison. The earlier reward-noise failure remains unresolved, and the seeded implementation stays isolated from the shared branch.

**Next.**

Test the exact pinned transport initialization with two GPUs and three bounded cases: original settings, receiver-only batch-invariance settings, and matching settings on both sides. Review the measured outcome before any further training attempt. The next milestone remains telemetry and the pause fix landed.

Seeded sync-in-async control (K4), family `2026.09.08.92`. Frozen Marin `c81a0ea208309b328b3d7ee39ba68a6e559a2ffc` / MarinSkyRL `13a1551ccf8839d13c60a4b591af2e15f69ef6f6`. 🤖 2 Snowball startup probes stop before rating any answers

**What we did and why.** We attempted a small inference-only qualification before rating Snowball's training pool. Both requests used the same 16 questions, four responses per question, original east-region BF16 weights and frozen sampling protocol. The intended result was a verified model load and 64 audited responses, allowing task selection for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality.

**Results.** Neither attempt generated an answer.

| Attempt | Physical H100s | Initiating failure | Task H100 hours |
|---|---:|---|---:|
| Tensor parallelism 8 | 8 | Model configuration rejects 20 attention heads split across eight ranks | 0.133373333333 |
| Tensor parallelism 1, data/expert parallelism 4 | 4 | Container OOM kill during model loading | 0.080462222222 |

The first CPU preparation checked architecture and context limits but missed the pinned model's parallelism restrictions. Subsequent source and native configuration checks established that its GPU implementation requires tensor parallelism one; expert parallelism provides the supported weight sharding. The second attempt reached all four intended expert ranks, each assigned 64 of the model's 256 experts, then was OOM-killed while loading. The task exited 137 after 72.416 seconds at a 128 GiB host-memory limit. No CUDA out-of-memory traceback was recorded, and peak host memory was not available in the retained task receipt.

The loader source exposes a concrete capacity mismatch: each worker defaults to a 40,000,000,000-byte CPU buffer. Four such buffers total 160 GB, exceeding the container's 137,438,953,472-byte limit before other memory use. Each worker streams the checkpoint tensors to CPU and clones them before model-specific expert selection; expert parallelism does not prevent those overlapping host allocations. This is source-backed capacity analysis, not a measurement of the failed run's peak memory.

Both attempts used one task, with no retries or preemptions. No model-load, GPU-headroom or response-rendering gate passed. Quality, tokens, core training throughput, age, ESS, truncation and confidence intervals are unavailable because no inference or learning completed.

**What this means.** The initial layout was incompatible with the pinned model. The corrected layout progressed further, but its loader memory was not bounded for four workers. The second failure does not establish that the model cannot fit on four GPUs.

**Next.** Keep the model, BF16 precision, expert layout and sampling fixed. Review an explicit 8 GiB buffer limit and concurrency four per worker, plus periodic container-memory evidence, before another bounded load probe. Require successful loading and all 64 response audits before expanding the rating job. The next related milestone is the eval and task system in place.

🤖 Eight controlled updates match training rewards across runners

### What we did and why

We compared synchronous training with the asynchronous runner restricted to zero rollout age, using Qwen3-0.6B. Both runners received the same prompt sets and request seeds, with matched communication settings before weight sync. This tests whether later comparisons can use the synchronous runner as their control (K4).

Each arm ran eight updates, with 64 prompts and four responses per prompt. We used seed 17 for the pair and seed 29 for an asynchronous repeat to measure variation. Evaluation was greedy on the same 128 development questions at startup and after training.

### Results

The seed-17 arms matched fingerprints of the consumed prompt-ID sets and raw training rewards at all eight updates. Both had zero rejected groups; the asynchronous runner consumed only age-zero rollouts. Every reward difference was therefore within the measured seed-repeat band.

Completed correctness counts answers that are correct under the task contract and finish with an accepted stop.

| Arm | Final completed correctness | Length stops | Consumed response tokens | Core training seconds | Task H100-hours |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Synchronous, seed 17 | 70/128 | 0/128 | 317,375 | 86.66 | 1.755 |
| Asynchronous, seed 17 | 68/128 | 1/128 | 317,375 | 123.90 | 1.901 |
| Asynchronous, seed 29 | 69/128 | 2/128 | 318,547 | 126.10 | 1.911 |

The full-ratio token effective-sample-size fraction ranged from 0.99875718 to 0.99901904 in both seed-17 arms and from 0.99874120 to 0.99900885 in the repeat. This measures importance-weight concentration on selected tokens.

Final asynchronous-minus-synchronous completed correctness was **−1.56 percentage points**, with a paired-question 95% interval of **[−7.03, +3.91] points**. Raw correctness equaled completed correctness at these endpoints. Semantic rescoring was unavailable for this legacy evaluation protocol.

Each seed-17 arm had one engine initialization failure caused by a port collision, followed by the runtime's built-in startup retry. All 50 observed worker processes, including failed and replacement starts, had the required settings. Scheduler retries and terminal telemetry export losses were zero. Total measured cost was 5.568 H100-hours.

### What this means

The prescribed control gate passes under these sampling and communication settings. The asynchronous runner was slower in this short, age-zero comparison. Core timing excludes startup and evaluation; this result does not rank production schedules.

The quality interval is conditional on the observed seed-17 models and is too wide to establish the 2-point non-inferiority claim. Consumed-set digests do not establish order within a batch. Earlier failed controls and the startup retries remain part of the record.

### Next

Integrate the qualified control, finish evaluation calibration, and complete the pause comparison needed for milestone 3, telemetry and pause fix landed. Quality-ranked sweeps will use the calibrated evaluation protocol.

🤖 20 pause measurements stand; final cleanup exposed a cancellation defect

**What we did and why.** We ran the original five-second-pause baseline under enough queued work to test whether a faster pause can preserve every native request. This is a stress qualification for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality (K7), using Qwen on 16 east H100s: eight learner GPUs and eight independent inference engines. Both prospective arms use 2,048 training rows, 512 generation workers, an admission-age limit of eight updates, four concurrent sequences per engine, and forced 1,024-token training responses. The candidate has not run.

**Results.**

| Arm | Updates | Consumed loss tokens | Core seconds | Task H100 hours | Final completed score | Semantic rating | Eval truncation | Consumed age mean / p95 | Token-weight ESS fraction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Original pause, failed final drain | 20 | 5,242,880 | 493.258 | 2.312793 audited for rank 0; rank 1 pending | 71/128 = 55.47%; Wilson 95% CI [46.82, 63.79]% | Not rated | 2/128 = 1.5625% | 2.202 / 7 updates | Mean 0.998550; range 0.997825–0.998854 |

All 5,120 consumed training sequences reached the forced length, and all 5,242,880 response tokens carried a loss mask. Initial raw and completed scores were both 8/128, with Wilson 95% CI [3.20, 11.85]%; final raw and completed scores were both 71/128. Initial evaluation had one length stop; final evaluation had two. These completed scores use the historical correct-answer-plus-accepted-stop definition; semantic correctness was not separately rated. No paired arm interval is available because the candidate has not yet run.

The 20 measured pauses had median 5.0999 seconds and nearest-rank p95 5.1792 seconds. Whole weight sync had median 6.2162 seconds and p95 6.3917 seconds. The audited completed-group stale-token fraction was 1,536,000 / 6,918,144 = 22.2025%, including stale-at-enqueue outcomes; this denominator excludes unfinished native work. All eight engines had real queued cohorts after the first two grace periods. Native stage coverage contains 903 events and 160 checked driver folds; per-origin CUDA durations and wall spans overlap and cannot be added into whole-sync latency.

The run then failed the frozen 30-second final idle acknowledgement. Its 3,945 request chunks reconstruct 488 receipts: initial state and all three snapshots for 20 syncs on each engine, but none of the eight required final receipts. The 29,077 native starts visible through the last recorded snapshots have matching terminal dispositions; requests resumed after those snapshots are outside that completed receipt prefix. Their final disposition is unavailable, so this is **not** a proof of whole-run conservation. W&B marks the run failed, and both the completion receipt and successful terminal manifest are absent.

The first failure was the final request-readback timeout at 19:27:09 UTC on September 8, 2026. Later metrics-endpoint connection failures occurred during teardown. Rank 0 used 1,040,757 ms on eight H100s; rank 1 is marked `cosched_failed` but still lacks a task/attempt finish timestamp. Its four-hour accounting reservation is not an observed duration or an actual-cost bound and does not delay another run. Total task cost and tokens per task H100-hour remain unresolved.

**What this means.** The workload exercises pause under a real backlog, and the final cleanup defect needs repair. The twenty measured syncs remain valid under the September 9 ruling; a final-accounting timeout after the last sync does not invalidate those measurements. A real-Ray CPU regression establishes that token-generation cancellation was not forwarded to the remote actor: the original path timed out, while routing it through the cancellation helper already used by chat stops the actor. This stress run does not establish production speedup, quality preservation, or a preferred admission-age range.

**Next.** Run the combined Snowball receiver readback and transport probe, then run the candidate with the cancellation fix and earliest first-token admission version. Keep the original baseline measurements and label the admission change when comparing the arms. Reconcile the missing task finish timestamp independently. The next milestone is completing telemetry and the pause fix (milestone 3).

🤖 Historical drift indicators do not establish a safe bound across 24 windows

**What we did and why.**

Before expanding the staleness ladder, this exploratory pilot (E4.5) tested whether existing indicators warned of the next decline in completed correctness. We reused six audited 100-update Qwen runs, all with training seed 17. Each prediction uses the preceding 20 updates and predicts the change between the current evaluation and the next one. This gives 24 dependent windows: five have a decline, and three decline by more than 2 percentage points.

The feature window, risk direction and two outcome definitions were fixed before calculating associations. Completed correctness uses the same audited verifier-plus-completed-stop endpoint as the historical reports. No new training ran. This informs the goal of faster Snowball training at the same answer quality.

**Results.**

| Indicator, fixed risk direction | AUROC: any next decline | AUROC: decline >2 pp |
|---|---:|---:|
| Lower legacy behavior-ratio ESS | 0.463 | 0.524 |
| Higher mean absolute log-ratio | 0.474 | 0.603 |
| Higher p99 absolute log-ratio | 0.442 | 0.619 |
| Higher mean squared log-ratio | 0.453 | 0.524 |
| Lower policy entropy | 0.547 | 0.619 |
| Higher raw gradient norm | 0.221 | 0.333 |
| Higher mean admitted age | 0.484 | 0.452 |

None of the available fixed-direction indicators reached AUROC 0.8 in this exploratory dataset. The whole-run bootstrap intervals are broad; for the primary endpoint, ESS is [0.159, 0.705], mean absolute log-ratio [0.206, 0.659], and low entropy [0.143, 0.798]. These intervals resample runs while retaining their dependent windows. They do not estimate variation across independent training seeds.

The existing ESS <0.5 flag never fired. A literal per-step mean-absolute-log-ratio >0.03 flag fired in two preceding windows; both were false alarms: 2/19, or 10.5%, for any subsequent decline. It missed all five declines. Applying the same threshold to each 20-update mean would erase both spikes, so that aggregation is reported separately.

The old worker absolute-log-ratio statistic is identically zero. Split stale-ratio ESS, split mismatch ESS, and gradient cosine are missing from these historical runs. In the new four-arm N1 correction screen, all 32 recorded stale-ESS values are exactly one, confirming that this particular statistic cannot discriminate rollout staleness when every batch has only one optimizer update.

All 7,800 native scalar values were recovered under exact run/job/region filters. Their 78 metric-family count/minimum/maximum/final summaries match the previous audited records in 312 checks. The pilot adds zero GPU-hours and zero optimizer updates; CPU analysis time was not separately benchmarked.

**What this means.**

The old indicators have not earned a predictive alert. The practical safe-bound rule is therefore closed for now: no predictive alert is adopted, and the ladders will be planned around the empirical quality knee. This is a design decision on the available evidence, not a universal statistical refutation. The held-out-seed AUROC ≥0.8 criterion remains untested; missing or structurally constant indicators remain untestable, not evidence of safety.

The legacy asynchronous behavior ratio combines engine mismatch and policy age. It must not be relabeled as either of the new split ratios. Type-A experiments need the actual split mismatch and age measurements; unit stale ESS in N1 is not a safe-bound signal. Health thresholds remain descriptive flags while the empirical quality knee and held-out-seed calibration determine the operating range.

**Next.**

Plan the staleness ladders around the empirical quality knee, with no predictive safe-bound alert. Keep the split-ratio and gradient-cosine telemetry and paired completed-score records so later held-out-seed evidence can reopen the rule. The next milestone is milestone 3, telemetry and pause fix landed.

<details><summary>Provenance</summary>

Historical six-arm source: the audited Qwen family `2026.09.06.16`, legacy GSM8K development battery of 128 questions, greedy evaluation at 0/20/40/60/80/100. This is an exploratory reanalysis of already observed runs, not a prospective training experiment. The historical source pairs and individual receipt URIs remain bound by `async-rl-v2-e0-audit-summary.json` and its per-run provenance; the analysis does not repin old runs.

Feature means use updates `(t−20,t]` at t=20/40/60/80; outcome is completed score at t+20 minus that at t. Startup→20 is excluded because no preceding training window exists. Risk directions are fixed; thresholds are not fitted. Whole-run bootstrap: 5,000 draws, seed 20260909; draws without both labels are omitted (4,913 valid primary draws, 4,569 sensitivity draws). The held-out-seed criterion remains untested.

Reproducible analysis: Marin analysis `fa612d1f16ae69f72042dee9b3442c9fc90dd569`, decision-wording follow-up `bb248dbade`, followed by the metadata-only operating decision in `bb248dbade`, `experiments/post_training/async_rl_indicator_audit.py`. 🤖 Two dormant correction masks stay within the observed seed noise

**What we did and why.**

For the fresh-data correction check (K12 N1), we ran eight synchronous Qwen3-0.6B updates with one optimizer update per rollout batch: behavior clipping at seeds 17 and 29, plus the off-policy mask and M2 mask at seed 17. This checks that enabling either transform leaves fresh-data updates numerically well behaved before testing stale data, toward faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. All arms used the same frozen legacy GSM8K train/dev recipe, 64 prompts × 4 responses per update, and greedy evaluation on 128 fixed questions at updates 0 and 8. Completed correctness means verifier-correct with an accepted completion stop.

**Results.**

| Arm | Final raw / completed correct | Length stops | Consumed response tokens | Core seconds | Task H100-hours |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| [Behavior clipping, seed 17](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/cbj0t3hi) | 70 / 70 of 128 | 4 / 128 | 316,946 | 79.330 | 1.606573 |
| [Behavior clipping, seed 29](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/erwlke3h) | 73 / 73 of 128 | 1 / 128 | 320,530 | 77.822 | 1.617778 |
| [Off-policy mask, seed 17](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/fhkcj239) | 72 / 72 of 128 | 3 / 128 | 317,920 | 78.919 | 1.619433 |
| [M2 mask, seed 17](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/wb97dzqc) | 69 / 69 of 128 | 3 / 128 | 318,745 | 78.571 | 1.632293 |

Both masks removed exactly zero tokens in the reported update metrics, and M2's pre-mask squared log-ratio statistic was zero. All four arms completed eight successful optimizer updates with positive gradients; each retained all 14 correction fields in both the batch aggregate and update-specific W&B records. The minimum raw gradient norm across the arms was 0.75685. These correction fields describe the last microbatch and rank mean; they are not token-pooled fractions for the whole update.

The frozen engineering noise band was the absolute difference between the two behavior-clipping seeds: 3/128, or 2.34375 percentage points. The off-policy mask differed from seed 17 by +1.5625 pp, with a paired 97.5% interval of [−4.6875, +7.8125] pp. M2 differed by −0.78125 pp, with [−8.59375, +7.03125] pp. Both meet the absolute noise-band rule. The intervals use 50,000 paired-question resamples and Bonferroni adjustment across these two contrasts for nominal 95% joint coverage, conditional on the observed training seeds.

The four runs used 6.476078 task H100-hours. All eight GPU tasks succeeded on their sole scheduler attempt. Retained hub logs contain no startup port-retry messages, but the incomplete telemetry coverage below prevents a whole-job zero-engine-death claim.

**What this means.**

The fresh-data numerical and final-score checks pass. This is an engineering check, not a non-inferiority result or a ranking of corrections. Zero masking here does not prove an active masking formula: the separate native numerical fixtures supplied that proof with nonzero retained gradients and actual parameter changes.

The full native telemetry audit is incomplete. The central query currently returns 23 of the expected 32 source-order events and eight of the expected 16 role-terminal receipts; every available terminal reports zero lost records. W&B and durable evaluation receipts cover all eight updates, but they cannot replace the missing complete source vectors and terminal counters. A direct regional query found neither the semantic training namespace nor its legacy parent namespace. This establishes a retrieval gap, not a correction or exporter failure. No full native telemetry gate or matched source-order union proof has been asserted.

**Next.**

Run a separately labeled eight-updates-per-batch M2 mechanism diagnostic using the numerical and fresh-data checks established here, with its own native coverage checks. The comparison of its full prompt set against all eight fresh-data batches remains unqualified while those source vectors are missing. The historical indicator pilot now supports planning the ladders around the empirical quality knee. The next milestone remains telemetry and pause fix landed.
