🤖 K18-D1 native gate: the D1 candidate fails both operands as written, and the second failure is the informative one — under the gate's own geometry no rollout was ever aborted at a weight sync (abort count 0 on every step, version spread 0 on every update), so the per-token version tags D1 adds had nothing to tag; the reward-band operand also fails, but a min/max band of three controls passes an identical run only 6% of the time over four cohorts

**What we did and why.** K18-D1 carries per-token policy-version tags through the existing abort-and-resubmit partial-rollout path, so that a group whose generation straddles a weight sync records which tokens came from which policy version. Shared promotion of D1 was gated on a native run: Qwen3-0.6B, C1/A1/N2, eight optimizer updates (four cohorts), P8 TP2 + I8 on RNO, three pre-change controls (seeds 17, 29, 43, control runtime `2750c83f` = shared 65fa9170 plus the staging-retry hunks) and one D1 candidate (seed 17, native runtime `a34d40c5` = control plus the D1 commit, patch-identical to `4a71789c`). The pass line, frozen before the candidate was released: every candidate update's admission reward inside the per-cohort min/max band of the three controls, never widened; at least one consumed update with `async/version_spread_max ≥ 1`; token-age fractions summing to one over the known tokens with coverage stated; schema-4 retained records validating through the frozen reader. Stage 1 froze the band from the three finished controls (identity by completion fingerprint, history read twice) and the candidate was launched bound to the band's digest; stage 2 evaluated it.

**Results.** Candidate `d1-seed17` ran clean (two tasks, one attempt each, zero failures, zero preemptions, on the same two physical nodes as control-seed17).

| cohort (updates) | candidate reward | band [min, max] | controls s17 / s29 / s43 | inside |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (1, 2) | 0.18199 | [−0.00142, 0.15390] | 0.15390 / 0.08841 / −0.00142 | no, above by 0.028 |
| 3 (3, 4) | 0.17302 | [0.18176, 0.20579] | 0.20579 / 0.19019 / 0.18176 | no, below by 0.009 |
| 5 (5, 6) | 0.31926 | [0.27083, 0.29098] | 0.27083 / 0.29086 / 0.29098 | no, above by 0.028 |
| 7 (7, 8) | 0.35091 | [0.34026, 0.39863] | 0.34026 / 0.38976 / 0.39863 | yes |

Version evidence, all eight updates: `async/version_spread_max` = 0 (mean 0); `async/staleness_newest_mean` 0, 1, 0.25, 1.19, 0.5, 1.5, 0.31, 1.25; `async/token_age_frac/{0,1,2,3plus}` sum to 1.0 at every update with `known_token_fraction` 1.0 (431,727 known loss tokens, 0 unknown) and complete-group fraction 1.0; `response_abort_count` = 0 at every step with abort-evidence fraction 1.0. Schema-4 retention: 188 archives, 297 records, 0 reader errors, 297/297 complete version runs, 0 null abort counts. Staging 6.9–7.7 s per node on all four arms. `K18_D1_GATE_FAIL reason=reward_outside_band`; the frozen reader's `validate_consumed_versions` raises `No consumed mixed-version evidence` independently.

**What this means.** Two separate things. First, the gate's geometry never exercised the code D1 changes: with C1/A1 and these response lengths, no in-flight rollout straddled a weight sync, the abort-and-resubmit path fired zero times, every consumed group carried a single policy version, and the tags were all trivially correct; the age fractions and the schema-4 records show the plumbing works end to end (known-token coverage 1.0, complete version runs on every record) but say nothing about mixed-version groups, which is what D1 is for. The gate cannot pass as specified until its geometry produces aborts, and that is a design correction, not a D1 defect. Second, the reward-band operand as written has no power at three controls: a null fourth run falls outside a min/max band of three exchangeable samples with probability 2/(n+1) = 1/2 per cohort, so it stays inside all four cohorts with probability 1/16; the candidate's one-of-four inside, missing above at two cohorts and below at one while sharing seed 17 with a control that itself sits at the band edge, is what a null draw looks like. The band was not widened and will not be; what it needs is more controls or an interval rule, which is a ruling above this session. D1 is not promoted by this run; nothing here argues against it either.

**Next.** Re-freeze the gate with a geometry that produces aborts (a sync interval shorter than the generation length, or forced abort at the boundary, so `response_abort_count > 0` and `version_spread_max ≥ 1` are reachable) and a band rule with stated power (more controls, or a tolerance interval) before the candidate is released again; the controls' histories and the candidate's archives are durable and can be reused for any re-analysis that does not change the rule after the fact.

🤖 All 12 correction runs crossed the 0.1-nat entropy stop threshold

**What we did and why.** We compared six off-policy correction methods at two rollout-age settings on Qwen3-0.6B, as a screen for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. The correction comparison (E4.3) is class R: the experiment decides whether any correction qualifies for selection. The first seed ran 96 optimizer updates per configuration, with two disjoint optimizer minibatches per prepared cohort and development evaluation every 32 updates.

**Results.** All 12 runs completed their requested updates, but every configuration crossed the pre-specified policy-entropy stop threshold. Each consumed the same 6,144 prompt groups and 24,576 responses. The 12 conditional second-seed runs are closed without launch because their first-seed configurations failed that scientific gate.

| Correction | Minimum entropy at age setting 1 / 2, nats | Updates below 0.1 at setting 1 / 2, out of 96 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Behavior clipping | 0.071165591 / 0.080584244 | 12 / 7 |
| Regular objective | 0.083199000 / 0.084338995 | 11 / 16 |
| Regular + capped importance sampling | 0.078978268 / 0.087671585 | 13 / 8 |
| Regular + importance-weight mask | 0.074850183 / 0.087887925 | 16 / 5 |
| Behavior clipping + importance-weight mask | 0.089487072 / 0.099840082 | 12 / 1 |
| Regular + M2 objective | 0.060714210 / 0.089728169 | 29 / 5 |

The two age settings produced distinct consumed-group distributions in every correction pair: mean age 0.958333333 versus 2.333333333 optimizer updates, with group-weighted 95th percentiles of 2 versus 3. The entropy measurement is actual policy vocabulary entropy; disabled diagnostic zeros were excluded. The runs continued to update 96 despite the observed stop condition.

Final held-out eight-draw completed correctness, semantic correctness and paired quality confidence intervals remain unavailable for all 12 runs. Native development scores were collected, but have not been joined to the frozen question-level harness evidence and do not support correction ranking. There is no selected correction or demonstrated quality-adjusted speedup.

**What this means.** This comparison concludes with 12 scientific failures and 12 conditional cells closed without launch. No method met the required health criterion, so the current behavior-clipping recipe remains an unselected baseline. The entropy failures prevent a clean correction recommendation; the realised-age separation alone does not establish how much staleness preserves answer quality.

**Next.** Carry the negative correction disposition into the cadence comparison and preserve the retained checkpoints for the outstanding held-out audit. The next correction milestone, “correction chosen and safe-bound rule,” remains incomplete; it must report that no correction qualified under this protocol.

🤖 Optimizer storage halves to 6 bytes per parameter; both 32-GPU learners fit

**What we did and why.** We compared Snowball's native optimizer with bf16 moments and
16-bit parameter remainders to measure how much learner memory the smaller state saves
(E7.2 3.2). Both arms ran five synchronous updates on 32 training and eight inference H100s
in RNO, with the same seed and frozen recipe. Reduced-precision moments are class T: this
memory test informs a tradeoff and does not establish answer-quality equivalence. The
separate class X remainders replay still owns the byte-equality qualification.

**Results.** All ten original GPU tasks and both coordinators succeeded. An independent
Finelog query reproduced the collector's exact row hashes and its complete memory panel:
32 ranks, four phases, five updates, 480 measured phase exits per arm, and five distinct
once-per-node staging receipts per arm. There were no memory-threshold excursions.

| Measured quantity | Native optimizer | bf16 moments + remainders |
|---|---:|---:|
| Updates / seed | 5 / 17 | 5 / 17 |
| Optimizer state, bytes per owned parameter | 12.0 | 6.0 |
| Maximum optimizer state per rank, GiB | 23.427 | 11.714 |
| PPO peak allocated / reserved, GiB | 56.673 / 57.322 | 55.382 / 56.871 |
| Learner log-probability forward peak allocated, GiB | 53.817 | 42.102 |
| Weight-sync peak allocated / reserved, GiB | 58.099 / 61.732 | 46.387 / 56.090 |
| Model-ready allocated, GiB | 35.264 | 27.455 |
| Minimum device free at a phase exit, GiB | 7.569 | 4.771 |
| Sum of five core step intervals, seconds | 349.768417 | 354.990983 |
| Training duration p50, seconds | 6.136462 | 6.624321 |
| Weight-sync duration p50, seconds | 12.246959 | 11.580481 |
| Response tokens selected for training | 813,606 | 816,222 |
| Task GPU-hours, including startup and evaluation | 10.774180 | 10.960813 |
| Per-node dataset-ready to model-ready interval, seconds | 181.452–188.923 | 179.874–190.216 |
| Minimum fraction of exactly unit behavior ratios | 0.007578094489872456 | 0.007396275876089931 |
| Retained learner-to-learner maximum absolute log-ratio, every step | 0 | 0 |

Total task GPU-hours were **21.734993**. The native state inventory reports fp32 master,
first moment and second moment; the candidate reports int16 remainder storage and bf16
moments, rather than a resident fp32 master tensor. The state reduction is 6 bytes per
parameter. It does not translate directly into the same reduction in peak allocated memory
or device-free memory. These are single-seed memory observations; no confidence interval or
quality ranking is inferred from five updates. Completed correctness, semantic score and
truncation were not independently harness-audited here and are not reported as quality results.

The core interval is the frozen synchronous trainer's `step` span: generation through the
post-update weight sync, excluding callback evaluation, checkpointing and startup. Training
and sync medians use all five measured updates, including the first. These are the original
non-shard sync runner's timings; they are not measurements of the expert-block transport.
Token counts are the positive loss-mask response tokens, independently equal in the retained
generation-alignment, learner-monitor and age-zero mismatch counts at each update; all
1,629,828 selected tokens across the pair are age zero on that telemetry.

The CPU collector's two attempts both emitted identical complete results and then exited 1.
Its frozen pair verdict remains **FAIL**: the approved card and collector require the named
exact-unit fraction to equal 1.0, which neither arm meets. The failure is not a missing row,
failed native execution or memory exhaustion. It is a mismatch between the requested
identity check and the configured loss's ratio operand.

**What this means.** Both configurations satisfy the measured memory thresholds at 32
training GPUs. The behavior-clipped loss explicitly discards recomputed old learner log
probabilities and calculates its ratio from current training probabilities divided by vLLM
rollout probabilities. Synchronous policy versions do not require those different engines
to emit bitwise-equal probabilities. Its exact-unit fraction therefore cannot serve as the
intended learner-forward identity check. The collector reads that metric faithfully; its
interpretation as “sync C1 identity” is the defect. The same requirement occurs in the
approved design, so this audit does not silently replace it or claim its literal gate passed.

There is separate positive identity evidence already retained: the learner monitor compares
the actual training forward with recomputed old learner probabilities. At all five updates
in both arms its maximum absolute log-ratio is exactly zero, validity is 1, diagnostics-failed
is 0, and selected-token counts are positive. The update-index-zero monitor independently
agrees. This evidence is reported separately from the failed named behavior-ratio criterion.
A CPU counterexample reproduces exact learner identity with a behavior exact-unit fraction
of 0.5; changing the old learner operand leaves the behavior metric unchanged, and mutating
its denominator to the old learner operand makes the counterexample fail.

Neither arm is rejected for memory. The approved rule rejects allocated memory above 72 GiB
or device-free memory below 3 GiB only at the same phase exit on two of three repeats;
reserved-only excursions are remeasured with `expandable_segments`. Neither arm crossed any
of those limits, including the retained collector's diagnostic reserved threshold of 76 GiB.
The five updates and 32 ranks are not independent repeats. No memory repeat is triggered by
these observations, and a ratio failure cannot count as a memory repeat. This result alone
does not establish that 16 training GPUs fit or adopt the precision setting.

**Next.** Conclude the pair as an audited failure of the frozen named criterion, with the
memory and retained learner-identity subresults recorded as passing. Preserve the precision
choice for the measured gradient comparison and the smaller-learner evidence. The next
milestone is the learner-size decision. No GPU rerun is needed to collect or explain this
pair. A bounded CPU-only collector revision can expose separate `frozen_verdict`,
`memory_verdict`, `learner_identity_verdict` and `behavior_ratio_diagnostic` fields, retaining
the original receipt and all identity/coverage checks. It must not turn the frozen verdict
into PASS or relax a tolerance. A change to the approved named done-when belongs to Ahmad;
it does not hold unrelated queue work or prevent this failed group from concluding.

🤖 16 learner GPUs exhausted memory before completing 1 update with FP32 gradient reduction

**What we did and why.** We tested whether Snowball could use 16 learner GPUs and
24 inference GPUs, freeing more of the allocation for answer generation. The two
40-H100 runs compared expert-block weight sync with the full-broadcast reference,
using the same BF16 optimizer moments, parameter remainders and FP32 gradient
reduction. The precision package is class T; the transport is class X and still
requires its separate byte-equality and timing gate.

**Results.** Both runs reached the first rollout batch and failed inside the first
optimizer step while allocating Adam's first-moment state. The training progress
remained at 0 of 20 completed updates. These are scientific trainer-memory failures;
the later metrics-connection errors and gang teardown did not initiate the failures.

| Arm | Completed updates | Failed allocation | Device free at failure | PyTorch allocated at failure | PyTorch reserved but unallocated |

whole-device PyTorch usage. Each device reported 79.18 GiB capacity; total process
usage including non-PyTorch memory was 79.17 and 79.16 GiB respectively. Each run
completed one rollout batch of 32 groups and 128 responses before training failed.

steady-state core time or 20-update transport result exists. Exact task GPU-hours

three identical repeats, so this result does not by itself satisfy the formal

**What we did and why.** We audited the retained 16-arm Qwen vLLM knob sweep (E5.5), including its gang orphan, to identify generator settings that could support faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. The runs offered 128 requests per inference engine, with two control seeds and one seed for each changed setting. This closes the retained-evidence audit as an **operational evidence-contract failure**, with useful timing and speculation observations; it does not qualify an adopted setting or admit the orphan as a scientifically complete run.

**Results.**

The two speed columns and core seconds are arithmetic means over trainer updates 2–5, as frozen. The first speed metric counts **consumed** response tokens over the full cycle, not standalone generation capacity. Task GPU-hours include startup and shutdown according to controller attempt timestamps.

The 14 changed settings yielded **0 joint ≥5% speed candidates**, **12 with both absolute effects below 5%**, and **2 mixed outcomes** (sequence limit 16 and batched-token limit 2,048). The two control seeds differed by +0.66% and −3.97% on the respective speed metrics. None of these single-seed effects has a confidence interval; the control repeat is not a sampling distribution. All 16 arms reported zero request preemptions. Mean buffer-wait fractions over updates 2–5 were 0.134–0.177%, so consumed throughput must not be called inference capacity.

Controller-accounted cost was **27.6932 H100 GPU-hours** across 32 attempts: 25.9103 for the 15 ordinary arms and 1.7829 for the orphan. This is a sum of `8 × (attempt_finished_ms − attempt_started_ms) / 3,600,000`, never coordinator wall time. The orphan's worker ended with `PodDeleted`, so 1.7829 is controller-attempt accounting, **not verified physical allocation release**. CPU history, preflight and failed exception jobs contribute zero GPU-hours.

Stage-1 speculation counters, cumulative through update 6:

| Plain n-gram setting | Drafts | Draft tokens | Accepted tokens | Acceptance rate | Accepted draft tokens/draft | Mean emitted length including bonus |

These are process-lifetime cumulative engine counters as sampled at update 6, not summed snapshots or isolated update-2–5 deltas. They may include startup evaluation and generation outside consumed training. Plain `ngram` disables async scheduling while the control retains it; therefore this is not a clean estimate of speculation's latency benefit. The Snowball stage-2 comparison is separately designed around `ngram_gpu`.

**What this means.** Retain the existing defaults: sequence limit 1,024, GPU memory utilization 0.75, batched-token limit 8,192, prefix caching on, speculation off. No class X/T setting is qualified by this audit. The speed-only threshold rejects 12 changed settings in this short measurement and leaves two conflicting results; the required reward veto is **not evaluable**, rather than passed or failed scientifically.

The reward defect affects the whole sweep, not just the orphan. All 15 recovered W&B histories lack `reward/avg_raw_reward` on updates 1–6, and their initial evaluation rows lack every step key accepted by the frozen reducer. The orphan's original stdout confirms the same namespace/cadence mismatch. Native N2 emits whole-cohort raw rewards as `async/cohort_preparation/reward/avg_raw_reward` only at steps 1, 3 and 5, while `loss/avg_final_rewards` describes each consumed partition. Substituting either into the registered per-update raw-reward check changes the statistic; no such substitution was made.

A second correction matters for work accounting: the manifest's “6 steps = 12 optimizer updates” is wrong for this runtime. The source requires exactly one successful optimizer update before each global-step advance; three cohorts × two partitions produce **six optimizer updates**. The orphan's Finelog rows independently report one successful valid optimizer update at every step 1–6. The frozen manifest is preserved as launch evidence.

**Next.** Stage-1 counter collection is complete and **unlocks Snowball speculation stage 2**, subject to its existing runtime and matched-packet checks. Compose the approved k=3/k=5/control comparison with `ngram_gpu`, raw logprobs and standard rejection sampling. This result does not adopt speculation. A future repair of the original reward/dump audit would need a reviewed scientific mapping and retained-object access; neither an identical CPU-audit retry nor a GPU rerun repairs the current evidence contract. 🤖 Sixteen inference GPUs used 23.4% more GPU-hours across 25 Snowball updates

**What we did and why.** The Snowball worker-split experiment (E5.2) compared P32/I8 with P32/I16 to identify an efficient allocation for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. Both runs used C1/A1/N1, seed 17, 32 prompts × four samples, and the shard synchronization path with proofs disabled. Each completed 25 updates; the first five were reserved for calibration and updates 6–25 for prediction validation.

**Results.**

|---|---:|---:|

| Successful original GPU tasks | 5/5 | 6/6 |
| Consumed loss/response tokens | 3,607,337 | 4,241,875 |
| Core seconds, all 25 updates | 955.647181 | 997.900548 |
| Mean core seconds/update | 38.225887 | 39.916022 |
| Core seconds, updates 1–5 | 216.376953 | 221.540670 |
| Core seconds, updates 6–25 | 739.270228 | 776.359878 |
| Cycle seconds | 957.839244 | 1,001.824993 |
| Whole task-allocation elapsed seconds¹ | 1,539.132 | 1,585.101 |

| Consumed tokens/core second | 3,774.758167 | 4,250.799348 |
| Consumed training sequences | 3,200 | 3,200 |
| Training length stops | 132 (4.125%) | 223 (6.96875%) |
| Training stop-reason coverage | 100% | 100% |

³ Arithmetic mean of the 25 per-update ESS fractions, not a newly pooled token-level ESS.

The timer records have complete 25-update coverage:

|---|---:|---:|
| `run_training` | 238.99819250963628 | 244.2718119006604 |

The independently emitted phase windows give publication/core shares of 15.593625% / 16.944301%, buffer-wait/core shares of 58.762565% / 57.871811%, and training/core shares of 25.008399% / 24.477991% for I8/I16. Their window boundaries differ slightly from the named timers; do not interchange the numerators. Full shard install/freeze/finish and proof-timer decomposition was not audited.

| Recorded rollout outcome | I8 groups / tokens | I16 groups / tokens |
|---|---:|---:|
| Consumed | 800 / 3,607,337 | 800 / 4,241,875 |
| Stale at dequeue | 72 / 687,611 | 56 / 528,824 |
| Stale at enqueue | 31 / 280,758 | 24 / 205,720 |
| Epoch discarded | 11 / 51,989 | 7 / 32,829 |

These are finalized rollout outcome counters. They do not establish complete engine-generated-token conservation, including unfinished or cancelled requests.

Evaluation failed before scoring. At the frozen runtime, `BasePPOExp.get_eval_dataset()` creates validation data only when `trainer.eval_interval > 0`; otherwise it returns `None`. Both envelopes set `eval_interval=-1`. The async driver skips evaluation when its dataset is `None`, even when the callback requests it. Consistently, the audited telemetry contains zero `eval/*` training metric rows and precisely initial publication plus 25 training publications per arm, with no evaluation publication. Expected dev input staging is present, but staging the input does not execute evaluation.

There is one run per arm, and no audited uncertainty interval or first-five-fit/remaining-twenty prediction result. The table is descriptive.

**What this means.** I16 used 23.4381% more task GPU-hours and 4.4214% more core time, while consuming 17.5902% more tokens. Its higher tokens/core-second rate therefore does not establish faster equal-work training, and the different consumed trajectories preclude treating this as a matched-reference timing pair. Keep the measurements, but leave the worker-split recommendation and the decision to close I16 undecided. The required evaluations and prediction validation remain unmet.

**Next.** Resolve the evaluation dataset guard and the missing native-dump-to-harness binding before making any quality statement. Complete the retained-counter throughput fit and its updates 6–25 validation before recommending an allocation for the system-balance milestone.

🤖 Snowball weight sync takes 5.76 s end to end with proofs off; transfer and install take 0.52 s

**What we did and why.** We measured the complete weight-sync interval to understand its remaining cost in faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. This proofs-off interval experiment (K10) ran Snowball 67B-A2B for 20 updates on 40 H100s: 32 Megatron policy GPUs (TP1/PP2/EP8) and 8 vLLM inference GPUs (DP8/EP8), on RNO. It used cadence 1, maximum age 1, one update per batch, seed 17, 32 prompts × 4 responses, 4,096 output tokens, 8,192 context tokens, learning rate 1e-6 and behavior clipping. We compared the durable phase receipts with native stdout, original task identities, completion evidence and Finelog; the earlier proofs-on pair supplies the full-byte qualification.

**Results.** All 20 updates and all five native tasks succeeded without a retry or preemption. Times below are seconds; the 95% intervals are exploratory within-run circular moving-block bootstrap intervals (block length 4, five blocks, 20,000 draws, seed 20260912). They describe this one sequential run and are neither between-seed uncertainty nor a paired speedup interval.

🤖 Newest-first admission lowers rollout age by 0.11–0.17 updates, but two seeds do not establish a quality gain

**What we did and why.** We tested whether changing which queued rollouts enter training can reduce their age while preserving answer quality and prompt diversity, as a step toward faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. This admission-order experiment (E5.3) is a class T lever because it changes the selected training trajectory. On Qwen3-0.6B, we compared first-in-first-out (FIFO) with last-in-first-out (LIFO) at seeds 17 and 29, and also screened freshest-first and age-weighted admission at seed 17. Each run used eight learner and eight inference H100s for 96 updates, with 64 prompt groups and four responses per group per update, publication cadence four and maximum admitted age four updates.

**Results.**

All six runs completed 96 updates. Age is the number of learner updates since generation of the first token; token mean weights each group's age by its consumed response-token count. Every optimizer batch retained 64 distinct canonical prompts, so the predeclared LIFO diversity kill of a drop strictly greater than 20% did not fire. Each run consumed 6,144 groups; all generated groups and response tokens reconcile to their terminal outcomes.

| Policy | Seed | Mean group age | Mean token age | Group / token age p95 | Stale groups discarded | Core seconds | Task H100-hours | Completed correct at update 96 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| FIFO | 17 | 2.458333 | 2.650071 | 4 / 4 | 0 | 559.999312 | 4.153762 | 145/256 |
| LIFO | 17 | 2.352214 | 2.240484 | 4 / 4 | 163 | 562.164481 | 4.033496 | 145/256 |
| Freshest-first | 17 | 2.341797 | 2.549011 | 4 / 4 | 179 | 567.203987 | 4.069702 | 156/256 |
| Age-weighted | 17 | 2.336589 | 2.372370 | 4 / 4 | 187 | 554.104825 | 4.034469 | 159/256 |
| FIFO | 29 | 2.458333 | 2.642055 | 4 / 4 | 0 | 561.758307 | 4.080498 | 148/256 |
| LIFO | 29 | 2.288411 | 2.174998 | 4 / 4 | 261 | 567.408816 | 4.178353 | 173/256 |

Against matched FIFO, LIFO lowered mean group age by 0.106120 updates at seed 17 and 0.169922 at seed 29; mean token age fell by 0.409587 and 0.467057 updates. LIFO did not lower core time in either pair. The six runs used 24.550280 task H100-hours in total, calculated from actual task-attempt start and finish times. Core seconds cover the measured training core; allocation includes the rest of each task's lifetime. These age and timing differences are fixed-update observations on different trajectories, with no uncertainty intervals or quality-adjusted speedup established.

The scoring session recovered all 24 dev evaluation points and 6,144 per-question rows through the pinned harness, using W&B as the independent metric reference. At update 96, LIFO minus FIFO on completed correctness is +0.0488. The question-resampled fixed-seed interval is [+0.0078, +0.0898], but the population interval across questions and observed training seeds is [−0.0352, +0.1367]. These are score-proportion differences and Bonferroni simultaneous percentile intervals at family alpha 0.05, using 10,000 bootstrap resamples. The whole observed gain comes from seed 29: the per-seed deltas are 0/256 and +25/256 (0.0000 and +0.0977). With only two observed training seeds, the population interval is the relevant decision evidence and includes zero; it does not establish behavior across a broader seed population. The seed-17 freshest-first and age-weighted contrasts also have intervals including zero at update 96. This is dev-256 evidence, not held-out evidence.

**What this means.** LIFO reduced the measured age of consumed rollouts in both matched seeds and preserved prompt diversity, but it discarded stale work, did not improve core time and did not establish a population-level answer-quality gain. No admission-order winner is selected and FIFO remains the default.

**Next.** Carry FIFO into the system-balance configuration and combine this result with the remaining cadence and resource-split studies for the system balance measured milestone. The final Snowball comparison will measure cadence, off-policy age, speed and held-out completed correctness on the chosen stopping package.

🤖 Speculative decoding saves only 0.523% of Snowball core time and worsens the slowest rollout groups

**What we did and why.** We tested whether proposing several tokens at once could deliver faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. This class T timing experiment compared speculation off with GPU n-gram proposals of three or five tokens. Each arm ran 25 updates with the same seed, 32 training GPUs and 8 inference GPUs, with native evaluations before and after training. The prespecified timing requirement was at least 10% improvement in both core time and rollout-group tail time.

**Results.** All three native arms completed their 25 updates successfully. Core time sums the training loop's measured core intervals; task GPU-hours include the full allocation of the five native tasks, including staging and evaluation.

| Arm | Core seconds | Change in core time | Task GPU-hours | Consumed response tokens |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Speculation off | 4,894.817773 | Reference | 64.777171 | 3,759,171 |
| Three-token proposals | 4,934.755394 | 0.815916% slower | 65.326487 | 3,693,246 |
| Five-token proposals | 4,869.219389 | 0.522969% faster | 64.563913 | 3,311,280 |

Tail time is the gap between the first and last response finishing within a group of four responses. These quantiles describe the 800 consumed rollout groups in each arm; they are percentiles, not confidence intervals.

| Arm | Tail mean (s) | Tail p50 (s) | Tail p95 (s) | Tail p99 (s) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Speculation off | 13.835998 | 9.761425 | 35.080760 | 39.745393 |
| Three-token proposals | 15.658771 | 10.555822 | 41.185270 | 45.418646 |
| Five-token proposals | 14.354397 | 9.304171 | 42.115421 | 46.355922 |

Five-token proposals improved median tail time by 4.684301%, but worsened p95 by 20.052759% and p99 by 16.632189%. They consumed 11.914622% fewer response tokens while barely reducing core time, so this comparison does not establish a gain at matched output volume. Three-token proposals worsened core time and every reported tail summary.

Across the full process, including both native evaluations, three-token proposals accepted 1,766,802 of 11,381,223 drafted tokens (15.523833%); five-token proposals accepted 1,682,810 of 16,623,020 (10.123371%). These are differences of cumulative counters, not sums of repeated snapshots. Exact throughput per request is unavailable.

No confidence interval across seeds or paired completed-correctness interval is available. The native aggregate evaluation diagnostics have not been joined to the original response rows and evaluation harness; completed correctness, semantic quality and truncation therefore have no qualified comparison here. The historical matched control seed band for importance-ratio drift is also unavailable. The three-token arm's auxiliary coordinator failed after its native child had succeeded; the retained original tasks and measurements remain valid.

**What this means.** Speculation remains off: neither candidate met the 10% core-and-tail requirement in this screen, and the better core-time candidate made the upper tail worse. This concludes the class T timing decision; the full quality card remains incomplete, so there is no quality-equivalence claim, adoption, or final training-speedup claim.

**Next.** Carry the speculation-off decision into the combined system-balance analysis while the remaining balance experiments are concluded. The next milestone is system balance measured.

🤖 Parameter remainders save 2 bytes per parameter with exact agreement after 10 updates

**What we did and why.** We checked whether storing the low bits of each parameter can reduce optimizer memory while preserving the full-precision update, a class X (exact) lever toward faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. The update-ten remainders check (K14/K29) re-audited a retained native two-H100 execution of the actual Megatron/Transformer Engine optimizer on a synthetic 256 × 256 matrix. It compared FP32 optimizer moments plus 16-bit parameter remainders against the precision-aware FP32-master control, with the same FP32 gradients and moments. This required no new GPU allocation.

**Results.**

| Rank | Weight decay | FP32 master elements compared | BF16 model elements compared | Mismatched master / model elements |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0 | 32,768 | 65,536 | 0 / 0 |
| 0 | 0.01 | 32,768 | 65,536 | 0 / 0 |
| 1 | 0 | 32,768 | 65,536 | 0 / 0 |
| 1 | 0.01 | 32,768 | 65,536 | 0 / 0 |

The native comparison covered every master and model bit: 262,144 bytes per rank/decay cell, or 1,048,576 compared bytes across the four cells, with 100% operand coverage. These are exhaustive checks of the retained operands, so a statistical confidence interval does not apply. All 20 embedded arm receipts matched their independently retained hashes, and every recorded gradient-shard oracle passed.

The remainders configuration retained 327,684 optimizer bytes per rank, versus 393,220 for the FP32-master control: exactly **2 bytes saved per owned parameter** in every cell. Both sides ran ten small-learning-rate updates at 1e-6, following a separate zero-gradient decay diagnostic at 1e-3. The original native execution used 0.084612 H100-hours; that historical allocation is reused as evidence and is not counted again.

**What this means.** Keep the exact remainders mechanism for this tested FP32-moment configuration. The broader combination with BF16 moments has a separate memory result; this comparison does not establish that BF16 moments reproduce FP32-moment arithmetic. At update ten the reconstructed masters moved, but the BF16 model changed-bit count was zero in every cell, so this is a mechanism proof rather than evidence of useful learning. It establishes neither Snowball/expert-parallel qualification, checkpoint resharding, nor answer-quality equivalence.

**Next.** Carry this scoped proof into the combined milestone on weight sync cut at least fourfold with bit-identical proof. Keep its optimizer-memory claim separate from the measured weight-sync speedup and the final quality comparison.

🤖 Standalone serving underpredicts training batch time by 19.1–26.0%

**What we did and why.** The inference-throughput study (E5.2) tested whether a controlled
serving measurement could predict training time and guide the policy-to-inference GPU ratio
for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. We ran one frozen
Qwen3-0.6B engine on one RNO H100 at requested concurrency 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and 256,
then fit `lambda_I(c) = lambda_max * c / (c + c_half)`. The audited collector used that curve
to re-predict batch time for four earlier trainer arms at their realised concurrency.
This is **class R research**: the ratio study decides whether the predictor supports a recommendation.

**Results.** All seven serving points passed their identity, steady-window and response checks.
The fit gave `lambda_max = 57,458.8` generated tokens/s/engine, `c_half = 106.34`, and maximum
absolute relative residual `0.128`.

| Requested c | Median running requests | Generated tokens/s |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 | 4.0 | 2,388.0 |
| 8 | 8.0 | 4,486.0 |
| 16 | 16.0 | 7,667.3 |
| 32 | 32.0 | 13,392.0 |
| 64 | 63.0 | 21,189.2 |
| 128 | 126.0 | 30,848.2 |
| 256 | 252.5 | 40,647.9 |

At the four trainer arms' realised concurrency, the resulting batch-time predictions were within
15% for **0/4 arms**. They underpredicted measured time by 19.1% to 26.0%. The same check at
nominal concurrency was also 0/4. None of the realised points was extrapolated below the sweep.

| Trainer setting | Realised requests per engine | Predicted batch s | Measured batch s | Prediction error |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 64 generation workers | 7.0000 | 11.023 | 14.897 | −26.0% |
| 128 generation workers | 9.0000 | 12.400 | 15.490 | −19.9% |
| 256 generation workers | 5.0625 | 12.381 | 15.459 | −19.9% |
| 256 generation workers, engine limit 16 sequences | 7.6875 | 13.192 | 16.315 | −19.1% |

Here a batch spans two optimizer updates; measured time is the median of the three batches
after the warm-up batch. These are single-run point estimates, with no confidence intervals.

**What this means.** The standalone curve fits the serving measurements, but its batch-time
predictions fail the training check. The Qwen ratio study closes as a negative result with
**no policy-to-inference ratio recommendation**. The standalone server and trainer used different
vLLM builds, and the model classified all four predictions as learner-bound, making the predicted
batch times insensitive to the tested inference concurrency. This check does not isolate the
cause of the prediction error or establish the trainer's actual bottleneck.

**Next.** Combine this negative result with the [completed Snowball ratio study](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5649672543)
at the **system balance measured** milestone. Use native training measurements when choosing
the Snowball configuration for the final comparison.

🤖 Non-expert export takes 0.075 seconds in the two-layer probe

**What we did and why.** We decomposed weight export to find where further work could help faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. This observation supports the class X, exact-overlap investigation (K11): it measures the existing export path and changes no production behavior. A randomly initialized, Snowball-width model with two decoder layers ran through the real Megatron exporter and streaming bucket packer on two H100s in one node, with three parallelism/filter configurations. No weights were transferred to inference workers, and no training or answer evaluation ran.

**Results.**

| Export configuration | Exported tensors | Packed payload, GiB | Median export union, s | Observed range, s | Peak extra allocation, GiB |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| One pipeline stage, two expert partitions | 46 | 10.74 | 0.173 | 0.173–0.174 | 6.25 |
| Two pipeline stages, one expert partition | 46 | 10.74 | 1.682 | 1.005–2.359 | 7.81 |
| Two pipeline stages, non-expert tensors only | 40 | 1.37 | 0.075 | 0.074–0.075 | 0.61 |

Each row summarizes two ranks × two measured passes after one warm-up pass per rank. These are dependent observations from one allocation; the ranges are descriptive, not confidence intervals. Export union is the time covered by export CUDA-event spans, not a full synchronization interval or isolated kernel time. Packed bytes are not measured network traffic.

| Export configuration | Largest measured components | Median component share of export |
| --- | --- | ---: |
| Two expert partitions | Expert gather | 63.5% |
| Two pipeline stages, all tensors | Pipeline tensor broadcast; object broadcast | 51.9%; 37.6% |
| Two pipeline stages, non-expert only | Conversion-task construction; pipeline tensor broadcast | 46.6%; 27.1% |

Shares are medians of the per-rank/pass ratios. The all-tensor pipeline configuration issued 1,058 tensor-broadcast calls and 524 object-broadcast calls per pass. The non-expert configuration selected 34 of 1,058 conversion tasks, while still paying the fixed cost of constructing the task list. Host waits for source-buffer release were measured separately: median 0.012 s, 0.013 s and 0.004 s in table order; they are not added to the contained export-component shares. Task GPU-hours were not reconciled in this observation receipt, and quality, consumed tokens and rollout age are not applicable.

**What this means.** Keep the decomposition as diagnostic evidence: export cost depends strongly on parallelism, and the non-expert remainder is small in this reduced model. It does not establish full-Snowball export latency, cross-node behavior, native overlap, receiver byte equality or a training speedup. The exact-overlap capability is not yet ready for adoption; this group closes only the observation probe.

**Next.** Preserve these measurements for choosing an overlap design after the final comparison runs have been launched. Work toward the final tradeoff statement remains ahead of this optional optimization; any later overlap candidate must demonstrate native overlap, byte equality and its measured effect on the full synchronization interval.

🤖 Partial-rollout version tagging fails the training-input identity check on 7 of 8 updates

**What we did and why.** We tested whether recording the policy version of each response segment preserves the training inputs when generation is interrupted and resumed (K18-D1 v2). These tags would help measure how old the data consumed by faster Snowball training actually is. This is a class X engineering change: its frozen gate requires identical consumed prompt-set digests and first-token admission-age summaries. We ran a control and tagged Qwen3-0.6B arm concurrently on RNO, each with 16 H100s, seed 17 and eight optimizer updates under an interruption-heavy configuration.

**Results.** Both jobs completed successfully, but the engineering identity gate failed.

| Check | Control | Version-tagged arm | Finding |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Optimizer updates completed | 8 | 8 | Both native jobs succeeded |
| Matching consumed prompt-set digests | — | 1 of 8 | Only update 7 matched |
| First-token age at update 8, mean / min / max | 7 / 7 / 7 | 6.828125 / 5 / 7 | Summaries differ |
| Consumed response aborts at update 8 | Not certified | 96 | Tagged arm reached interrupted/resumed generation |
| Maximum consumed version spread at update 8 | Not certified | 2 | Mixed-version responses were consumed |
| Known token-version / abort-evidence fractions | Not certified | 1.0 / 1.0 at every update | Population telemetry is present |
| Measured task H100-hours | 7.006907 | 6.843211 | Accounting only; no timing ranking |

The tagged arm consumed 262,144 known loss tokens per update, 2,097,152 in total, with zero unknown tokens. Both arms consumed 256 sequences of 1,024 tokens per update; every sequence was length-stopped. Raw GSM8K optimization rewards are preserved below, but they are not completed correctness.

| Update | Prompt-set digest equal | Control raw reward | Tagged raw reward |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| 1 | No | 0.14453125 | 0.14453125 |
| 2 | No | 0.12890625 | 0.12890625 |
| 3 | No | 0.15234375 | 0.14843750 |
| 4 | No | 0.12500000 | 0.11328125 |
| 5 | No | 0.12109375 | 0.13281250 |
| 6 | No | 0.09765625 | 0.10156250 |
| 7 | Yes | 0.08984375 | 0.09375000 |
| 8 | No | 0.17578125 | 0.18750000 |

This single-seed engineering screen supplies no harness-verified held-out quality estimate, semantic score or confidence interval. Length-stopped responses do not count as accepted completions under the frozen answer contract.

**What this means.** X, not yet: the version-tagging change is not qualified for adoption, and the dependent partial-rollout comparison remains gated. The stress test exercised the intended mechanism, but that cannot override the failed input-identity check. Independently scheduled runs can consume different completed groups; this pair does not isolate a causal effect of the tagging code, and the first digest mismatch occurs before any consumed mixed-version group. The negative gate decision is complete; archive completeness, every resubmitted prefix, the measurement-guard object, resolved training receipts and stable W&B history remain explicitly uncertified.

**Next.** Keep this failed screen in the system balance measured milestone and continue the independent balance experiments. Any future causal diagnosis or replacement identity protocol must be frozen before another candidate is observed; this result does not authorize changing the gate after the fact.

🤖 Reviewed task selection retains 1,947 Qwen and 1,853 Snowball questions

**What we did and why.** Faster Snowball training at the same answer quality needs tasks that
produce both successes and failures, so the task-selection study (E6.2) built training views
from retained model ratings and the reviewed source-question exclusions. This is **class R
research**: this study decides task membership; subsequent training decides its effect on quality.
We applied the resolved-response rule separately to each model and admitted eligible questions
using evidence from either model. An independent CPU audit checked all six source objects and
seven output objects, replayed the Qwen records, and reproduced the selected counts and statistics.

**Results.** The materialized views contain **1,947 Qwen questions** from arithmetic hard and
MATH L1–2, and **1,853 Snowball questions** from arithmetic medium, GSM8K, MATH L1–2 and MATH L3.

Each source bin must have an equal-question completed-correctness mean in [0.3, 0.6] and
an informative fraction strictly above 0.4. The latter measures four-response subsets containing
both a completed correct answer and an unsuccessful answer. Responses unresolved by the semantic
verifier supply no evidence. A question needs at least one resolved response for its rate
and four for its informative statistic. Both denominators are reported. Membership requires
a resolved rate strictly between zero and one from either model; each rung retains its own
measured population. No unrated Snowball question receives an invented Snowball measurement.

🤖 FP16 gradient scaling passes 3 finite updates and an injected overflow on 4 H100s

**What we did and why.** We qualified the native dense-gradient runtime needed to test lower-precision gradient reduction (E7.1b runtime qualification). This class T lever may reduce gradient storage and communication, but its quality and performance tradeoff must be measured before adoption for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. A synthetic diagnostic ran on four H100s on RNO with tensor parallelism 2 and data parallelism 2, using actual NCCL reduction, Transformer Engine backward and Adam, FP16 gradients and BF16 model parameters. We deliberately injected an overflow on one rank to check that every rank skipped the same update, reduced its loss scale and recovered together.

**Results.** All four ranks passed the same finite-update and overflow-recovery checks in one successful original task attempt.

| Optimizer attempt | Loss scale before → after | Update applied | Overflow observed | Result on all four ranks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8 → 8 | Yes | No | Finite update |
| 2 | 8 → 16 | Yes | No | Finite update and scale growth |
| 3 | 16 → 8 | No | Yes, deliberately injected | Coherent skip and backoff |
| 4 | 8 → 8 | Yes | No | Finite recovery update |

The gradient buffer was FP16 at 131,072 bytes per rank throughout; model parameters remained BF16. The diagnostic checked exact finite parameter changes, FP32 master gradients and Adam moments, and a learning-rate scheduler that did not advance on the skipped update. This is a small synthetic layer, so its buffer size is not a production-model memory estimate.

| Potential benefit | Evidence here | Tradeoff still to measure |
|---|---|---|
| Lower gradient storage and communication | Native FP16 buffer/reduction path works on the tested dense topology | Full-model memory, step time and completed-answer quality are not measured by this group |
| Dynamic loss scaling | Growth, unanimous overflow skip/backoff and recovery pass | Unexpected non-finite training steps still trigger the scientific kill rule |

There is no held-out quality estimate, semantic score, consumed rollout count or confidence interval from this runtime diagnostic. The intentional overflow is a test condition, not a scientific training observation.

**What this means.** Keep the runtime available behind its opt-in flag for the separate gradient-precision comparison; it is not selected as the default. This qualification cleared a prerequisite for the full Qwen experiments, without qualifying their quality or production memory. The implementation remains limited to dense training with pipeline, expert and context parallelism each equal to 1; Snowball's expert/pipeline-parallel FP16 path and checkpoint/scaler restoration are unqualified.

**Next.** Complete the separate full-Qwen evidence and paired quality analysis to decide the precision tradeoff for the learner-size decision milestone. Any Snowball FP16 extension still needs its own implementation and qualification after the small-model scientific result; this kernel pass does not release it.

🤖 Paused Snowball weight sync is 1.99 seconds after diagnostics move outside the pause, 66.38% below the preceding 10 updates

**What we did and why.** We measured whether counter reads and durable diagnostic capture could
move out of Snowball's generation pause while preserving the exact expert-block installation path.
This class X engineering run used 32 learner and 8 inference H100s for 20 updates, with diagnostics
inline for updates 1–10 and outside the pause for updates 11–20. Proofs were off throughout; the
earlier proofs-on run remains the full-byte qualification.

**Results.** All five original GPU tasks and all 20 updates succeeded with no failure, preemption or
measurement retry. Times are seconds from one chronological run; p50 and p95 use the 10 updates in
each half.

| Measured interval | Inline p50 | Inline p95 | Outside-pause p50 | Outside-pause p95 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Paused weight sync | 5.905570 | 6.768338 | 1.985379 | 2.186016 |
| Full call including diagnostics | 5.905710 | 6.768487 | 4.921344 | 5.481481 |
| Transfer and install | 0.507843 | 0.729860 | 0.506619 | 0.851359 |
| Capture inside the shard interval | 1.702940 | 1.800022 | 0.344357 | 0.353839 |
| Generation-buffer wait | 23.159469 | 41.774695 | 37.041286 | 39.619861 |
| Core time per update | 40.258421 | 67.650862 | 50.736572 | 52.905863 |

The paused-sync median fell **66.381246%**, while the full call including diagnostics fell
**16.668027%**. In the second half, diagnostic completion capture took 1.365490 seconds p50 and
diagnostic interval capture took 1.563229 seconds p50 after the pause. Across all 20 updates,
transfer and install measured 0.507280 seconds p50 and 0.861726 seconds p95, and paused sync
measured 3.699174 seconds p50 and 6.326437 seconds p95. The install and whole-sync medians both
pass the 4-second timing line; p95 is reported but is not a gate.

The run consumed 3,604,983 tokens and 842.457425 core seconds. Original-task accounting is
17.001469 task GPU-hours. It produced no audited completed-correctness or semantic-quality result.

**What this means.** Keep the outside-pause diagnostic placement as the candidate for the selected
class X sync path: the measured paused interval is below four seconds and the expert-block install
remains about half a second. Most of the diagnostic work moved rather than disappeared, as the
smaller reduction in the full call shows. Generation-buffer wait and core time were higher in the
second half, and the two halves used evolving weights, trajectories, response lengths and cache
state, so this is a descriptive timing result rather than a causal whole-run speedup or a
between-seed interval.

This proofs-off run emitted no source-replica proof or frozen-sender full-byte replay row, and it
adds no sampled byte-comparison tripwire. It therefore makes no new bit-equality claim; exactness
continues to rely on the retained proofs-on qualification, which covered 20 publications with zero
mismatches. No answer-quality claim is made from this timing run.

🤖 Sixteen inference GPUs save 4.2% of Snowball core time and use 15.8% more GPU-hours

**What we did and why.** We repeated the Snowball worker-split comparison with its evaluation schedule repaired, comparing 32 learner GPUs with either 8 or 16 inference GPUs (E5.2 v3). Each arm ran 25 updates at cadence one and maximum age one, using the qualified expert-block sync path with proofs disabled. This class T experiment asks whether extra generation capacity improves the time and GPU-hours required for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality; it also tests a step-time prediction frozen after the first five updates. The [earlier result](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5649672543) remains the record of the original evaluation-defective runs.

**Results.** Both corrected arms completed with no failure or preemption. Cost includes each original task’s staging, evaluation and teardown. These are single-seed trajectories with different consumed-token counts; no between-seed confidence interval or equal-work speedup is available.

| Audited measure | 32 learner / 8 inference GPUs | 32 learner / 16 inference GPUs |
|---|---:|---:|
| Updates | 25 | 25 |
| Consumed tokens | 3,431,182 | 3,572,903 |
| Core seconds | 920.208349 | 881.335310 |

| Prediction error | +39.985394% | +12.660747% |
| Final completed-correct answers / 256 development questions | 25 / 256 | 4 / 256 |
| Final length-limited responses / 256 | 179 / 256 | 197 / 256 |

Doubling inference GPUs reduced core time **4.224374%**, increased consumed tokens **4.130384%**, and increased task GPU-hours **15.804963%**. The step-time model fails its 15% error requirement at the smaller inference allocation. The scoring session independently joined the development responses through the frozen harness and W&B; the final completed-correct counts agree with the native audit. These development numbers are descriptive, with no held-out quality ranking or paired semantic-quality interval.

**What this means.** Keep **32 learner and 8 inference GPUs**. More inference GPUs made this run modestly shorter and less GPU-efficient, while the failed prediction prevents a validated optimum from being claimed. High truncation in both arms keeps answer-stopping qualification central to the final comparison; raw reward is not a substitute for correct answers that finish. The prediction experiment is concluded as an audited negative, and these results do not justify a repeat or a worker-split change.

**Next.** Carry this negative into **system balance measured**, alongside cadence, admission order and speculative decoding. The final comparison will use the qualified answer-stopping recipe and held-out scoring before making a quality-versus-speed claim.

🤖 Milestone 5: Snowball weight installation is below 0.55 seconds, and the generation pause is 1.99 seconds

**What we did and why.** We combined the weight-sync experiments since the telemetry milestone to choose the exact synchronization path for the final comparison of faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. The evidence includes matched full-broadcast comparisons at [32 learner / 8 inference GPUs](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5634012950) and [32 / 16 GPUs](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5638365943), the [production-shaped interval with proofs disabled](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5649672660), and the [diagnostic-placement experiment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5652299558). This is class X engineering: the intended change is timing and data movement, with byte equality qualified separately.

X, ready for adoption: [placement configuration support](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/3093cf4adecdf30791c6c241068e9cab7953290c), preserving the existing default requests; this qualifies configuration plumbing, not the smaller learner’s memory fit.

Class T correction masks remain opt-in; [the selector repair](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/027a4ee1c69b657c02f5e39f280d6549cf59cf94) makes each requested mask reach the learner without changing treatment defaults.

X, not yet: the newer expert-block topology passes its tiny byte-equality and corruption checks, but general adoption still lacks the full Snowball timing and byte matrix; the selected, previously qualified 32-learner path remains the final-comparison candidate.

**Results.** The intervals below measure different parts of synchronization and must not be treated as interchangeable.

| Evidence | Measured result | Decision and scope |
|---|---|---|
| Matched transfer and installation, 32 / 8 GPUs | 0.5088 s candidate versus 19.8909 s reference, p50 over 20 publications; 39.1× shorter | Keep this geometry; all receiver bytes match at every publication |
| Matched transfer and installation, 32 / 16 GPUs | 0.5452 s versus 20.6459 s; 37.9× shorter | Transport qualifies here too; this does not select more inference GPUs |
| Per-receiver collective payload | 0.1465 of the reference at both geometries | Passes the 0.2 limit; physical ingress per receiver host was essentially unchanged |
| Earlier proofs-off whole-sync interval | 5.756 s p50; installation 0.5240 s | Exposed substantial work outside installation |
| Diagnostics inline → outside the generation pause | Paused-sync p50 5.905570 → 1.985379 s; 66.381246% reduction | Keep outside-pause placement; full call including diagnostics falls only 16.668027%, to 4.921344 s |
| Smaller learner, 16 / 24 GPUs | Both [FP32-gradient](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5649672213) and [BF16-gradient](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5649672315) pairs exhausted memory before completing an update | No transport or steady-state timing qualification at this geometry |
| [Parameter-remainders replay](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5649716093) | Zero mismatches after 10 updates; 2 bytes saved per owned parameter | Exact mechanism proof with FP32 moments on the tested synthetic two-rank configuration; no Snowball or BF16-moment equivalence claim |

The diagnostic-placement run used one seed, with ten updates per chronological half. Its outside-pause p95 was 2.186016 s. Generation-buffer wait and core time increased in the second half, so the 66.381246% pause reduction is not a causal whole-training speedup or a between-seed confidence interval. The proofs-off run adds no byte-equality evidence; the earlier proofs-on runs retain that qualification.

The [sync-share analysis](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5649715487) also resolves a negative: after algebraically subtracting proof time, sync plus generation-buffer wait was 73.646683% of core at 32 / 8 GPUs, with exploratory within-run 95% interval [64.843132%, 78.844274%], and 74.640969% at 32 / 16, [68.401215%, 78.421549%]. The proposed “below 15%” simplification is false. Buffer wait does not isolate delay caused by synchronization, and algebraic proof removal does not replay production execution.

**What this means.** Keep the qualified expert-block path, pause handshake and outside-pause diagnostics for the final comparison. The matched transfer-and-install reductions exceed fourfold, and the selected pause is below four seconds. We have not measured a matched fourfold reduction in the complete training-run synchronization interval, established an end-to-end training speedup, or qualified the smaller-learner topology. Those scopes remain explicit rather than being inferred from the install timer.

Carry the measured negatives forward: more engines at age one, n-gram speculation, partial rollouts, the small-model engine knobs, both smaller-learner gradient recipes, and the standalone throughput curve supplied no adopted speed improvement. Tensor-parallel decode per engine, FP8 KV cache, larger maximum sequence counts and faster MoE kernels remain excluded by their recorded placement or implementation evidence; these are not new GPU measurements. BF16 gradient reduction remains a memory lever: its measured Snowball training phase was 6.5% slower.

**Next.** Carry this selected sync path into the answer-stopping qualification and final Snowball comparison; additional sync experiments stay behind that comparison. The next numbered milestone is **correction chosen and safe-bound rule**, using the scoring session’s held-out results rather than development rewards.

🤖 Snowball fits on 32 FSDP2 learner GPUs; the exact-ratio test fails at all 5 updates

**What we did and why.** We tested Snowball's FSDP2 learner backend for memory use and
probability-ratio consistency during synchronous training (E7.2). This class R experiment
asks whether that backend can support faster Snowball training at the same answer quality;
this short run tests the prerequisite memory and identity criteria. We ran five updates with
32 learner and 8 inference H100s on RNO, seed 17, a 4,096-token response limit and an
8,192-token context.

**Results.**

The coordinator and all five original child tasks succeeded, with zero failures or preemptions.
All five optimizer updates completed and the native scalar packets contain no nonfinite values.
Original task allocation cost was **10.118909 H100-hours**. The five recorded step intervals sum
to **323.394024 seconds**; their median is **64.122324 seconds**. Median policy-train and weight-sync
intervals are **10.524136** and **6.611690 seconds**, respectively. The run consumed 640 responses
and 642,590 response tokens. These are one-run timing observations, with no paired confidence
interval or quality claim.

The literal frozen gate fails on all five updates:

| Update | Exact-unit ratio fraction; required 1.0 | Clip fraction; required 0 | Retained learner absolute log-ratio max | Retained learner ESS fraction |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0.007425455 | 0.013779840 | 0 | 1 |
| 2 | 0.007785902 | 0.007027224 | 0 | 1 |
| 3 | 0.005799257 | 0.016684116 | 0 | 1 |
| 4 | 0.007363379 | 0.010158457 | 0 | 1 |
| 5 | 0.007696266 | 0.004965419 | 0 | 1 |

All 32 learner ranks have the required model-ready observation and every entry/exit for the three
learner phases at updates 1–5. There are 1,056 memory events, including initial publication.
Every event joins to an original task UID, node and allocation interval; every phase exit has
allocated/reserved peaks and more than 4 GiB of device headroom.

| Phase | Exit receipts | Maximum allocated peak, GiB | Maximum reserved peak, GiB | Minimum free device memory, GiB |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Learner log-probability forward pass | 160 | 26.738799 | 28.892578 | 47.056763 |
| PPO forward, backward and update | 160 | 38.596513 | 45.480469 | 30.449402 |
| Weight publication | 192 | 14.932481 | 15.664062 | 63.447388 |

**What this means.** The learner fits on 32 learner GPUs in this run. The retained learner
comparison reports a maximum absolute log-ratio of zero and an effective-sample-size fraction of one
at every update. The failing test compares the learner's probabilities with the vLLM
probabilities recorded during generation. The pinned loss explicitly ignores the retained
learner probabilities when constructing this behavior ratio, so training-versus-inference
mismatch can remain under synchronous scheduling. The source establishes that these are
different comparisons; the measured exact-ratio and zero-clipping criteria still fail.

FSDP2 remains unadopted after this scientific gate failure. The run supplies no 16-GPU
qualification, matched speedup or held-out quality result. The planned 1.5× training-time
comparison against Megatron is unevaluated. The audit uses retained task records, native scalar
packets and Finelog; it does not independently read back the terminal objects from S3.

**Next.** Carry the memory measurements and failed ratio test into the **learner-size decision**
milestone. Keep Megatron as the trainer and preserve this negative result without repeating the
unchanged configuration. A revised identity criterion would need to name which probability
comparison it is testing.

🤖 BF16 gradients lower Snowball's observed PPO memory peak from 57.65 to 51.67 GiB; 20 updates do not select a precision

**What we did and why.** We compared FP32 and BF16 gradient reduction at the same 32-learner / 8-inference-GPU Snowball geometry (E7.1b). Each class T arm ran 20 updates on 40 RNO H100s with seed 17, cadence one, maximum age one and one update per batch. The only scientific configuration change was the precision of the model's gradient-reduction buffer; this asks whether lower-precision gradients can reduce memory or time while preserving the evidence needed for faster Snowball training at the same answer quality.

**Results.** Both arms completed all 20 updates. All ten original tasks succeeded once, with no failure, preemption, nonfinite metric or memory-threshold crossing. Every one of the 5,120 training records was consumed exactly once across the two arms; archived response-token and loss-token totals match the native consumed metrics at every update.

|---|---:|---:|
| Consumed training responses | 2,560 | 2,560 |
| Consumed response/loss tokens | 3,095,273 | 2,882,292 |
| Core seconds, 20 updates | 4,160.557082 | 3,867.269630 |

| PPO maximum peak allocated, GiB | 57.654356 | 51.669019 |

BF16 used 5.985337 GiB less memory at the PPO peak and 9.150394 GiB less at policy publication. Its measured training phase was 6.508062% longer. Its core time was 7.049235% lower and task GPU-hours were 5.860094% lower, but it also consumed 6.880847% fewer tokens on a different realized trajectory, so those whole-run differences are descriptive rather than an attributed speedup.

| Completed-correct answers, update 0 → 20 | 38/256 → 63/256 | 42/256 → 27/256 |

These are single-seed, 20-update observations with no confidence interval, and the arms already differ at update zero.

**What this means.** BF16 gradient reduction is a memory tradeoff, not a demonstrated speed lever. Keep it behind its precision flag when memory headroom matters; this pair does not support changing the default or selecting a precision on quality. No FP16 result, 16-learner-GPU qualification or precision-winner claim follows.

🤖 The Snowball cost model misses the 32/8 core time by 44.6%

**What we did and why.** We tested whether a fitted cost model could choose the worker split for
faster Snowball training by predicting core time within 15% on a separate experiment family. The
cost-model study (E2.1) is class R: its value is whether the model predicts well enough to guide a
later experiment, rather than a runtime default. We froze the model from the first five updates of
the cadence study, then evaluated it without rescue tuning on updates 6–25 of the already-inspected
32-learner-GPU runs with 8 and 16 inference GPUs. We also audited the model's token and timing
operands and tested its sensitivity to the unresolved critical-path response-length proxy.

**Results.** The model passes the 15% threshold for one of two geometries. The uncertainty intervals
resample the 20 validation core times in blocks of three while holding the calibration model fixed;
they do not include calibration, model-selection or training-seed uncertainty.

| Geometry | Predicted core seconds | Measured mean core seconds | Relative error | Conditional 95% interval | 15% result |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| 32 learner / 8 inference GPUs | 51.339496 | 35.507430 | +44.588040% | [+28.857717%, +58.274565%] | fail |
| 32 learner / 16 inference GPUs | 36.414891 | 33.273470 | +9.441221% | [−2.466976%, +20.018617%] | pass |

The admitted-batch maximum response length is only a proxy for the response that blocks the
learner. Varying that proxy changes the prediction substantially:

| Critical-path proxy setting | 32/8 predicted core seconds | 32/16 predicted core seconds |
|---|---:|---:|
| No latency term | 13.748757 | 13.356273 |
| Minimum from calibration | 41.794617 | 29.983490 |
| Median from calibration | 51.339496 | 36.414891 |
| Maximum from calibration | 89.662700 | 62.237315 |

The accounting audit joins 1,854 successful generated groups exactly to their dispositions and
token counts; 1,600 were consumed, 190 rejected and 64 discarded at the terminal boundary. Across
40 validation core windows, completed-arrival event balances close exactly for both geometries.
Those balances exclude unfinished partial tokens and are not physical buffer snapshots. The data
also lack a clock-calibrated response-to-learner-wait mapping, a prospective outcome freeze and full
predictive uncertainty.

**What this means.** The current cost model is an audited negative: it misses the working 32/8
geometry by far more than 15%, and the apparent 32/16 pass is not robust to the critical-path proxy.
We therefore do not use the model to recommend a worker split or claim a validated optimum. The
remaining physical accounting and prospective-validation fields stay explicitly incomplete; they
would be required to validate a future revised model, but they are not required to dispose this
frozen model after its independent-family failure.

**Next.** Carry this negative and its incomplete-accounting limits into **system balance measured**.
The final comparison keeps the empirically selected 32/8 geometry and does not launch another
cost-model measurement unless a revised model and a prospective measurement contract are proposed
as a new study.

**What we did and why.** We examined whether the observed relationship between rollout age and
training informativeness survives adjustment for response length, to avoid choosing an off-policy
range from a misleading association. This stratification and replay study (E4.4) is class R: it
informs the research interpretation of faster Snowball training at the same answer quality. We
analysed 100 retained Snowball update summaries from one seed and used two CPU storage inspections
to search for the individual records and sequential Qwen policies required by the original tests.
The evidence audit is concluded; the requested individual-level stratification and fixed-sample
policy replay were not measured.

**Results.** The retained aggregate covers 25 four-update cadence cycles, with one update at each
realised age from 0 through 3 per cycle. Each update contains 32 prompt groups and 128 responses.
Length below means the update's mean response length, so these are aggregate observations rather
than an individual-response analysis. Informativeness is the retained training metric, not
completed-answer accuracy.

| Realised age | Updates | Informative groups / groups | Informative fraction | Mean response tokens |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 25 | 79 / 800 | 9.8750% | 628.273 |
| 1 | 25 | 128 / 800 | 16.0000% | 827.888 |
| 2 | 25 | 156 / 800 | 19.5000% | 1,048.613 |
| 3 | 25 | 310 / 800 | 38.7500% | 1,733.244 |

| Aggregate model | Age slope, percentage points per additional age unit | Conditional 95% interval |
|---|---:|---|
| Age alone | +9.0125 | [+7.5125, +10.4125] |
| Age plus fixed bins of cohort mean length | +0.9084 | [−3.4873, +4.2513] |
| Age plus continuous cohort mean length | −4.7351 | [−11.3824, +0.6708] |
| Age plus continuous cohort mean length, controlling for cadence cycle | +0.5637 | [−1.4279, +2.4454] |

The intervals use 20,000 bootstrap resamples of complete cadence cycles and are conditional on this
one run. The fixed-bin model omits 101 singular draws. Its length bins use the fixed edges 512,
1,024, 2,048 and 4,096 tokens; age zero appears only in the lowest occupied bin, while the highest
occupied bin appears only at age three. Sparse overlap and changing signs across the continuous
length models limit interpretation. These intervals contain no training-seed uncertainty.

| Requested measurement | Final evidence disposition |
|---|---|
| Snowball informative fraction by individual group length and consumed age | Not measured. Recovery found 577 training records in 268 archives with the intended stable run ID, but original physical-attempt ownership, complete four-response membership and first-token-to-consumption version bindings remain unestablished. |
| Qwen fixed-sample absolute log-ratio and effective sample size versus injected age | Not measured. The generation buffer survives, but its aligned sample arrays remain unverified. The bounded checkpoint listing exposes only update 96 and no sequential nine-version series. |

The follow-up reader incorrectly required the physical attempt identifier inside the stable run
ID before computing nested length and group statistics. Consequently its zero target counts are
skipped calculations, not evidence of absent responses or groups. Correcting that filter alone
would not establish the missing ownership and consumption bindings. The Qwen listing is limited
to the inspected checkpoint root and depth; it does not prove that no other copy exists anywhere.

**What this means.** Coarse length adjustment reduces the observed age slope in this aggregate
diagnostic, with an adjusted interval spanning zero. This is consistent with length and completion
order affecting the association, but does not identify a causal effect of age, establish that
older rollouts are harmless, or satisfy the original individual-level test.

We conclude the retained-evidence audit as **not evaluable under the requested measurement
contract**, with the aggregate diagnostic preserved. No scientific hypothesis is rejected from
missing data, no quality-ranked setting is selected, and no operating-age range or default changes
on this evidence. The literal tests remain unmeasured; concluding the audit does not turn them
into passes. The randomised-delay extension remains offloaded.

**Next.** Carry the diagnostic and both missing-measurement limits into **system balance measured**.
Do not repeat blind reads of the same objects. Reopen these analyses only if a concrete
original-attempt/consumption manifest or sequential-policy source becomes available; the final
operating-range recommendation must rely on the measured confirmation studies.

🤖 The parser-only treatment completes 100 of 256 answers correctly; the top four treatments are statistically indistinguishable

**What we did and why.** We compared five ways to address Snowball's unfinished answers, because faster Snowball training at the same answer quality requires answers that are both correct and completed. This stopping-treatment screen (E6.1 stage 2) is class R: it selects the answer contract and stopping package for confirmation. Each treatment trained for 25 updates at one seed on 32 learner and eight inference H100s, with weight publication every two updates, maximum admitted age one update, and one update per batch. We evaluated the same 256 development questions before training and at update 25, using one greedy response per question.

**Results.** All five corrected runs completed 25 updates, with all 25 original GPU tasks succeeding and no retries, failures or preemptions. Earlier startup failures remain separate and supply no scientific observations.

Completed correctness is the fraction of responses with both a correct answer and an accepted stop. The table reports each treatment with its package enabled. Length-limited responses are only one kind of incomplete response; repetition-triggered stops also remain incomplete.

| Treatment | Completed correctness, update 0 → 25 | Completed correct at update 25 | Contract correctness at update 25 | Length-limited fraction at update 25 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Post-thinking parser only (`parser_only`) | 0.15625 → 0.39062 | 100/256 | 0.39453 | 0.41797 |
| Forced thinking close (`force_close`) | 0.23438 → 0.37891 | 97/256 | 0.38672 | 0.31641 |
| Negative advantage for truncation (`negative_truncation_advantage`) | 0.15625 → 0.37109 | 95/256 | 0.37109 | 0.41406 |
| Soft overlength penalty (`soft_overlong`) | 0.14453 → 0.36719 | 94/256 | 0.38281 | 0.44141 |
| Repetition-triggered stop (`repetition_stop`) | 0.17188 → 0.26562 | 68/256 | 0.27734 | 0.25000 |

The frozen deterministic selector chooses the parser-only treatment on its first key, highest package completed correctness at update 25. There is no tie, so neither later comparison keys nor the tie order are used. Its lead over forced thinking close is three questions.

| Treatment minus parser only, update 25 | Completed-correctness difference | Simultaneous interval | Holm-adjusted p |
|---|---:|---:|---:|

Only repetition-triggered stopping separates from parser only. The top four treatments are statistically indistinguishable on this evidence; deterministic selection does not establish that parser only is better than forced thinking close.

The two treatments that alter generation also have separate evaluations with the intervention disabled. At update 25, forced thinking close scores 0.35156 disabled versus 0.37891 enabled; repetition-triggered stopping scores 0.31641 disabled versus 0.26562 enabled. These are descriptive endpoint comparisons, with no paired intervention-effect interval reported.

The fleet used 92.793609 task H100-hours, calculated from actual task start and finish times. Each run consumed 3,200 training responses; every per-update age p95 was between zero and one. Core time covers the measured training core, while task hours include the rest of each task's lifetime. These are fixed-update observations on different trajectories, with no timing intervals or quality-adjusted speedup established.

`records.parquet` was not produced. The frozen harness correctly rejected dumped rewards that disagree with its pinned verifier mapping: the post-thinking parser changes how truncated responses are scored, and the soft overlength treatment deliberately reshapes rewards. At update 25, 116 of 256 soft-penalty rewards disagree with that binary mapping. A reviewed verifier mapping is required to join these treatments through the full frozen harness.

The scorer authenticated all 14 endpoint views and 3,584 rows, decoded responses with the pinned tokenizer, and independently computed correct-answer × accepted-stop under the frozen completion rule. **What this means.** Keep parser only as the mechanically selected treatment for confirmation. The screen does not establish a quality advantage over the other three leading treatments, and its 0.41797 length-limited fraction leaves nontermination unresolved. This is one-seed development evidence after 25 updates; it supplies no held-out result, graduation or faster-training-at-equal-quality claim.

**Next.** Carry the selected parser-only settings into the planned 100-update, two-seed confirmation and retain the frozen control roles. That study must measure completed correctness and whether truncation falls below 10% on both seeds before the **answer contract and tasks fixed** milestone.
