As before, the reported count is the number of complete pairs at the moment of posting — an arm seed and its matched synchronous control, both at update 100 and both through the membership gate — and a final replaces this comment when the wave ends.

**Results — age cap one, interim at five matched pairs.** Same 256-question development set, one response per question, update-100 endpoint, completed correctness (correct answer with an accepted stopping reason).

| Seed | Synchronous control | Age cap one | Difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|

| 43 | 53.516% | 35.938% | −17.58 pp |
| 79 | 44.531% | 54.688% | +10.16 pp |
| 97 | 46.875% | 45.703% | −1.17 pp |
| **Mean** | **47.89%** | **48.20%** | **+0.31 pp** |

The fixed-observed-seed interval is [−2.03, +2.73] points with Holm p 0.818; the primary population interval, resampling seeds and questions, is [−10.23, +9.92] points with Holm p 0.960. The one-sided lower bound is **−11.12 points**, which excludes both the 15-point margin and the 20-point outer bound. **Non-inferiority is established at 15 points.**

Achieved power at five pairs is **74.2% at 15 points and 91.7% at 20**, from a paired-difference SD of 11.99 points; the pre-observation unpaired 10-point basis would have read 86.2% / 97.5%. Power below the 80% target does not weaken this result and the two statements are not in tension: power is a property of the design — the chance of establishing non-inferiority if the true difference were exactly zero — while the claim rests on the interval actually observed, and that interval excludes the margin.

**The swing is the part worth carrying.** At three pairs this configuration read −2.47 points and unresolved; at five it reads +0.31 points and non-inferior. That is a 2.8-point move and a sign flip on two added seeds — exactly the caution attached to the three-pair figure, which now attaches with equal force to this one. Five pairs on a 12-point paired SD is not a precise estimate either, and seven or eleven pairs may move it again.

Two consequences follow. The earlier comparison of this configuration's level with age cap four's is **withdrawn in the form it was given**: at five pairs the two are +0.31 and −2.60 points and both resolve at 15 points, so "same level, one resolved and one not" no longer describes them. The method point it illustrated — the seed count a configuration needs is a property of that configuration, not of the protocol — stands on its own and does not need that pairing.

On the margin's justification: the control's own spread across five seeds is SD 4.17 points, range 9.77, against the 5.04 points on three seeds that the 15-point margin was set against. The reasoning holds, and the control is if anything tighter than assumed.

Integrity of the two new controls, checked before their numbers were read: both clean at every panel — 256 questions, one sample per question, question ids matching the frozen battery. **What this means.** On the deep pool, the supported range is now age caps **one and four non-inferior at the 15-point margin**, with age cap two unresolved at three seeds. The [milestone claim](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5663169886) is unchanged: its chosen configuration is age cap four and its speed numbers are untouched. Nothing here is a decision against age cap two — it is unresolved, which is not the same as rejected.

🤖 Raw `main` measured at 100 updates at every staleness allowance: this branch is 22 to 36% faster at the same allowance and 65% faster end to end, and three defects in `main` had to be repaired or disclosed to make the measurement at all

**What we did and why.** Every speed claim so far compared this branch's configurations with its own staleness-0 control. This comment adds the comparison a reader outside the programme wants: the asynchronous implementation as it stands on `main` today (fork point `8e33e017`, stock parser and loss, 64 generation workers), run to 100 updates at seed 17 at each of staleness 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4, on the same 32-trainer / 8-generator H100 shape.

**Results, wall-clock to 100 updates, seed 17, one arm each (cycle-sum convention as in every earlier audit).**

| Staleness allowance | `main` | This branch | Saving | Of which `main` spends in weight copies |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 8,524 s | 6,235 s | **26.9%** | 2,141 s |
| 1 | 5,583 s | 4,360 s | **21.9%** | 2,068 s |
| 2 | 5,093 s | 3,544 s | **30.4%** | 2,092 s |
| 3 | 4,913 s | 3,142 s | **36.0%** | 2,206 s |
| 4 | 4,301 s | 2,942 s | **31.6%** | 2,066 s |

Core time falls 27 to 47% by the same rows. Full-task GPU-hours from the scheduler's task durations, single attempt each: staleness 0, 103.1 on `main` against 76.7 here (−25.6%); staleness 1, 70.4 against 55.9 (−20.7%); staleness 2, 64.9 against 46.8 (−27.9%); staleness 4, 55.8 against 40.3 (−27.8%); staleness 3 withheld because that `main` run took two attempts. `main` spends about 2,100 s of every run in weight copies whatever the allowance, the 20-second copy repeated 100 times; this branch spends about 500 to 545 s. End to end, from what `main` does at staleness 0 to this branch's staleness-4 configuration is 8,524 → 2,942 s, **−65.5%**; to the staleness-1 configuration, −48.8%. GPU-hours in the training window scale with wall on both sides.

**What it took to measure, each a finding about `main`.**

1. *Served-model identity.* `main`'s generation client and server disagree about the model's name under the launcher's automatic short alias; every request fails with HTTP 400. Fixed by one configuration key that restores the full path on both sides.
2. *No trainable tokens on Snowball's template.* `main`'s HTTP path re-tokenises each answer and takes its loss mask from the chat template's generation markers; Snowball's template has none, so every answer is fully masked and rejected, and the loop re-queues forever without logging. We added the two marker lines around the assistant turn, nothing else: the rendered prompt is byte-identical with and without them, and the template hash is in the provenance. The `main` column is therefore "`main` plus the annotation it needs to train this model".
3. *Training on re-tokenised text.* On that path `main` trains on token ids re-encoded from the generated text with special tokens stripped, not the ids the model sampled: no thinking-start prefill, the thinking-end marker dropped, a spurious header inside the response at mask zero, and no behaviour log-probabilities to expose the mismatch. The staleness-3 arm's entropy rose above 2 from update 49 and it logged sixteen zero-reward training steps from update 57 on; that is consistent with what this defect would predict, and the cause is not established. This is why the `main` column carries no quality claim beyond the descriptive figures below.
4. *Evaluation dumps never reached storage.* `main` builds the dump directory with `pathlib.Path` on an `s3://` export path (`skyrl_train/evaluate.py:177-186`, and the same for training-data dumps at `trainer.py:1629-1635`), which collapses the URI into a local path, and writes it with the built-in `open`; the files land on the pod's disk and vanish with it. Confirmed by listing every object under all ten run prefixes: zero dump keys. Quality for the `main` arms is therefore the runtime's own logged metric at updates 0 and 100, which the four held-out panels show agrees with our frozen contract to within about 0.1 pp at update 100 and disagrees by about 1.5 pp at update 0.

**Quality, descriptive only, under `main`'s own metric.** `main` logs pass@1, which is "correct answer" with no stop or length condition at all; every quality figure earlier in this thread is "correct answer and accepted stop". So these are upper bounds against any earlier figure, by the truncated-but-correct fraction, which cannot be sized without the dumps. Read them for shape, not for level, and never beside an earlier number.

| `main` at staleness | pass@1 at update 0 | pass@1 at update 100 |
|---|---:|---:|
| 0 | 0.172 | 0.418 |
| 1 | 0.117 | 0.461 |
| 2 | 0.121 | 0.398 |
| 3 | 0.145 | 0.000 from update 60 |
| 4 | 0.145 | 0.531 |

The staleness-3 arm collapsed at update 60 and stayed at zero; on the training side it logged sixteen zero-reward steps from update 57 with entropy above 2 from update 49, so two independent instruments agree the arm degraded. The cause is not established; re-tokenised training is the candidate, not the finding.

**One operational note, not a `main` finding.** On this runtime's coordinator route a post-training export step failed on every arm and each coordinator's single retry re-ran the training; the reruns finished or failed on their own, every audit is from the first complete run of its arm (for staleness 3, the attempt that followed a preemption at update 63), and the cost was GPUs.

**What this means.** The weight-copy work alone is worth about 27% of wall-clock against `main` at the same allowance with no quality trade (option 1 in the report). The staleness configurations add their own savings on top, and the combined number against `main` as it stands today is about two thirds of the wall-clock. `main` itself cannot currently train this model without the annotation, and trains on tokens it did not sample when it does.

<details><summary>Provenance</summary>

Prepared 2026-09-15. `main` arms: `async-rl-v2-e93-raw-main-c1-s{0,1,2,3,4}-seed17-u100-v5` on MarinSkyRL `8e33e01707b7225ecde1d6b8ad172a3dd4dc8661` with the annotated template SHA256 `a770431392d970d106aeada8ae1c6594bba5d520659f3c7b606a62d4880ee667` (original `60180a4f…275e4`, diff two inserted lines); the added key `++generator.engine_init_kwargs.served_model_name=null`. This branch's rows: the synchronous control seed 17 (`async-rl-v2-e90-control-abort-s17-u100-e57-v2`), the E9.2 staleness-2 and -4 arms at seed 17, the staleness-1 and -3 arms at seed 17 (`…-s2s-e92-a5-s1deep-s17-u100-v1`, `…-a3-s3deep-s17-u100-v1` attempt 1), all on `ba5ba171`. Independent cold reviews before launch: the v4 and v5 startup reviews and the config-route audit, all in the experiment records.

comments.body:
🤖 All four staleness arms on one statistical basis; age cap one falls to the 20-point outer margin at ten matched seeds; age cap three complete and unresolved; four held-out update-100 panels

**What we did and why.** Since the [five-pair interim](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5668561187), five more matched pairs completed for age cap one (seeds 61, 113, 149, 167, 185), an age-cap-three arm was added at three matched seeds so the ladder has no gap, and every arm was recomputed as its own pre-registered family so the rows are comparable. Four held-out update-100 panels were also scored on the frozen 3,294-question battery.

**Results — the four arms, each against its matched synchronous controls.** Same 256-question development set, one response per question, update-100 endpoint, completed correctness. Each row is its own non-inferiority test at the approved 15-point margin; the rows share the same controls, so their differences are correlated, and no row is compared with another.

| Configuration | Matched seeds | Mean difference | Population interval | One-sided lower bound | Non-inferior at 15 points | Achieved power at 15 |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---|---:|
| Age cap one, 64 generation workers | 10 | −9.22 pp | [−17.81, −0.39] | −17.48 pp | **no**; yes at the 20-point outer bound | 92% |
| Age cap two, 96 workers | 3 | −8.72 pp | [−23.05, +4.69] | −33.54 pp | not established | 33% |
| Age cap three, 128 workers | 3 | −6.51 pp | [−17.06, +6.64] | −27.42 pp | not established | 41% |
| Age cap four, 160 workers | 3 | −2.60 pp | [−8.59, +3.00] | −9.07 pp | **yes** | 99% |

One arm establishes non-inferiority at 15 points: age cap four. Age caps two and three do not, and for them that is a failure to establish, not a demonstration of inferiority: three seeds cannot resolve an arm whose paired spread is 12 to 15 points against a 15-point margin. Age cap one is different: at ten pairs and 92% power it is resolved, and it resolves outside the 15-point margin, non-inferior only at the pre-registered 20-point outer bound, with a population interval that excludes zero for the first time in this wave. The four point estimates sit within about 7 points of one another and share the same controls, so nothing here ranks the arms. Only the age-cap-one row is a single-variable contrast with the control; the other three pair a larger allowance with a larger generation pool chosen for it, and the design cannot separate the two.

**Age cap one at ten pairs.**

| Seed | Synchronous control | Age cap one | Difference |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 17 | 50.781% | 48.438% | −2.34 pp |
| 29 | 43.750% | 56.250% | +12.50 pp |
| 43 | 53.516% | 35.938% | −17.58 pp |
| 61 | 55.078% | 41.797% | −13.28 pp |
| 79 | 44.531% | 54.688% | +10.16 pp |
| 97 | 46.875% | 45.703% | −1.17 pp |
| 113 | 60.156% | 50.391% | −9.77 pp |
| 149 | 54.297% | 35.938% | −18.36 pp |
| 167 | 57.812% | 23.828% | −33.98 pp |
| 185 | 61.719% | 43.359% | −18.36 pp |
| **Mean** | **52.85%** | **43.63%** | **−9.22 pp** |

The point estimate has read −2.47 points at three pairs, +0.31 at five, −2.80 at six, −5.02 at seven, −6.47 at nine and −9.22 at ten. Non-inferiority at 15 points held at five, six, seven and nine pairs, its cushion going 3.9 → 1.4 → 0.16 → 1.12 points, and from six pairs onward we wrote that one more adverse pair the size of the worst so far could take the bound past 15. Pair 149 arrived at exactly that size and the claim survived by 0.16 points; pairs 61 and 113 were adverse and it survived; pair 167, at nearly twice that size, took the one-sided lower bound to −17.48 points. The caution was right and the cushion is gone. This is not the underpowered outcome of age caps two and three: with a paired spread of 14.2 points and 92% power the arm is resolved, and it resolves outside the margin; the population interval, [−17.81, −0.39], excludes zero, so under seed-population inference this configuration is shown to differ from its control, for the worse, by about 9 points with a wide interval. Per the pre-registered rule it falls back to the 20-point outer bound, where it is non-inferior. One pair remains outstanding, and this arm has moved on every pair added, twice reversing sign and now reversing a margin verdict, so ten is not final either; the eleven-pair figure will be reported when it exists. The control's own spread on ten seeds is SD 6.29 points, range 17.97, still in the region of the margin's justification rather than comfortably inside it. The fuller table also shows that the control mean rose from 49.35% at three seeds to 52.85% at ten while the arm mean fell, so the rows are not independent observations.

**Age cap three, three matched seeds.** Per-seed differences −13.67, +7.81 and −13.67 points. The two identical values are a coincidence of the 256-question grid (both exactly −35/256) and should not be read as agreement between seeds; seed 29's positive value shows the arm is not consistent across seeds. Truncation at update 100 was 43% and 49% on two seeds, above the controls' 25 to 35%, with no weight put on two seeds.

**Held-out update-100 panels.** Four panels on the frozen battery (3,294 questions, four responses each, 13,176 responses, membership gate exact on every panel), frozen-contract completed correctness:

| Panel | Score | Runtime parser | Gap |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Age cap zero, seed 17 | 0.6617 | 0.6604 | 16 responses |
| Age cap two, seed 17 | 0.5083 | 0.5082 | 1 response |
| Age cap four, seed 17 | 0.6285 | 0.6279 | 8 responses |
| Synchronous control, seed 29 | 0.5276 | 0.5276 | 1 response |

At update 100 the runtime parser and the frozen contract agree to within 16 responses in 13,176 on every panel, so the choice of parser is immaterial there, unlike at update 0 where it moved the number by 1.5 points; that was predicted in writing before the panels existed. The three seed-17 panels share one lineage: 0.662, 0.628 and 0.508 for age caps zero, four and two, where the development set at seed 17 gives 0.508, 0.438 and 0.266 for the same three configurations, the same non-monotone shape with held-out gaps about half the size. That is one seed and no statistic: a single seed can reproduce an ordering by chance. The seed-29 control panel is a different lineage and is not compared with them. The held-out goal at three seeds is not claimed demonstrated.

**What this means.** With the deep in-flight pool, the only configuration whose quality is settled inside the 15-point margin is age cap four; age caps two and three are unresolved at three seeds; age cap one, the only single-variable contrast, is shown under population inference to differ from its control, for the worse, at ten pairs, and is non-inferior only at the 20-point outer bound. The [milestone claim](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5663169886) for age cap four stands. The earlier interim statements that age cap one was non-inferior at 15 points are superseded by this one.

**Next.** Pair 131's control is being resubmitted under its fifth name after four runs died on restart under the write-once measurement guard; the eleven-pair figure is reported when it lands. The raw-`main` baselines are in the [previous comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5687648447).

comments.author: atqamar
comments.body:
🤖 **E10: in-loop generation throughput versus pool depth, one seed, 25 updates**

**What ran.** Five arms on MarinSkyRL `ba5ba171`, copied from the E9.1 A4-abort seed-17 action that E9.2 reused as
its seed-17 member. Each arm is 40 H100 at cw-rno2a, seed 17, 25 updates, 32 prompts × 4 samples, `max_staleness_steps`
64 so admission never throttles on age, and `generator.max_num_seqs` 2048 per DP rank so the engine cap never binds.
The arms differ only in the generation-worker count: 128, 256, 512, 1,024, 2,048. A worker
is a concurrent *group* producer, and each group is 4 samples.

**Timing and realised depth.** Steady window = updates 5-19 and 21-24 (updates 20 and 25 carry evaluations, and 25
also the forced checkpoint). Burst window = updates 1-4. Throughput is the mean over the 8 engines, per engine. Median depth and KV use are per-engine means; peak and burst-peak depth are summed over the 8 engines and are window means of the per-update peaks.

| Workers | Wall (s) | Core (s) | Buffer wait (s) | Sync (s) | Response tokens | Steady tok/s per engine | Median depth (per engine) | Peak depth (all engines) | Burst peak depth (all engines) | Peak KV % (per engine) | Preempted requests |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 128 | 529.3 | 425.7 | 16.0 | 145.3 | 3,884,813 | 1,148.9 | 29.1 | 290.7 | 295.8 | 6.4 | 0 |
| 256 | 523.5 | 415.1 | 15.0 | 138.8 | 3,879,436 | 1,169.0 | 30.0 | 301.8 | 500.5 | 6.7 | 0 |
| 512 | 545.8 | 426.6 | 18.5 | 145.5 | 4,249,435 | 1,779.5 | 44.0 | 423.8 | 968.8 | 10.8 | 0 |
| 1,024 | 611.0 | 467.8 | 36.3 | 174.4 | 3,062,524 | 524.0 | 166.4 | 1,557.4 | 1,877.8 | 41.4 | 0 |
| 2,048 | 637.3 | 480.1 | 50.1 | 191.2 | 2,337,546 | 298.2 | 92.8 | 1,490.7 | 3,272.5 | 60.7 | 0 |

**The knee.** Per-engine steady throughput relative to its own maximum: 64.6%, 65.7%, **100% at 512**, 29.4%,
16.8%. Under the pre-registered rule (first depth below 90% of the peak) the knee is at **1,024 workers**, so it
lies between 512 and 1,024. 512 is a single peak rather than a plateau: 128 and 256 sit at two thirds of it.

**What the numbers do and do not support.**
- **Depth saturates at the consumption rate**, a property of the loop's code that these rows confirm: the trainer
  admits one 32-group cohort per update and the completed queue holds 32, so producers beyond that block holding a
  finished group. 128 and 256 workers are therefore
  indistinguishable in steady state (29 versus 30 running requests per engine); they differ only in the burst
  window, where peak requests rise 296 → 500 → 969 → 1,878 → 3,273. Read the curve against realised depth, never
  against the configured worker count.
- **The fall past 512 is not scheduler preemption.** No vLLM request was preempted in any arm. Peak KV use rises
  6.4% → 60.7%, wall time rises from 529 to 637 s (not monotonically: 256 workers is 6 s faster than 128) and buffer
  wait more than triples. No mechanism for the fall is claimed from these rows.
- **The deepest arm is data-capped.** The train set holds 1,853 rows, of which 1,824 are served per pass, and 32
  are consumed per update, so 2,048 workers cannot all hold a group: its steady median depth (92.8) sits below the
  1,024 arm's (166.4) despite twice the workers.
- **Scope.** One seed, one run per arm, 25 updates, one model and one cluster. These are timing rows, not a
  quality result, and no arm-versus-arm quality claim follows.

**Operational notes on the runtime** (not results):
- Every arm's training survived; three arms lost or had preempted tasks immediately after their final update, which
  cost the terminal step only.
- Where a child retry then restarted training in place, the write-once measurement guard killed it within minutes,
  which is the guard working as intended.
- The two deepest arms waited about 44 minutes for placement while 200 H100 were in flight; their measured wall
  time is unaffected, since wall runs from each arm's own first rollout.

🤖 Two additions to the raw-`main` comment: the staleness-3 arm rerun under a fresh name did not collapse, and every asynchronous arm on this branch discards about a fifth of its groups as stale while the synchronous control discards none

**The staleness-3 rerun.** The [raw-`main` comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8955#issuecomment-5687648447) reported `main`'s staleness-3 arm collapsing at update 60. It was rerun under a fresh name, seed 17, same annotated template, and completed on its second attempt after a worker loss at update 99 of the first. Timing: 4,754 s wall against 3,142 s on this branch, a 33.9% saving (the collapsed run had read 4,913 s); 2,096 s of that in weight copies. Quality under `main`'s own pass@1, upper bound as before: 0.137 at update 0, 0.238 at update 100, with no zero-reward evaluation anywhere but a peak of 0.395 at update 80 and a 15.6-point fall over the last twenty updates. So the collapse did not reproduce, and the rerun is not a clean completion either; the cause of the first run's collapse remains unestablished. The comparison table's staleness-3 row now reads 4,754 s.

**A caveat on every staleness comparison on this branch.** The runtime discards a group that outlasts the staleness allowance and regenerates it from the same prompt. Over the same 90 updates at seed 17 the counters show 0 groups discarded in the synchronous control and 897, 968, 967 and 925 in the age-cap-one to age-cap-four arms, a rate of 21 to 23%, every one tagged stale. That is a large selection process on the asynchronous side of every quality comparison posted in this thread and absent on the other, separate from the staleness of the gradients. Whether it moves any quality number is not known; it is recorded as a caveat, not a correction, and a comparison that controls for it is queued. Response-length distributions differ in shape across arms too (dispersion down about 30%, cap hits concentrated into fewer updates) while their means do not fall; two stronger length claims were withdrawn on cross-checking. The abort pause itself is ruled out as a cause: an aborted answer keeps exactly its remaining budget.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
A retried evalchemy run leaves two complete results trees: the canonical task tree and a second tree under the harness's scratch directory (`tmp<random>/`). For single-task runs the dashboard averages both attempts into the run's overall score and doubles the item count, reporting a score that equals no actual attempt.

Reproduce:
1. Open https://marina.oa.dev/evaldash/runs/20260806-193519-qwen3-8b-olympiadbench-5172 — the overview reports OlympiadBench accuracy 10.0.
2. The run's record (s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/20260806-193519-qwen3-8b-olympiadbench-5172/record.json) carries two metric entries:
   - `olympiadbench`: num_solved 2/30, accuracy 0.0667 (canonical tree `olympiadbench/qwen3-8b/`, 2026-08-06T21:03)
   - `tmpvu7bt1e4`: num_solved 4/30, accuracy 0.1333 (scratch tree `olympiadbench/tmpvu7bt1e4/qwen3-8b/`, 2026-08-06T22:15)

   The attempts share a resume fingerprint; 22/30 generations are byte-identical and 8 were re-generated against a second inference endpoint.
3. `measurement_from_record` averages the two entries — mean(0.0667, 0.1333) = 0.10 — and sums n_scored to 60 for the 30-item task (lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/eval_measurements.py:151).

Both defenses miss single-task runs:

- Write side: `is_scratch_artifact` (lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/lm_eval_samples.py:77) excludes `tmp<random>/` trees when globbing results files (lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/result.py:72), and `tmpvu7bt1e4` matches its pattern — but this record was written with the scratch entry present, so the path that keyed these metrics did not apply, or predates, the filter.
- Read side: `_task_scores` deduplicates same-task entries by leaf name, first-wins (lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/eval_measurements.py:67). That catches group tasks (`tmpXXXX/mmlu_anatomy` shares the `mmlu_anatomy` leaf with the canonical key) but not single-task runs, where the scratch entry's key is the bare tmpdir leaf (`tmpvu7bt1e4`) and never matches the task leaf.

Expected: one authoritative attempt per (task, model) — the canonical-tree rule the write side already encodes — also applied at read time over record metric keys, so legacy records like this one repair on display. The run overview then shows the canonical attempt's score (6.67% here) with n=30, never a cross-attempt mean.

The same run renders all 30 samples "ungraded"; that is a producer-side gap tracked in marin-community/evalchemy#128.

comments.author: weaverbot
comments.body:
🤖 Architecture and plan for the evaldash issues, peer-reviewed as requested: https://loom.oa.dev/s/m6bfst8b/artifacts/evaldash-stats-engine (rev 2)

The four subissues are the same gap seen from four angles. Evaldash has no representation of *a measurement and how much of it happened* — a matrix cell is `value: float | None`, so there is nowhere to put "236 of 240 intended trials, 4 agent timeouts", and nothing to filter or aggregate on except presence. #8084 needs that representation to admit a partial run, #8085 needs it to qualify an aggregate, #8086 needs it to decide which result is admissible, #8087 needs a query object over it.

So the pre-work is one engine, shared by the eval runners and the dashboard: a typed measurement carrying its item counts and interval, plus an explicit selection query over a set of measurements. Each issue is then a call into it.

**Statistical core.** One estimand: the success rate over the items a run set out to grade. With `c = n_scored / n_attempted`, θ splits into an identified part and an unidentified one, and the missing part gets bounded rather than imputed — missingness correlates with task difficulty, which is exactly why #8084 needs a gate rather than an average. The reported interval is Wilson on the scored items, scaled by `c` and widened by `1 − c`, with an Imbens–Manski critical value so it covers the parameter at 95% instead of over-covering at ~97.5%. Width is at least `1 − c`: a run that graded 92.3% of its trials reports an interval at least 7.7 points wide however many trials it ran.

**Three things fall out that are worth flagging before implementation.**

1. Harbor already publishes a biased number, and the gate would expose it. `_aggregate` divides by `len(trials)` while an errored trial is read back with reward 0.0, so `accuracy` scores every timeout as a wrong answer — the Manski lower bound, computed by accident and labelled a point estimate. It is masked today only because any failed trial aborts the run. Relaxing that without fixing the denominator would ship the bias. The intended-trial count also cannot come from the result glob: a trial that dies before writing leaves no file, so the runs with the worst attrition would report perfect coverage.
2. Ranking cannot use `k / n_scored`. It is a complete-case estimate, so ranking on it rewards a model for timing out on hard items — #8085's complaint re-entering through the sort key. Ranking uses the interval's lower bound. At `c = 1` the two coincide, so the 368 evalchemy runs are unaffected.
3. A 90% gate admits results for display but cannot support ordering claims. Resolving a 5-point gap between two models needs coverage above 0.975 on both, and 2 points needs 0.99. Display admission and comparison admission are two thresholds, not one.

**Evidence.** Everything above is checked against the 387 records under `gs://marin-eval-metadata/evals` (CoreWeave needs credentials this session did not have). Item counts are already there — 1204 of 1249 per-task metric dicts carry `sample_len`, and Harbor carries `total`/`solved` — so the primary adapter is the record, not the archive, which matters because only 6 of 387 runs have a finestore archive today. A cross-check worth knowing about: the llama-3.1-8b mmlu record has 124 task entries because the run wrote the whole 62-entry panel twice, once under `mmlu_5shot` and once under a task directory named `tmp6jnnx8cc`, scoring 0.63502 and 0.63488. Benchmark identity cannot be the raw evalchemy task directory, and that duplicate looks like a separate launcher bug.

**Peer review** changed the design materially, so the artifact records it. Adopted: the Imbens–Manski correction; asymmetric difference bounds; demoting paired comparison, which provably buys zero attrition-width reduction; the Harbor denominator fixes; dropping a fleet-max denominator inference and a new Postgres table that would have been write-only; and moving the engine out of `lib/finestore` — `marin-core` already depends on `marin-finestore`, so an engine there naming `RunStatus` would create a distribution cycle and break that wheel's CI leg. It lives in `marin/evaluation/` under the same import-light contract as `records.py` and is vendored into the dashboard image by one `COPY`; "on top of finestore" holds on the data path, not the package path. One of my own claims did not survive: the apparent mmlu panel drift between models was my triple-count of group and leaf rows.

Proceeding to implementation as one PR: engine and tests, the record coverage contract, the Harbor gate, the evaldash panel API, then the SPA. Item-level tallies, paired comparison intervals, and evidence-based suspect-zero detection are deferred and will be filed separately.

comments.author: weaverbot
comments.body:
🤖 Plan and first PR are up.

**Artifact (architecture + plan, peer-reviewed twice):** https://loom.oa.dev/s/m6bfst8b/artifacts/evaldash-stats-engine
**PR:** #8122 — CI green.

## What the four issues have in common

evaldash had no representation of *a measurement and how much of it happened* — a cell was `value: float | None`. That single gap produces all four symptoms: a Harbor batch with one timed-out trial in 240 is either discarded or silently scored as if the trial were wrong (#8084); a cross-benchmark mean is reported without saying which benchmarks, at which metric, or what it did about the ones a model never ran (#8085); a partial re-run hides older results that are still the newest available for their own benchmark (#8086); and filtering has nowhere to express "complete coverage only" because coverage isn't a thing the data carries (#8087).

So the PR is mostly the engine, with the four issues as applications of it — the pre-work-plus-applications shape you suggested, in one PR rather than five.

## The engine

Each result is stored as sufficient statistics (items graded, items attempted, correct count, recorded dispersion, per-cause counts of ungraded items) and intervals are derived on read. The estimand is θ over the items a run *set out* to grade. With `c = n_scored / n_attempted`, `θ = c·θ_obs + (1−c)·θ_miss`, and θ_miss is bounded to [0, 1] rather than imputed — a trial that times out is more likely to be a hard trial, so imputing anything for it is a guess about difficulty. The interval therefore widens by at least `1−c`: admitting a partial batch costs width proportional to what was missed, which is your "unknown interval around the missed answers" made concrete.

Two details worth flagging:

- The critical value is Imbens–Manski, not the ordinary 1.96. Applying the two-sided quantile to an interval that already spans an unidentified region covers the identified *set* at 95% and over-covers the parameter (~97.5% at realistic coverage rates). Because Δ is known exactly here rather than estimated, the usual objection to that correction doesn't apply.
- Binary metrics use Wilson, because eval results really do sit at the boundary — 0 of 8 agentic trials has a normal interval of *zero width* and a Wilson interval of [0.000, 0.324].

Every ordering in the system sorts on the interval's lower bound, so losing items cannot buy rank.

## Per issue

**#8084** — Harbor takes its attempted-trial count from the job's own bookkeeping (counting result files misses every trial that died before writing one, so preempted runs would report perfect coverage), divides rates by the trials a verifier actually graded, and keeps the per-error-type counts of the rest. A batch below a 90% completion gate fails as `infra_failed` and still records its coverage, so the rejection reads as counts. Run detail shows the breakdown. An unreadable job record leaves the count *unknown* rather than equal to results-found — the runs where it's unknown are exactly the interrupted ones a found-count would certify as complete.

**#8085** — No cross-benchmark mean is shown at all unless a caller names a missing-data policy, and one that is shown renders its panel, per-benchmark metrics, and policy inline. The primary surface is a panel table: one row per model, one column per benchmark. `ComparePage`'s client-side mean, which scored a missing shared benchmark as 0, is gone; comparison goes through the engine and answers orderings with a difference interval per benchmark rather than two error bars to eyeball.

**#8086** — Each benchmark comes from the newest run that clears the request's admission rules, across cohorts, so a partial re-run no longer hides results still newest for their own benchmark. `cohort=` pins to one launch when you want that instead. Every cell carries its run id, version, git sha, and timestamp; a `(model, benchmark)` with no admitted cell reports why and links the offending run, so an empty cell is explained rather than blank.

**#8087** — Benchmark column selection, a one-action complete-panel filter, cohort selection, model search, and run-metadata facets (accelerator/platform/backend/mechanism/user) are all in the request, so a panel is a shareable URL. The active ones render as removable chips: a number on screen should never be the product of a filter the reader can't see.

## Deliberately not in this PR

Filed as follow-ups: item-level tallies so binary intervals stop depending on inverting a rate (#8123), paired comparisons on shared items (#8124), the evalchemy launcher writing the same mmlu panel under two task directories (#8125), attempted-item counts for lm-eval runs so their intervals stop being sampling-only (#8126), and pyrefly/test-selection coverage for the evaldash server tree (#8127).

One caveat on #8126 worth knowing before reading the dashboard: today nearly every evalchemy run's interval is labelled `sampling_only`, because lm-eval records how many documents it graded but never how many it attempted. That's the honest label — completeness is unknown, not established — but it applies fleet-wide until the producers record the count.

comments.body:
🤖 #8122 is merged (`fb91b3dc94`). #8084, #8085, #8086 and #8087 closed with it; leaving this thread open for whatever comes next.

What landed, briefly. Every eval score now carries an interval that covers the items its run did not grade, from one engine (`marin.evaluation.eval_stats`) that the producers and evaldash share. The estimand is fixed once — θ over the items a run set out to grade — and the unobserved part is bounded rather than imputed, so admitting a partial run costs interval width instead of quietly biasing the number upward. Two things worth knowing if you use the panel:

**evalchemy results are no longer "completeness unknown."** lm-eval publishes no attempted-item count beside its metrics, so the honest reading of every evalchemy run was sampling error with unknown completeness. **A benchmark where nothing parseable came back is held out of the panel** rather than standing as a model's newest score. issues.title: [epic][eval] evaldash request tracker megathread

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
**What is this document?** This document is an attempt to formalize Marin’s policy towards what constitutes reportable, public-facing, canonical eval results for Marin models as well as the baselines we compare against.

**Why do we need this document?** With the first “snowball” cool-down, Marin is entering a regime where we regularly compare Marin models to existing open and closed-source models. Because Marin’s unique claim is that we are open development, we will need to hold ourselves to a high standard of transparency on how we report eval scores of Marin models and what claims we make about Marin model capabilities based on those scores.

**What is in scope for this document?** This document is intended to act as a living snapshot, trustworthy for any given period in time, as to the *what* and the *how* of Marin’s canonical set of evals. By what, we mean “which evals did we run, with what consistent set of hyperparameters and experimental constraints”. By how, we mean “where is the self-contained codebase that is both necessary and sufficient to reproduce our eval results independently”.

**What is not in scope for this document?** Everything else. More explicitly, this policy will not cover bespoke, custom “val set” evals we use for data mixing, RL, etc., which can have distinct pipelines; it will not cover what benchmarks we should add or remove from the in-distribution (hill-climbed) set in the future; it’s not for roadmapping or future planning; and it will not cover how we present results or talk about them in public.

## How

Use [Running Evaluations with Marin](https://marin.readthedocs.io/en/latest/tutorials/run-lm-evals/) as the launch runbook. The [source on `main`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/docs/tutorials/run-lm-evals.md) tracks the current launcher, model registry, suites, placement, durable records, and result inspection. Use [Harbor evaluation](https://marin.readthedocs.io/en/latest/harbor-integration/) for supplied Harbor `JobConfig` files and Daytona credentials.

Routine post-hoc evaluations use the shared launcher:

```bash
uv run python -m experiments.evaluation.cli launch \
  --model <registered-model-key> \
  --evals <registered-suite-or-eval-keys> \
  --dry-run
```

Remove `--dry-run` after the plan resolves the intended model, tasks, accelerator, target cluster or region, and records prefix.

### Eval tracks

| Track | Measures | Framework | Selection |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Non-agentic | Single-turn generation or loglikelihood | Evalchemy + lm-eval-harness | `--evals <registered-suite-or-eval-keys>` |
| Agentic (registered) | Tool use, coding, multi-turn agent rollout scoring | Harbor | `--evals <registered-harbor-key>` |
| Agentic (supplied policy) | Tool use, coding, multi-turn agent rollout scoring | Harbor | `--harbor-config <job.yaml>` |

`--evals` accepts only entries from `experiments/evaluation/evals.py` and its named suites. `--harbor-config` is repeatable and accepts supported external Harbor YAML or JSON policies. File-backed Evalchemy and lm-eval definitions are not supported; [#7990](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/7990) tracks that follow-up.

## What

### Benchmark suite

**Status legend:** ✅ production-ready · 🔧 in development (PR open) · ⚠️ has known issues · ❌ not started

**AA-II column:** Maps each benchmark to the AA-II component(s) it serves as a surrogate for (see [AA-II proxy weights](#aa-ii-proxy-weights) below). “—” means the benchmark is a canonical baseline outside the AA-II scheme.

#### Evalchemy chat benchmarks (`eval.eval`)

| Benchmark | Metric | Seeds | AA-II component | Status | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| MATH500 | pass@1 | 1 (42) | — | ✅ | |
| AIME24 | pass@1 (mean ± std) | 10 (42–51) | — | ✅ | |
| HumanEvalPlus | pass@1 | 1 (42) | — | ✅ | |
| MBPPPlus | pass@1 | 1 (42) | — | ✅ | |
| OlympiadBench | exact match | 1 (42) | HLE (math) + CritPt (physics) | ⚠️ | PR #24 merged; multi-part scoring + tolerance handling needs follow-up (vendor official `auto_scoring_judge.py`) |
| MMLU-Pro | accuracy | 1 (42) | HLE | ⚠️ | Issue #32: dataset download failure on some configs |

#### Harbor (agentic through the shared launcher)

| SWE-bench-verified random-100 | `swebench` | `DCAgent/swebench_verified_eval_set` | 32 | — | ✅ | |

| DS-1000 | — | `harbor ds-1000` | — | SciCode + GDPval-AA v2 | ✅ | |

Use a registered Harbor key with `--evals`, or pass one `--harbor-config` file per dataset. The benchmark table remains canonical when a file-backed config is required. ID mean = average per-benchmark z-score over SWE/`dev_set_v2`/`tb2` (`dev_set_v2` excluded from SE/ranking). Tool-using models require the correct `tool_call_parser`. Daytona uses `DAYTONA_API_KEY`, with the approved `DAYTONA_EVAL_API_KEY` secret as the launcher fallback.

#### pass@k (standalone vLLM driver)

`passatk_driver.py`—one batched `llm.generate(SamplingParams(n=128, temperature=0.7, seed=42))`, sub-sample k ∈ {1, 8, 32, 128}.

Estimator: `pass@k = mean[1 − C(n−c,k)/C(n,k)]`.

#### Shared rules

- **Runs per benchmark:** 3. Run every benchmark 3 times (seeds 42, 43, 44); report the mean.

- **Decoding:** `temperature=0.7`, `top_p=1.0`, `num_fewshot=0`, `repetition_penalty=1.1`. Applied consistently across all frameworks.

- **Context length:** standard = 32k (`max-model-len=32768`); extended = 131k. Set `max_gen_toks=32768` (standard) or `131072` (extended). Shared across all frameworks.

- **Reasoning parser:** every model, every benchmark—verify the correct reasoning parser (e.g. `hermes`, `deepseek_r1`) is configured and applied for models that emit `<think>`/reasoning tokens.

- **Chat template:** Ensure the correct template via `--apply_chat_template` (override to the correct template, e.g. `delphi_v0.jinja2`) whenever templates are available.

- **Logging:** `--log_samples` always on; set `--output_path` to durable storage (never `/tmp`). Never pair with `--predict_only`. Per-sample records for **lm-eval-native** tasks persist correctly as of evalchemy **#28** (`676fb85f`, merged 2026-07-19)—before that the flag was accepted but native-task samples weren’t written (blocked offline rescoring, e.g. the `drop` re-score).

### Report format

| Suite | Row format |
| --- | --- |
| Math | `scale \| mix \| stage \| model \| MATH500 \| AIME24(mean/std) \| gsm8k \| notes` |
| NLP | `model \| params \| MMLU \| HellaSwag \| ARC-c \| ARC-e \| PIQA \| WinoGrande \| OBQA \| BoolQ \| TruthfulQA \| LAMBADA \| TriviaQA \| NQ \| DROP \| template` |
| Agentic | `model \| SWE-100 \| dev_set_v2 \| tb2 \| ID mean \| ID SE \| traces` |
| pass@k | `model \| type \| p@1 \| p@8 \| p@32 \| p@128 \| n \| job \| status` |

### Quality gate + re-fire discipline

**Gate:** A leg registers iff valid-complete ≥ 90% and non-benign ≤ 10% (use `scripts/database/eval_guardrail.py`). `AgentTimeout` is benign (passthrough-scored, counts as valid-complete)—do not flag on timeout rate. Benchmarks are resumed until valid-complete ≥ 90%. For certain publication-quality results, we should consider setting this gate even higher, perhaps >95% or >99%.

> **Technical note:** Harbor main already has rich error classification and resume capability. Evalchemy is currently less mature. [evalchemy PR #19](https://github.com/marin-community/evalchemy/pull/19) tracks the attempt to create similar infra-aware gating in Evalchemy.

### AA-II proxy weights

| Component | Weight | Surrogate(s) | Surrogate status |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- |
| GDPval-AA v2 | 20% | FinanceBench + IFBench + DS-1000 | FinanceBench 🔧 · IFBench 🔧 · DS-1000 ✅ |
| τ³-Banking | 14% | τ²-Bench-Verified Retail (or BFCL, or a small BFCL parity subset) | τ²-Bench-Verified Retail 🔧 · BFCL ✅ |
| Terminal-Bench | 16% | OT-TBLite | ✅ |
| SciCode | 8% | DS-1000 + CruxEval | DS-1000 ✅ · CruxEval ⚠️ |
| HLE | 12% | MMLU-Pro + OlympiadBench (math) | MMLU-Pro ⚠️ · OlympiadBench ⚠️ |
| GPQA Diamond | 6% | GPQA Diamond | ✅ |
| CritPt | 6% | OlympiadBench (physics) | ⚠️ |
| AA-Omniscience | 12% | SimpleQA or TriviaQA | SimpleQA ✅ · TriviaQA ✅ |
| AA-LCR | 6% | MRCR | 🔧 |

Composite replacements: normalize each constituent, macro-average within the component, then apply weight. Publish every component alongside the aggregate.

**Coverage gaps:** MRCR, FinanceBench, and IFBench have open PRs awaiting review. CruxEval, MMLU-Pro, and OlympiadBench have known issues blocking production use. Until these are resolved, the corresponding AA-II components cannot be fully computed.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Canonical evaluation model configs expose tensor and data parallelism, but not pipeline parallelism. This prevents the blessed `experiments.evaluation.cli launch` path from serving an evaluation model across multiple Iris tasks.

The immediate failure is [GLM-5.2 AWQ INT4 on TB2.1](https://evaldash.oa.dev/runs/20260813-011602-glm-5.2-awq-int4-glm-5.2-awq-int4-tb21-aa-7bc9). At `max_model_len: 1048576`, TP8 on one H100x8 node loaded 62.35 GiB of weights per rank, then vLLM failed before any trial ran:

```
ValueError: No available memory for the cache blocks. Try increasing `gpu_memory_utilization`
```

PP2 with TP8 inside each node would reduce stage-local weight memory while retaining NVLink for tensor parallelism. Marin already has Iris gang rendezvous and native vLLM PP support from #7758. That implementation is currently exercised as PP2/TP1/DP8 for Grug; its helper fixes local TP to 1, and the evaluation path does not call it.

The remaining gaps are visible in [`ServeConfig`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/66487ec75071fe96d04459aabfab8cf806c905f2/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/model_config.py#L63-L89), [GPU topology validation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/66487ec75071fe96d04459aabfab8cf806c905f2/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/hardware.py#L170-L180), and [evaluation serving lowering](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/66487ec75071fe96d04459aabfab8cf806c905f2/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/serving_config.py#L258-L278). They model one GPU slice and validate only `TP × DP`.

Done when:

- Evaluation model YAML can declare pipeline parallelism separately from per-node tensor and data parallelism.
- The launcher validates per-node GPU use and total gang geometry.
- PP2/TP8 lowers to two coscheduled H100x8 Iris tasks and starts one distributed vLLM endpoint.
- Dry-run output and durable evaluation records preserve the resolved PP, TP, DP, task count, and per-task accelerator shape.
- A behavioral test covers a multi-node evaluation topology and rejects inconsistent geometry before submission.

Tracked from #8083.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Marin cannot run FinanceBench or SimpleQA with a Together-backed judge without replacing or exposing candidate-endpoint credentials. A direct Together probe confirmed that `openai/gpt-oss-120b` supports the Chat Completions API used by FinanceBench and the Responses API request shape used by SimpleQA, so provider compatibility is not the blocker.

Reproduce:
1. Launch FinanceBench with a distinct external judge credential. [`runner.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/93251781092fa281077dff0a9c7b455fd6cc9677/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runner.py#L229-L235) overwrites `OPENAI_API_KEY` with `local-endpoint` in the Evalchemy child.
2. Launch a supplied Harbor SimpleQA policy whose verifier requires a separate provider key. [`HarborDefinition.secret_env_for`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/93251781092fa281077dff0a9c7b455fd6cc9677/experiments/evaluation/evals.py#L117-L120) resolves only the Daytona credential, so the isolated verifier does not receive the judge key.
3. Observe that FinanceBench cannot authenticate to the judge and SimpleQA has no verifier credential. Passing the Together key as the process-wide `OPENAI_API_KEY` would also send a judge credential through the candidate client boundary.

Expected: Evalchemy judges and Harbor verifiers receive explicit provider key, base URL, and model settings at verifier-only boundaries. Candidate endpoint authentication remains unchanged. Judge transport and parsing failures fail evaluation coverage instead of becoming incorrect answers.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 **Research**

Current main already resolves Harbor verifier placeholders through [`HarborDefinition.secret_env_for`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5b15614b09f7a976a8e075d2b36233b59991cb7e/experiments/evaluation/evals.py#L124-L128), so that part of the report is fixed. Evalchemy still has no judge configuration and its child reserves `OPENAI_API_KEY` for candidate authentication in [`runner.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5b15614b09f7a976a8e075d2b36233b59991cb7e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/runner.py#L226-L236). The pinned FinanceBench and SimpleQA graders accept ambiguous output as a grade; SimpleQA also needs a new immutable generated-dataset revision. PR [#9128](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9128) owns hosted judge provisioning and does not provide the external credential path.

**Proposed Fix**

Add a FinanceBench-only typed judge block that maps a `SecretSpec` to `JUDGE_API_KEY`, passes its URL and model separately, and records only those non-secret fields. Tighten both grader parsers so malformed labels and provider failures reduce coverage instead of producing zero rewards. Regenerate and pin the corrected SimpleQA dataset, then validate isolation with separate local candidate and judge HTTP stubs.

The equivalent point in this run would be about step 150k. We see step change in slope of the final rms norm when moving to dropless: However the prior 1e23 run had large final rms norm growth and trained fine: The total grad is driven 95% by the output projection. Output proj sits in AdamH. Incoming activation goes through rms norm and gated norm. Likely take no intervention as long as loss curve looks good, given data from prior 129B-A16B. If we were to see loss curve degrade, potential interventions would be: - higher logit z loss. - weight decay on final rms-norm. - lower LR on lm_head. It is not obvious that any of these would be a 'fix', or even that there is a problem to fix. As a result, would want to compare to baseline for at least 1 day of steps. The growth is specifically in just the lm_head:

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Frozen-gradient probes at checkpoint 101,316 rule out a kernel artifact and a direct effect of dropping; the lm_head rise is a trajectory effect, and the lm_head gradient is tangential. No intervention recommended on this evidence. Details below; the same material was filed as #9149 before this issue was seen, and that issue is now closed in favour of this one.

Method: restore the hero checkpoint at step 101,316 on one NVL72 rack, take no updates, and compute the training gradient on the hero's own next six batches under three variants: the production ragged transport on QuACK 0.6.4, the same transport on the XLA `ragged_dot` fallback (exact sigmoid), and the pooled-wave transport at capacity factor 1.15 (3.4% drops). Each also with the logit z-loss off. For every parameter the probe records the gradient norm, the weight norm and their inner product. Records are under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/mwittmann/grad-norm-20260914/`; W&B runs `gradnorm-101316-ragged-v2-20260914` and `gradnorm-101316-pooled-20260914` in `marin_moe`. First-batch values; the pattern holds on all six.

| variant | loss | grad total | lm_head grad | cos(grad, W) lm_head | final_norm gain grad |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ragged, QuACK 0.6.4 (production) | 1.25651 | 0.6024 | 0.5735 | −4.9e-5 | 4.4e-4 |
| ragged, QuACK, z-loss off | 1.25614 | 0.6015 | 0.5720 | −4.9e-5 | 4.7e-4 |
| ragged, XLA `ragged_dot` fallback | 1.25652 | 0.6019 | 0.5736 | −4.9e-5 | 4.4e-4 |
| pooled-wave cf 1.15 (drops on) | 1.26849 | 0.6047 | 0.5665 | −1.0e-4 | 4.8e-4 |

The lm_head gradient is tangential. Its cosine with the weights is −5e-5 on every batch and variant, so the radial (logit temperature) component is a few parts in 10⁵ of the norm, and the final-norm gain sits near its optimum (cosine −0.07 on a 4.5e-4 gradient). Turning the z-loss off changes the lm_head gradient by 0.28%. So the growth is a steepening of the loss along model-changing lm_head directions; it is not a temperature pull that the z-loss or a final-norm weight decay would be absorbing.

Kernels: QuACK and the XLA fallback agree on the loss to 1e-5, on the lm_head gradient to 1e-4, and on expert weights, latent projections and attention matrices to about 1%. The lm_head gradient does not pass through the expert backward, so an expert-kernel error cannot move it directly. The hero's per-tensor gradient history is also continuous across the switch from the pooled einsum path to QuACK at 81,716. One caveat: the RMSNorm gain gradients (latent_norm about 1e-2, token embeddings about 1e-3) differ between the two kernels by up to 7× on some batches in either direction (ratios 6.9, 0.93, 1.1, 0.99, 0.41, 0.26). They are cancellation-dominated sums that flip under QuACK's 0.5% approximate SwiGLU, contribute under 1e-3 of the squared total, and the same executable reproduces them to 6e-3. A systematic component is not excluded and is cheap to test by saving the gain-gradient vectors from both kernels and an fp32 reference on the same batches.

Dropping has no direct effect at fixed parameters: the pooled-wave arm gives a lm_head gradient 1.2% below the ragged one and a total 0.4% above it, averaged over the six batches. Over the paired 200-step replay at 81,716 the ragged-to-pooled lm_head ratio was 1.06 ± 0.07 across 20 samples. The pooled arm's loss is 0.012 nats worse; the offset was 0.0065 at the switch, so the model has grown more dependent on complete expert outputs.

From W&B: the lm_head share of the squared total went from 84% at 58k to 95% at 100k; every other parameter group is flat, including the routed expert weights (0.0094 to 0.0104). The slope of the total per 1k steps was 0.0040 (62–72k), 0.0062 (72–82k), 0.0133 (82–91k) and 0.0085 (91–101k), so it was already accelerating before the switch and has been falling since. The d768 rungs trained dropless from scratch (`l2-abl-d768-ragged` vs `l2-abl-d768-ep`; `mhep-main-c13d1-d768-20260902` vs `rav-ladder-d768-v2`) show equal or lower gradient norms than pooled-wave in every tenth of the run and the same final-norm gain trajectory within 1%, so dropless training does not raise the norm in general; the effect is tied to switching a model that had adapted to noisy experts.

Reading: among the bundled changes at 81,716 (transport, kernels, fp32 weights on device, PJRT wheel), the transport is the only one that alters what the model computes beyond rounding, so the slope change is attributable by elimination to the reduced dropping acting through the trajectory. A demonstration would need paired multi-thousand-step continuations from 81,716, which does not look worth the compute. Today's data-mixture swap will move the norm on its own, so the slope is best judged from a new post-swap window. The QuACK 0.6.1 to 0.6.4 frozen-state probe in the #8959 validation found the two versions' gradient norms identical to 3e-6 relative, for reference on the earlier +10% A/B difference.

issues.author: mcwitt-agent
issues.body:
A FineStore archive under a `tmp/ttl=30d/` prefix stops serving reads once any object its `HEAD` manifest references expires, and nothing repairs it. Bucket lifecycle rules expire each object 30 days after its own last write (CoreWeave reports `X-Amz-Expiration` as last-modified plus 30 days; GCS `age` rules behave the same). `HEAD` is rewritten on every commit, so it outlives the write-once objects it points at. #9202 handles the first casualty, the `_archive.json` marker. The schema objects and the data shards fail the same way.

Schema objects are written once per table (`lib/finestore/src/finestore/commit.py:118`, skipped when present). After one expires, every `scan`, `point`, `keys`, and `read_blob` on that table raises `FileNotFoundError` from `_meta` (`lib/finestore/src/finestore/reader.py:554`). `PersistentKvCache` treats that as a miss, so every process recompiles until process 0 stores again and `table()` re-registers the schema. The `marin-us-east-02a` `cutlass-kernels` schema object is already gone as of 2026-09-16.

Data shards at generation 3 and above are never compacted: `maintain()` iterates only `DEFAULT_COMPACTION_LEVELS = (16, 4, 4)` (`lib/finestore/src/finestore/store.py:46`, `:361`), so they age without bound. `_read_plan` opens every shard of the table (`reader.py:279`), so one expired shard makes every read fail, permanently, because no code path removes an unreadable shard from the manifest. If an overfull level 0-2 contains an expired shard, `compact_table` raises `FileNotFoundError` (`compaction.py:85`), `_run` stores it as `self._error` (`store.py:412-413`), and every later `flush` in that process raises (`store.py:432-434`). The cache adapters catch it, so the process survives, but the archive never accepts a write from that process again. Recovery today is deleting the root.

Dates on live archives: the hero cluster's `cutlass-kernels` archive references a `g=3` shard written 2026-08-30, expiring about 2026-09-29. The `marin-us-east-02a` archive references a `g=544` shard written 2026-09-07, expiring 2026-10-08. After those dates every process on those clusters recompiles every CuTeDSL kernel on every start. The fused cross-entropy autotune cache (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/fused_cross_entropy_loss/api.py:230`) and the XLA per-fusion autotune cache (`lib/iris/src/iris/runtime/jax_init.py:204`) live on the same kind of prefix and rot the same way.

Reproduce:
1. Open a `DataStore` on a local root, write a blob, close it.
2. Delete one active shard under `data/blobs/` (or the object under `schemas/`).
3. `ReadView(root).read_blob(name)` raises `FileNotFoundError`; `PersistentKvCache.at(root).load(name)` returns `None` with a warning.
4. Open a `DataStore` again and write enough blobs to overfill level 0 (17 flushes with default limits). The maintenance thread fails and the next `flush` raises.

Expected: an archive on a TTL prefix keeps serving the entries that still exist, and a writer keeps accepting writes. Two structural options: rewrite the top generation on a schedule so no shard outlives the TTL, or have `_read_plan` and `compact_table` drop shards that return `FileNotFoundError` and commit a manifest without them. A third option outside FineStore is to rotate the cache root on a period shorter than the TTL and read from the current and previous roots.

Done when:
- A `PersistentKvCache` archive whose oldest active shard expired still serves reads for entries in the remaining shards.
- A writer on that archive commits and compacts without poisoning its maintenance thread.
- A test covers a deleted shard on the read and the compaction path.

issues.author: dlwh
issues.body:
Add a standalone Levanter entry point that reads original documents from a JSONL/Parquet file or bucket prefix, or a Hugging Face dataset ID, and writes a JSONL export with `doc_id`, `corpus_id`, `loss`, and `bits_per_byte`.

Loss is mean next-token negative log-likelihood in nats. Bits per byte is the same loss sum in bits divided by the original document's UTF-8 byte length. Score complete documents in context-length windows with one token of overlap, counting each next-token target once and combining chunk sums before computing means. Use the existing Levanter perplexity scorer's tokenization and BOS/EOS insertion policy: the first token is conditioning context, subsequent tokens including any inserted EOS are scored, and synthetic tokens add no bytes to the denominator. Exclude training auxiliary losses.

Done when:
- Source text and ID fields are configurable; provided document and corpus IDs are preserved, with deterministic fallbacks for missing IDs.
- Scoring streams documents and emits one output row per original document, including null metrics for empty or unscorable documents.
- Tests cover JSONL, Parquet, the HF loading boundary, long-document chunking, masking, Unicode byte counts, and export schema.
- A Snowball run validates the input-to-export path and records its checkpoint, source, and output artifacts here.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Scope:** new evaluation output path across `eval.py`/`packing.py` plus cross-checkpoint identity design and a Snowball smoke run — larger than a self-contained fix, so this is analysis for review rather than a PR.

**Research**

Loss evaluation runs through `TaggedEvaluator`. Per-position loss, weight, and next-token id are already produced by the loss fn and reduced to scalars per batch/tag; nothing per-document is retained today.

- [`_default_lm_eval_loss_fn`](lib/levanter/src/levanter/eval.py#L225-L239) returns `(per_pos_loss, per_pos_weight, per_pos_token_id)` with shape `[EvalBatch, Pos]`.
- [`TaggedEvaluator._make_accum_for_batch`](lib/levanter/src/levanter/eval.py#L546-L594) computes `weighted_loss = losses * weights` then immediately sums to scalars — the insertion point for per-segment retention.
- [`per_segment_loss`](lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/packing.py#L153-L174) already groups `losses * loss_weight` by segment id from the packed example; `eval_harness.py`'s `_eval_loglikelihood` calls it via `hax.vmap` as precedent.
- Segment ids live on the packed example's attn mask ([`SequencePacker.pack`](lib/levanter/src/levanter/data/packing.py#L79-L93)); padding uses `loss_weight == 0`, so masked/pad tokens drop out for free.
- Existing per-step JSONL sink: [`cb_tagged_lm_evaluate`](lib/levanter/src/levanter/eval.py#L362-L382) writes `eval_metrics.jsonl` under `checkpoint_path` from process 0.

**Key design problem — stable identity across checkpoints.** `per_segment_loss` returns *local* segment ids (0..N within one packed sequence), which are not stable document identities. The issue requires ids stable across checkpoints for the same dataset + eval config. Local segment id must be composed with a deterministic example key. Since eval iterates the dataset in fixed order (`DomainTaggedDataset`), a stable key is `(dataset_tag, global_example_index, local_segment_id)`. The fixed-length-split path (non-packed eval sets) has no segment ids, so source-document identity and fragment reassembly are unavailable there — the record must mark this explicitly rather than fabricate ids.

**Proposed approach** (maps to the Done-when list)

1. Add an optional per-document sink to `TaggedEvaluator`/`cb_tagged_lm_evaluate` (e.g. `document_loss_path: str | None`), off by default so aggregate metrics and their code path are untouched.
2. In `_make_accum_for_batch`, when enabled and the batch carries segment ids, `hax.vmap(per_segment_loss)` to get per-segment weighted-loss sums and per-segment token-weight sums (a second vmap summing `loss_weight` per segment gives scored-token count / total weight). Emit alongside the batch's tag one-hot. When no segment ids exist, emit one record per example flagged `segmentation="fixed_length"` with unavailable document identity.
3. Buffer records host-side in `evaluate()` (avoid GCS chatter inside the jit/step loop) and write one JSONL per eval step from process 0, reusing the `checkpoint_path` fsspec pattern. Fields: `step, dataset_tag, example_index, segment_id, weighted_loss, token_count, token_weight, segmentation`.
4. Reproduce the aggregate: `sum(weighted_loss)/sum(token_weight)` over records must equal the reported token-weighted (micro) loss — this is the natural regression assertion.

**Tests** (`lib/levanter/tests`, following `TESTING.md`): a packed batch with ≥2 documents plus padding — assert per-document weighted losses and token weights match a direct reference computation, masked/pad positions contribute zero, and the reconstructed aggregate equals `TaggedEvaluator`'s reported loss; a partial final batch; and the fixed-length path emitting the unavailable-identity flag.

**Open questions before implementation**
- Output granularity: per-segment only, or also per-token arrays? The Done-when list reads per-segment.
- Identity: is `(dataset_tag, example_index, segment_id)` an acceptable stable id, or is a content hash / original document id required (needs plumbing through the data pipeline)?
- Where should the JSONL land relative to `eval_metrics.jsonl`, and is there a size/row cap for large eval sets?
- Snowball smoke run: which checkpoint + data config should I use, and do you want me to run it or leave it to a human?

Happy to implement once the identity scheme and smoke-run target are confirmed.

issues.author: mcwitt-agent
issues.body:
Diagnose the recurring excess of time between W&B history rows over `throughput/duration` on the 535B-A23B hero run. The pattern occurs before and after disabling QuACK programmatic dependent launch (PDL) in #9183. Its cause and end-to-end throughput cost are unresolved.

A September 16 read of consecutive W&B history rows found:

| Measurement | [Control, PDL enabled](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-mix-996f4891-step108k) | [Trial, PDL disabled](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/hero-nopdl-step108k) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| History steps | 108000–108981 | 108778–112667 |
| Eligible adjacent intervals | 976 | 3,886 |
| Intervals with excess >1.2 s | 40.37% | 40.84% |
| Median timestamp interval, quiet / slow | 16.963 / 18.369 s | 16.661 / 18.172 s |
| Median training duration, quiet / slow | 16.704 / 16.717 s | 16.387 / 16.417 s |
| Median excess, quiet / slow | 0.236 / 1.584 s | 0.240 / 1.645 s |

Reproduce the measurement:

1. Fetch unsampled history for the linked runs over the listed step ranges, including `_step`, `_timestamp`, `throughput/duration`, `throughput/hook_time`, and `throughput/loading_time`.
2. For adjacent rows whose `_step` values differ by exactly one, compute `interval = timestamp[i] - timestamp[i-1]` and `excess = interval - duration[i]`. Retain `0 < interval < 60` seconds and `duration[i] < 40` seconds to exclude startup and large interruptions.
3. Classify quiet intervals as `excess < 0.8` seconds and slow intervals as `excess > 1.2` seconds. Compute each column's median independently; median excess need not equal the difference of medians.
4. To locate sustained stretches, take a trailing 12-interval median of excess and retain runs above 1.2 seconds lasting more than 20 intervals. The start-to-start spacing on the trial grows from roughly 67–73 toward 75–83 minutes after startup; control stretches recur roughly 32–42 minutes apart excluding the 116-minute spacing that spans its interruption. The period is not fixed at 80 minutes.

In both groups and both runs, median `throughput/hook_time` is about 4.6 ms and `throughput/loading_time` about 25 microseconds. These recorded timers do not explain the roughly 1.6-second excess in slow intervals.

The [trial build’s training loop](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8f6f33bebe681ed12ff88a6ed14121990bf2cec3/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/train.py#L1160) stops the step timer before callbacks, later metric materialization, and checkpoint handling; the next batch load also falls outside it. [Background tracking](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8f6f33bebe681ed12ff88a6ed14121990bf2cec3/lib/levanter/src/levanter/tracker/background.py#L12) prepares payloads on the training thread and performs tracker I/O on a worker thread. Flat step duration therefore does not establish that the extra timestamp gap is harmless, and timestamp gaps alone do not establish GPU idle time.

The [run tracker](https://mtracker.oa.dev/hero-run-535b) currently attributes the recurring gap to the trial build in its summary, while its September 16 03:25 entry reports the same effect in the control. The evidence above does not establish a PDL regression. The trial also changed the PJRT wheel (#9179), so the build comparison does not isolate PDL's effect on cadence.

Done when:

- Independent trainer progress timing establishes how much of the timestamp excess is real time between completed optimizer steps and how much is deferred logging.
- Measurements locate the delay within the full iteration, explain the recurring stretches, and quantify their end-to-end throughput cost against quiet periods.
- A fix, if needed, is validated across multiple slow/quiet cycles using full-iteration timing; moving time outside `throughput/duration` is insufficient.

Related: #9180 tracks checkpoint-associated spikes in measured training duration; whether it shares a cause with this pattern is unknown. #8870 tracks silent hangs, and #8506 tracks hero operations.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Root cause observed on `hero-nopdl-step108k`: staggered full Python garbage collections delay ranks reaching the every-step checkpoint-decision broadcast. Other ranks wait there, after both `throughput/duration` and recorded `throughput/hook_time` have stopped.

Read-only probes observed three generation-2 collections lasting 1.432–1.501 seconds while scanning about 4.67 million long-lived objects per affected rank. One consumed 1.430 seconds of main-thread CPU time. Rank-0 profiles showed 1.3- and 1.4-second waits in `Checkpointer.on_step → broadcast_one_to_all → device_get`, while rank 0 itself performed no full GC. Independent trainer progress confirms real cadence loss: matched multi-step intervals average 16.715 seconds/update in the quiet group versus 18.458 in the slow group, using each group's median. CPython's long-lived-object threshold and measured promotion rates imply a 258–273-update recurrence, close to the recent 261–278-update spacing. The phase spread supports the extended stretches; it does not quantitatively predict their width.

Proposed fix: disable automatic cyclic GC during steady-state training and explicitly collect on all ranks at shared step boundaries. Start validation with every 100 updates: synchronize after checkpoint handling, then run `gc.collect()` before the next step. Restore the prior GC policy on exit. Measure retained host memory to select the final interval, and include synchronization and GC in full-iteration timing.

The historical trial's slow intervals have about 8.3% lower throughput than quiet intervals. Excess above a quiet baseline matched by `step % 10` accounts for 3.83% of eligible elapsed time, including other residual tails; this is not a measured fix benefit. No training settings were changed. Keep this issue open until the fix is validated across multiple slow/quiet cycles, including checkpoint behavior and memory trends. The control was not directly instrumented for GC, and the build comparison does not isolate PDL.

[Incident record with measurements, source links, and evidence provenance](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/455).

issues.body:
The GPU canary (`grug-train-canary-gpu-35108393797-1`) crashed on every task attempt in the first training step. The persistent CuTeDSL kernel cache at `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/cutlass-kernels` is in a half-present state: its `HEAD` commit token exists but its `_archive.json` format marker is gone. Reading it raises `ValueError`, which is not caught by the cache's read path, so a recoverable cache miss became a fatal training crash. All 4 attempts failed identically; the job never reached step 1. Reproduce: 1. Point the CuTeDSL kernel cache (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/cutlass_kernel_cache.py`) at a FineStore archive whose `HEAD` object exists but whose `_archive.json` is absent. 2. Run any grug MoE step that compiles a cutlass kernel (`experiments/grug/moe/train.py:532` → `get_or_compile_kernel` → `cache.load`). 3. Training aborts with `ValueError: archive at has HEAD but no format marker`. Expected: an unreadable or inconsistent kernel cache degrades to a cache miss and recompiles the kernel (`cutlass_kernel_cache.py:152` falls through to `original(fn, spec)` at line 160). It must not crash the training loop. Two defects combine:
Defect 1 — read path only tolerates OSError `PersistentKvCache.load` catches `OSError` and treats it as a miss, but `ReadView.__init__` raises `ValueError` for an inconsistent archive: ```python # lib/finestore/src/finestore/cache.py:76 try: value = ReadView(self._storage_root()).read_blob(key) except OSError as exc: # ValueError is not caught logger.warning("FineStore cache is unreadable, treating %s as a miss: %s", key, exc) return None ``` ```python # lib/finestore/src/finestore/reader.py:513 if archive_metadata is None and self._snapshot.token is not None: raise ValueError(f"archive at {self.root} has HEAD but no format marker") ``` The cache is best-effort, so this `ValueError` should be treated as a miss rather than propagating.
Defect 2 — the archive lost its format marker to TTL expiry `_archive.json` is written once at archive creation and never rewritten (`initialize_archive`, `lib/finestore/src/finestore/commit.py:87` — conditional write only when absent). `HEAD` is rewritten on every commit (`commit`, `lib/finestore/src/finestore/commit.py:246`). The archive lives under `tmp/ttl=30d/`, a prefix with a 30-day per-object S3 lifecycle expiration (`lib/rigging/src/rigging/filesystem/cluster_config.py:453`). The write-once marker ages past 30 days and is deleted while `HEAD` stays young, leaving `HEAD` without `_archive.json`.
Stack trace (attempt 2) ``` File "/app/experiments/grug/moe/train.py", line 532, in _run_grug_local state, metrics, watch_stats = train_step(state, batch, compute_watch=compute_watch) File ".../cutlass/jax/primitive.py", line 329, in cutlass_call_inner_p_impl kernel = get_or_compile_kernel(fn, spec) File "/app/lib/levanter/src/levanter/cutlass_kernel_cache.py", line 152, in get_or_compile_kernel module = cache.load(key) File "/app/lib/finestore/src/finestore/cache.py", line 76, in load value = ReadView(self._storage_root()).read_blob(key) File "/app/lib/finestore/src/finestore/reader.py", line 514, in __init__ raise ValueError(f"archive at {self.root} has HEAD but no format marker") ValueError: archive at s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/cutlass-kernels has HEAD but no format marker ``` The subsequent `wandb AlreadyJoinedError` and XLA coordination-service `Connection refused` lines are teardown after this fatal error, not the cause.
Fixing defect 1 restores the canary immediately (recompile on miss). Fixing defect 2 stops the archive from becoming inconsistent again; options include refreshing `_archive.json` on write or excluding the marker from TTL expiry. Canary run context: - Lane: gpu (CoreWeave, `cw-us-west-04a`) - Iris job: `/runner/iris-run-job-20260916-143234/grug-train-canary-gpu-35108393797-1` - GHA run: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/35108393797 - W&B run: https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin/runs/canary-gpu-35108393797-1 - Date: 2026-09-16

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Research

Confirmed against the live archive. `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/cutlass-kernels/_archive.json` is absent, while `HEAD` exists (last modified 2026-09-12, sequence 10018). The bucket lifecycle rule for `tmp/ttl=30d/` ([`expiration_rules`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5b15614b09/infra/pulumi/src/iac/buckets/coreweave.py#L80-L88)) expires each object 30 days after its own last write. The marker is written once at archive creation ([`initialize_archive`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5b15614b09/lib/finestore/src/finestore/commit.py#L87-L102)) and `HEAD` is rewritten on every commit, so the marker aged out first. The archive was created shortly after #8210 landed on 2026-08-15, which puts the marker's expiry at about 2026-09-15; the canary failed on 2026-09-16.

The reader raises `ValueError` for `HEAD` without a marker ([`ReadView.__init__`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5b15614b09/lib/finestore/src/finestore/reader.py#L511-L514)), and [`PersistentKvCache.load`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5b15614b09/lib/finestore/src/finestore/cache.py#L74-L79) only converts `OSError` to a miss. Nothing repairs the archive because the crash happens before any store: a writer open would re-create the marker (`initialize_archive` writes it when absent), but the kernel cache reads first. The fused cross-entropy autotune cache ([`api.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5b15614b09/lib/levanter/src/levanter/kernels/pallas/fused_cross_entropy_loss/api.py#L230)) shares the same `for_prefix` path and will fail the same way once its own marker expires. Content-addressed schema objects ([`write_schema`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/5b15614b09/lib/finestore/src/finestore/commit.py#L118-L133)) are also written once and expire on the same schedule; a missing one is already an `OSError` miss, so it degrades rather than crashes.

Proposed Fix

1. `PersistentKvCache.load` treats `ValueError` from the read view as a miss, like `OSError`. This restores the canary: the miss compiles, process 0 stores, and the writer open re-creates the marker.
2. A write-open refreshes the marker and schema objects when they already exist (same bytes, compare-and-swap on the marker version), so their last-modified date is never older than the commits that follow. This keeps a TTL-hosted archive consistent for as long as it receives writes.

Regression tests: deleting `_archive.json` from a populated archive makes `load` return `None` and a later `store` repairs the marker; opening a store for writing advances the marker mtime.

comments.author: mcwitt-agent
comments.body: 🤖 Fix in #9202 (draft). `PersistentKvCache.load` now treats the reader's `ValueError` as a miss, and a write-open rewrites `_archive.json` and the schema objects with their existing bytes so their lifecycle clock is never older than HEAD's. The bucket confirms the mechanism: `X-Amz-Expiration` on `HEAD` (modified 2026-09-12) is 2026-10-13, and a flat kernel object from 2026-08-18 expires 2026-09-18. The PR body lists the operational steps: an optional manual marker recreate to unblock the canary before the fix ships, the canary rerun, and a 2026-09-24 deadline for the TPU-side autotune archive in `gs://marin-us-central2`.
